    0.1 What this handbook covers

    Five codebases work together. Two Python builders read nGenue’s Delphi source and write knowledge graphs as JSON files. A small .NET service parses T-SQL for them while they build. Two Python MCP servers load those graphs into memory and answer questions from AI assistants through tools.

    CodebaseWhat it isWritten inProduces or serves
    delphi-kgThe graph builder for the new nGenue UI (version 0.5.2)Python 3.11graph_full.json
    delphi-kg_old_UIIts fork for the legacy nTrack UI, installed as delphi-kg-legacy (version 0.6.0)Python 3.11graph_old.json, one per client
    delphi-scriptdomThe T-SQL parser service the builders call during a buildC#, .NET 9Parsed SQL: tables, columns, procedures, write targets
    ngenue_mcpThe MCP server for the new UIPython 3.11144 tools at /mcp
    ngenue_mcp_legacyThe MCP server for the legacy UI, one instance per clientPython 3.11148 tools at /<client>/v1/mcp

    The servers also read files that other projects make: the SQL object graph (database_graph.json, from graph_builder v5.x), the stored-procedure code flows, the data dictionary, the business workflow graph and the documentation vectors in Qdrant. Their source isn’t covered here, so those files are explained from the server’s side: what they contain and how the server reads them.

    About this snapshot

    Everything here was read from the code as uploaded on 4–7 November 2026. The live connectors run slightly older builds (135 and 139 tools rather than 148 and 144), so a tool described here may not exist on a server until it is redeployed.

    0.2 The big picture

    Read the figure from left to right. On a developer laptop, the builders parse the Delphi source and the SQL inside it into graph files. On the Windows Server VM, eleven MCP server processes each load one client’s graphs into memory at start-up. Every request that reaches them carries a token from Microsoft Entra ID, and each server checks it before doing anything. In Claude or ChatGPT, the AI decides which tools to call, reads the answers and writes its reply.

    Follow one question

    The team checks every new graph with the same question: “What happens when a user clicks Save on the End User screen?” This is the path it takes. Part 3 repeats it with real calls captured from the live servers.

    1. The AI reads the server’s playbook. When Claude connects, the server sends an instructions text that explains the graphs, the tools and how to chain them. The legacy server’s playbook is about 75,000 characters, roughly 10,000 words.
    2. It finds the screen. Claude calls find_form_by_name with "End User". When exactly one screen matches, the answer ends with a STATE UPDATES block that sets active_form to the screen’s id. The server keeps no memory of this: Claude passes the value back on its next calls.
    3. It traces the Save action. Claude calls get_action_chain, passing active_form back with action_filter set to save. Over the wire, that is one HTTPS POST carrying a JSON-RPC message:
    4. The server answers from memory. IIS passes the request to the AEP instance, which checks the token, checks the arguments and runs the tool on a worker thread. The graph is already in RAM, so the tool follows the Save action to the method it runs and the calls and SQL beneath it, then trims the answer to fit its size budget.
    5. The AI keeps going or stops. Claude may follow up with a stored-procedure tool or a read-only SQL query, then writes its answer. The server never decides when to stop; the AI does. Part 6 explains exactly how that works.

    0.3 Two product lines, one design

    nGenue’s Delphi application exists in two UI generations. Each has its own builder, its own graph format and its own server, but the design is the same.

    Legacy lineNew UI line
    User interfaceLegacy nTrack UI (Delphi VCL)New nGenue UI
    Builderdelphi-kg_old_UIdelphi-kg
    Delphi graphgraph_old.json, one per client (AEP’s is about 470 MB)graph_full.json (about 1 GB)
    Server codengenue_mcp_legacyngenue_mcp
    Instances10, one per client1
    Addresshttps://mcp.ngenue.net/<client>/v1/mcphttps://mcp.ngenue.net/mcp
    Tools in this snapshot148144

    The ten legacy instances serve AEP, Interconn, PEP, Snyder, Texican Retail, Texican Wholesale, TwinEagle, UGI, V26 and WRWE. Each client runs its own build of the legacy source, so each gets its own Delphi graph, its own SQL graph and its own server process.

    Likely reason

    One graph per client keeps answers exact. A screen, a method or a stored procedure can differ between client builds, and a shared graph would answer with another client’s code.

    In the code

    “Legacy” names the UI, not the age of the code. Comments in both repositories mark fixes ported from the other (“from the new MCP’s …”). From graph version 2.6 on, the legacy builder stamps _metadata.line = "legacy" into every graph, and the legacy server refuses a graph from the other line at start-up.

    0.4 How to read this handbook

    The handbook is long on purpose: it assumes nothing and covers every package, module and setting. You don’t have to read it in order. Pick the path that matches what you’re about to do.

    • I’m new to all of itRead in order. Part 1 explains every concept the rest of the handbook relies on.
    • I’ll change the MCP serversChapters 1.2 to 1.6, then Parts 3, 4 and 6, with the tool catalogue in Appendix A open beside you.
    • I’ll change a graph builderChapters 1.7 and 1.8, then Part 2 and the schema reference in Appendix E.
    • I run the serversParts 4 and 5, then the risks in Part 7.
    • I want the design answersPart 6: context, stopping, failures, approvals, and why there’s no framework.

    What the labels mean

    Verified in code

    Read directly from the source, a config template or a real build log.

    Likely reason

    The code shows what happens but not why. This is the most likely explanation, and it is marked as one.

    Planned

    Not built yet: Azure Key Vault, per-client Entra apps, the Jenkins pipeline.

    Watch out

    Something that can break, leak or mislead. Part 7 collects all of them.

    Conventions

    • File paths are relative to each repository’s root, for example server/handler.py in ngenue_mcp_legacy.
    • “Legacy” always means the legacy nTrack UI line, and “new UI” means the nGenue UI line.
    • Code excerpts are real. Where lines are left out, you’ll see “…”.
    • A word with a dotted underline shows a short definition when you point at it or move to it with the Tab key.
    • The handbook remembers where you stopped reading and offers to take you back there next time.

    Part 1

    Foundations, from zero

    Every idea the rest of the handbook relies on: the Python features this code uses, how it does several things at once, the web and MCP protocols, sign-in with tokens, parsers, graphs, search by meaning, SQL Server access and Windows hosting.

      Each chapter explains one idea from zero, with small examples you can run, and then shows exactly where the nGenue code uses it. If you already know a topic, skim it for the boxes labelled In the code: they tell you something about this system that a general tutorial can’t.

      1.1 Python you need for this code

      Both builders and both servers are plain Python 3.11; only the ScriptDOM service is C#. They use no exotic tricks, but they lean on about ten language features again and again. Learn these and every file becomes readable.

      Modules, packages and imports

      A module is one .py file. A package is a folder of modules with an __init__.py file in it. When you write import tools, Python looks for a module or package called tools in each folder listed in sys.path, in order, and uses the first match.

      The server repositories keep server/, auth/ and loaders/ at the top level, so running from the repository root makes them importable. The tool code lives one level down in tools/, so the loader adds that folder to sys.path at start-up. After that, tool files can write from models import ToolResult and import tools.

      Almost every file starts with from __future__ import annotations. It tells Python to store type hints as plain text instead of evaluating them when the module loads. That makes imports faster and lets a hint mention a class that is defined later in the file, or one that is only imported for type checking.

      Installing: virtual environments, requirements.txt and pyproject.toml

      A virtual environment is a private folder of installed packages for one project, so two projects can use different versions of the same library. You create one with python -m venv .venv, activate it, and install into it.

      Each repository describes its dependencies twice, for two different readers:

      • requirements.txt is a list for pip install -r: the quickest way to get a working environment.
      • pyproject.toml describes the project as an installable package: its name, version, required Python version, dependencies, optional extras and command-line entry points.

      The servers declare an optional docs extra (Qdrant, OpenAI, sentence-transformers, torch, numpy), because a server without documentation search doesn’t need those heavy packages. They also declare an entry point, mcp-server = "server.app:main", which creates an mcp-server command that calls main() in server/app.py. The builders declare delphi-kg = "delphi_kg.cli:main" (and delphi-kg-legacy for the fork).

      Why it’s built this way

      The version pins carry real reasons, written next to them. The builder needs Python 3.11 exactly, because tree-sitter-languages 1.10 ships no installable wheels for newer Pythons. pydantic is held to 2.10 because the JSON Schema it generates changes between minor versions, and two machines would otherwise publish different schemas under the same version number.

      Try it

      On Windows, from a server repository folder: py -3.11 -m venv .venv, then .venv\Scripts\activate, then pip install -r requirements.txt. Run the server with python -m server.app once a .env file is in place (chapter 4.6 and Appendix C list every setting).

      Type hints

      A type hint says what kind of value a variable, argument or return value should hold. Python doesn’t check them while the program runs; editors and checkers such as mypy do, and they make code far easier to read. The forms you’ll see most:

      HintMeans
      def find(name: str) -> dict | NoneTakes a string; returns a dict or None
      list[str], dict[str, list[str]]A list of strings; a dict from strings to lists of strings
      frozenset[str]An unchangeable set of strings (used for fixed lists such as blocked SQL words)
      Callable[[], Any]A function that takes no arguments and returns anything
      Iterator[Token]Something you can loop over that yields tokens one by one

      One trick appears in tools/tools/base.py: imports inside if TYPE_CHECKING: only run for type checkers, never at runtime. That lets ToolDeps mention DelphiIndex and the vector-search classes in its hints without importing heavy modules or creating import cycles. The hints are written as strings for the same reason.

      Dataclasses

      Writing a class that only holds data normally means writing __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ by hand. The @dataclass decorator writes them for you from the field list. Two options matter here:

      • frozen=True makes instances read-only after creation. ToolDeps (above) is frozen: every tool shares one instance, and no tool can swap out a graph by accident.
      • field(default_factory=…) computes a default each time an instance is created, instead of once when the class is defined. The server configuration uses this to read each environment variable when ServerConfig() runs, not when Python first imports the file.

      The builder’s parser uses frozen dataclasses for its intermediate results too (ObjectIR in extractors/dfm/ir.py): once a DFM object is parsed, nothing downstream can change it. The vector-search embedder adds __slots__, which fixes the attribute list and saves a little memory per instance.

      Classes, inheritance and abstract base classes

      Every one of the 148 legacy tools is a class that inherits from BaseTool. BaseTool is an abstract base class: it inherits from ABC and marks execute() with @abstractmethod, so Python refuses to create a tool that forgot to implement it.

      It also uses a less common hook, __init_subclass__, which runs once for every class that inherits from it. BaseTool uses it to give each tool a readable title and the standard MCP safety annotations, unless the tool sets its own.

      The builder uses the other way of describing “anything with these methods”: a Protocol. SqlParserBackend in extractors/sql/backends.py lists parse(), parse_batch(), health_check() and name. Both ScriptDomBackend and LexicalHintsBackend provide them, so the rest of the builder can use either one without knowing which it has. Nothing has to inherit from the protocol; matching the shape is enough.

      Decorators

      A decorator is a function that takes a function (or class) and returns a replacement. Writing @something above a definition is shorthand for f = something(f). You’ll meet three kinds:

      • Built in: @dataclass, @property (a method you read like an attribute), @staticmethod, @abstractmethod.
      • From frameworks: @app.post("/mcp") registers an HTTP route in FastAPI; @click.command() and @click.option(…) build the builder’s command line; @asynccontextmanager turns a generator into an async with block.
      • Written here: _retry in tools/vectorstore/searcher.py wraps every Qdrant call so that temporary failures are retried.

      Context managers

      A with block guarantees that clean-up happens even if an error is raised inside it. You’ll see it for files (with open(…)), locks (with _lock:), HTTP clients (async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:) and worker pools (with ProcessPoolExecutor(…) as pool:, which waits for workers and shuts them down).

      The server’s start-up and shut-down live in one context manager. FastAPI runs the code before yield before it accepts any request, and the code after yield when the process stops.

      Exceptions

      Errors in Python are exceptions: raised with raise, handled with try … except, with finally for code that must always run. Defining your own exception classes lets callers handle one kind of failure differently from another.

      The code follows one rule throughout: a problem with a request becomes an answer, not a crash. A tool that fails returns an error result the AI can read. A problem at start-up, such as a missing graph, stops the process at once with a clear message. Some examples:

      • NGenueLoadError (start-up) ends in _fatal_exit(), which calls os._exit(). The comment explains why: uvicorn swallows a normal SystemExit raised during start-up and replaces its exit code.
      • ToolExecutionError carries a tool’s error text up to the protocol layer, which sends it back with isError: true.
      • LiveSqlError and its children LiveSqlBusy, LiveSqlTimeout and LiveSqlDisabled hold messages that are safe to show: no server names, no connection details.

      Two spellings matter when re-raising. raise NewError(…) from exc keeps the original error attached for the logs. raise NewError(…) from None deliberately hides it; live SQL does this so a database driver’s message, which can name servers, never reaches the AI.

      Logging

      The logging module writes timestamped messages at five levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL. Each module gets its own logger with logging.getLogger(__name__), so every line shows where it came from. The server sends all of it to standard error, which NSSM captures into log files on the VM (chapter 1.11).

      Notice the %s placeholders instead of an f-string. The logger fills them in only if the line is actually written, so a DEBUG line costs almost nothing when the level is INFO. The tool_call line is the most useful one in production: one per call, with the tool name, duration in milliseconds, answer size, and whether the answer was cut.

      Loading code by name

      The server never imports a tool by name. It discovers them. Two functions from importlib make this possible:

      • importlib.import_module("loaders.ngenue") imports a module whose name is only known at runtime. server/app.py uses it to load whichever loader LOADER_MODULE names, so the same server core could serve different tool sets.
      • importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(…) imports a file by its path. tools/tools/__init__.py walks every tools/<category>/<tool>/tool.py, imports it, and keeps each BaseTool subclass defined in that file.

      Adding a tool therefore means adding a folder with a tool.py and adding its name to loaders/tool_manifest.txt. Nothing else has to be edited, and the manifest check at start-up (chapter 3.2) catches a tool that failed to import.

      Settings from the environment

      Settings arrive as environment variables: named text values that a process inherits from whatever started it. os.getenv("PORT", "8000") reads one, with a default. Because they are always text, the server converts them with small helpers (_env_int, _env_set, _env_list) that fall back to a default and log a warning when a number doesn’t parse.

      On the VM, the values come from a .env file next to each instance’s code. load_dotenv() from python-dotenv reads that file into the environment when server/config.py is imported. When it isn’t given a path, it looks next to the calling file and then in each parent folder, so it finds the .env in the repository root. It never overwrites a variable that is already set, which is how tests and a future Key Vault loader can override it.

      Key takeaways

      • Tools are classes that inherit from BaseTool; the server finds them by walking folders, not through a hand-written list.
      • Dataclasses hold configuration and shared state; frozen ones can’t be changed by accident.
      • Errors in a request become answers; errors at start-up stop the process with a clear message.
      • Every setting is an environment variable, usually loaded from the instance’s .env file.

      1.2 Processes, threads and asyncio

      The builder has to parse about 1,600 files as fast as possible. The server has to keep answering while one tool spends ten seconds walking a graph and another waits for SQL Server. Those are two different problems, and Python has a different tool for each.

      Two kinds of slow

      • CPU-bound work keeps the processor busy: parsing Pascal, walking syntax trees, building indexes, serialising a big answer to JSON.
      • I/O-bound work mostly waits: for Microsoft Entra ID, Azure OpenAI or Qdrant to answer over the network, for SQL Server to run a query, for the disk.

      Making CPU-bound work faster needs more processor cores working at the same time. Making I/O-bound work faster needs something useful to do while waiting.

      Processes, and the GIL

      A process is a running program with its own memory. Two processes can run on two cores at the same moment. The cost is that they share nothing: data has to be copied (pickled) to send it from one process to another, and starting a process takes time.

      In standard Python, threads can’t spread CPU-bound work over cores, because of the GIL. Only one thread runs Python code at a time. So for CPU-bound work the answer is several processes.

      That is what the builder does. With --parallel (or --workers N, default: number of cores, at most 8), Phase 2 (PAS), Phase 4 (DFM) and the behavioural walkers run in a ProcessPoolExecutor: a pool of worker processes that each take one unit at a time.

      Three details are worth copying in your own code. Work is sent as plain dictionaries (item_dicts), because only simple data can be pickled cheaply. A worker that crashes becomes a diagnostic, not a failed build. And results are merged in the order they were submitted, not the order they finished, so two builds of the same source produce byte-identical graphs.

      Threads

      A thread runs inside a process and shares its memory. Threads are cheap and good at waiting: a thread blocked on a network read or a database call releases the GIL, so other threads keep running. Many C libraries also release it while they work, including pyodbc during a query and torch inside the reranker.

      Shared memory brings one obligation: when two threads may change the same data, a threading.Lock must protect it. The server has several such locks. One guards the pages kept for get_more_results (tools/budget.py), and another guards the live-SQL counters that track how many queries are running.

      The server keeps three thread pools:

      PoolSizeRuns
      asyncio’s default poolPython’s default: CPU cores + 4 threads, at most 32Every ordinary graph tool, so one slow tool can’t freeze the server
      live_sqlSQL_QUERY_MAX_CONCURRENT, default 4sql_query and get_menu_path; extra calls wait up to 10 s, then get “busy”
      docsDOCS_MAX_CONCURRENT, default 4Documentation search: embedding, Qdrant and the reranker

      Watch out

      Python can’t stop a running thread. When a tool passes its 90-second limit, the server stops waiting and answers with a timeout, but the thread keeps working in the background until it finishes, and its result is thrown away. Live SQL goes further and cancels the database statement itself through a “safety net” (chapter 3.8).

      asyncio and the event loop

      asyncio runs many waiting tasks on one thread. An async def function is a coroutine: when it reaches await on something slow (a network reply, a timer), it hands control back to the event loop, which runs another task until the reply arrives. One thread can juggle thousands of open requests this way, as long as no task holds on to the thread for long.

      That is the golden rule: never block the event loop. A CPU-heavy loop or a blocking call inside an async function freezes every other request until it ends. uvicorn and FastAPI run the server on an event loop, so the server follows the rule in three ways:

      1. Ordinary tools are synchronous functions, sent to a thread pool with loop.run_in_executor(…) and awaited from there.
      2. Truly asynchronous work, such as fetching Entra ID’s signing keys with httpx.AsyncClient, is awaited directly.
      3. Heavy start-up work, such as loading a 470 MB graph with json.load, also goes to a thread, so the process stays responsive while it loads.

      Other asyncio pieces you’ll meet: asyncio.gather(…) runs the items of a JSON-RPC batch at the same time; asyncio.Lock makes sure only one request refetches Entra ID’s keys when an unknown key appears; asyncio.wrap_future lets the event loop await a job submitted to the live-SQL pool.

      A Windows detail

      On Windows, Python’s default event loop is the “Proactor” loop. server/app.py replaces it with the older “Selector” loop when it runs on Windows. The comment gives the reason: in Python 3.11, the Proactor loop could close its listening socket after a particular network error (WinError 64), leaving the process running but no longer accepting connections.

      Which one, when

      SituationUseWhere in our code
      Lots of CPU work that splits into independent piecesProcessesBuilder: parsing and walking units in parallel
      Blocking calls (a driver, a library without async)ThreadsServer: graph tools, pyodbc queries, the reranker
      Many requests that mostly wait on the networkasyncioServer: the HTTP layer, the OAuth proxy, key fetching
      A limit on how long to waitasyncio.wait_forThe 90 s tool limit; the live-SQL safety net

      Key takeaways

      • The builder is CPU-bound, so it uses a pool of processes and merges results in a fixed order to stay deterministic.
      • The server is mostly waiting, so it uses one asyncio event loop and pushes every blocking tool onto a thread.
      • Timeouts stop the waiting, not the work: a thread keeps running until it finishes.

      1.3 JSON, pydantic and JSON Schema

      Everything in this system is passed around as JSON: the graphs on disk, every MCP message, every tool answer. This chapter covers JSON itself, how the builder guarantees its JSON has the right shape (pydantic), and how both sides describe a shape so others can check it (JSON Schema).

      JSON in Python

      JSON has six kinds of value, and Python’s json module maps each to a Python type: an object becomes a dict, an array a list, a string a str, a number an int or float, true/false become True/False, and null becomes None.

      Three options do real work in this code:

      • default=str turns anything JSON can’t represent (a date, a path) into a string instead of raising an error. Tool answers are serialised this way.
      • sort_keys=True writes object keys in alphabetical order. The builder uses it, with compact separators, so the same input always produces exactly the same bytes.
      • allow_nan=False rejects NaN and Infinity, which Python allows but JSON doesn’t. The server’s plain_json() turns them into null first, so no client ever receives invalid JSON.

      The servers read the graphs with one json.load call each, which turns the whole file into Python dicts and lists in memory. Chapter 1.8 explains what they build from them.

      pydantic models

      pydantic lets you declare a data shape as a class with typed fields, and then enforces it: building an instance with a missing field, a wrong type or an unknown field raises a clear error. The builder declares every node and edge this way, so a bug that produces a malformed node fails during the build instead of reaching the server.

      Two pydantic methods matter: model_dump() turns an instance back into plain dicts for writing, and model_json_schema() produces a JSON Schema describing the class. The builder generates graph.schema.json from the models with the second one. It is never edited by hand, and a test fails if the committed file and the models disagree.

      The servers don’t define pydantic models of their own. FastAPI depends on pydantic internally, but the servers’ data travels as plain dicts and dataclasses, checked against JSON Schema where it matters.

      JSON Schema

      A JSON Schema is itself a JSON document that describes what another JSON document may contain: which keys, which types, which are required, which values are allowed. It is the shared language between the AI client and the server, because MCP describes every tool’s arguments with one.

      Here is the real input schema the legacy server publishes for get_action_chain, shortened:

      The tool’s own file only declares action_filter and include_vendor. The other two are added by BaseTool.advertised_input_schema() from the tool’s required_state and optional_state: the state fields (chapter 6.2) are described once, in tools/tools/state_schemas.py, and copied into every tool that needs them.

      Schemas also describe answers. A tool that declares an output_schema sends its answer twice: as text, and as a JSON object called structuredContent. The handler checks that object against the schema with the jsonschema library before sending it.

      Why it’s built this way

      The code comments give the reason: Claude Code rejects a tool answer that has an output schema but no matching structuredContent. So the server checks first. When an answer doesn’t match, it is sent as an error result that still contains the full text, which every client passes on to the model, instead of a malformed answer that a client would silently drop.

      Key takeaways

      • The builder writes sorted, compact JSON so identical input gives identical bytes.
      • pydantic models in the builder enforce the graph’s shape, and the JSON Schema is generated from them, never written by hand.
      • In the servers, JSON Schema describes every tool’s arguments, and for some tools their answers too, which are checked before sending.

      1.4 HTTP, JSON-RPC, ASGI and FastAPI

      An MCP server is, underneath, a small web server. This chapter covers the layers a request passes through before any tool runs: HTTP, the JSON-RPC message format inside it, and the Python pieces that receive it.

      HTTP in one page

      An HTTP request has a method (GET, POST…), a path (/aep/v1/mcp), headers (named text values) and an optional body. The response has a status code, headers and a body. The headers this system cares about:

      • Authorization: Bearer <token> carries the Entra ID token or API key.
      • Content-Type: application/json says the body is JSON; the server rejects anything else.
      • MCP-Protocol-Version says which MCP revision the client speaks.
      • WWW-Authenticate, sent back with a 401, tells the client how to sign in.

      The status codes the servers actually send:

      CodeMeaningWhen our servers send it
      200OKEvery answered MCP request, including a tool that failed: the failure is inside the answer (isError: true)
      204No contentThe request was only notifications, which get no answer
      302Redirect/oauth/authorize sends the browser on to Microsoft’s sign-in page
      400Bad requestBad JSON, an unknown method or tool, bad arguments, an unsupported protocol version
      401UnauthorizedNo token, or an invalid or expired one
      404Not foundOAuth metadata asked for when OAuth isn’t switched on
      405Method not allowedA GET on the MCP path: only POST is routed there
      500Server errorJSON-RPC internal error, such as a request arriving before start-up finished
      502Bad gatewayThe token proxy couldn’t reach Microsoft Entra ID
      503Unavailable/health while the server is still loading graphs

      JSON-RPC 2.0

      REST APIs use many URLs and HTTP methods. JSON-RPC uses one URL and puts everything in the body: which method to call, its parameters, and an id to match the answer to the question. MCP is built on it.

      JSON-RPC reserves a few error codes, and MCP adds its own:

      CodeNameHTTP status our server uses
      -32700Parse error: the body isn’t JSON400
      -32600Invalid request: not a proper JSON-RPC object400
      -32601Method not found400 (deliberately not 404)
      -32602Invalid params, including an unknown tool name400
      -32603Internal error500
      -32022MCP: unsupported protocol version400

      JSON-RPC also allows a batch: an array of requests in one body. MCP stopped using batches in its 2025-06-18 revision, but the servers still accept them for older clients and run the items at the same time with asyncio.gather. A batch made only of notifications gets a bare 204.

      ASGI, uvicorn and FastAPI

      Three pieces turn network bytes into a Python function call:

      1. uvicorn is the web server. It listens on a port, speaks HTTP, and hands each request to the application through a standard interface.
      2. ASGI is that interface: a contract that any async Python server and any async Python framework can both follow.
      3. FastAPI, built on Starlette, is the application. It maps a method and path to your function, parses the request, and runs middleware and start-up code.

      The same app also serves GET /health, GET / (name and version), the OAuth discovery documents and, through an APIRouter added only in OAuth mode, the two OAuth proxy endpoints.

      Middleware

      Middleware is code that wraps every request: it can inspect it, reject it, or pass it on and then look at the response. In Starlette a middleware class implements dispatch(request, call_next); calling call_next passes the request inward.

      The servers add two middlewares: CORS first, then the auth check (API key or Entra ID token). Starlette runs the one added last on the outside, so every request meets the auth check first. Only the MCP path is protected. /health and the discovery documents stay public, because a client must be able to read them before it has a token.

      CORS

      Browsers block a web page from calling another site’s API unless that site allows it. That rule is called CORS, and only browsers enforce it. Claude’s and ChatGPT’s back-end servers, Claude Code and Cowork are not browsers, so CORS doesn’t affect them; it only matters for browser-based tools such as some MCP inspectors. The servers allow the origins listed in ALLOWED_ORIGINS, or every origin when it is empty. They allow POST, GET and OPTIONS, accept the Authorization and MCP-Protocol-Version headers, and let a browser read the MCP-Protocol-Version header in answers.

      Behind a reverse proxy: PUBLIC_URL

      Each Python server listens only on 127.0.0.1 at its own port. IIS receives https://mcp.ngenue.net/aep/v1/mcp from the internet, strips the /aep/v1 prefix and forwards the request to the AEP instance as http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp. A program behind a reverse proxy can’t see the address people use to reach it, so PUBLIC_URL tells it. The server needs it to write correct links in its OAuth discovery documents and in the WWW-Authenticate header.

      Key takeaways

      • Every MCP message is one HTTPS POST carrying a JSON-RPC request; the answer is plain JSON.
      • A failed tool still returns HTTP 200: the failure is in the answer, where the AI can read it.
      • uvicorn serves HTTP, FastAPI routes it, middleware checks the token, and PUBLIC_URL makes links correct behind IIS.

      1.5 MCP from zero

      The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Before it, every AI app had its own plugin format. With it, one server, like each of ours, works with Claude on the web, desktop and mobile, Claude Code, Cowork and ChatGPT without changes.

      Hosts, clients and servers

      • The host is the AI application the person uses: Claude, Claude Code, Cowork or ChatGPT.
      • The client is the part of the host that holds one connection to one server, such as the “AEP-MCP” connector.
      • The server is our program on the VM.

      The language model never talks to the server directly. When the model decides to use a tool, the host sends the request and passes the answer back into the conversation. That is why approvals, retries and stopping are the host’s business, not the server’s (Part 6).

      What a server can offer

      MCP defines three things a server can provide: tools (functions the model calls), resources (data the host can read) and prompts (ready-made instructions a person can pick). The registry in server/registry.py supports all three, but the nGenue loader registers only tools, so the servers announce a single capability: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}. listChanged: false tells clients the tool list never changes while the server is running.

      A server can also send instructions: text the host gives the model about how to use the server. Ours send the playbook from ngenue_old_ui_instructions.md (legacy) or ngenue_instructions.md (new UI), prefixed with one line naming the client and graph build this instance serves.

      A tool, as the client sees it

      A client asks for the tool list with tools/list. Each entry has a name, a title, a description the model reads to decide when to use it, an inputSchema (chapter 1.3), sometimes an outputSchema, and annotations: hints such as readOnlyHint: true that help a host decide how cautious to be.

      Calling a tool is tools/call with the tool’s name and arguments. The answer’s content is a list of blocks; ours always send one text block. A tool that failed sets isError: true and explains why in the text.

      There are two different kinds of failure, and the difference matters. A protocol error (an unknown tool, a malformed request) is a JSON-RPC error: the request never reached a tool. A tool error (a screen not found, a timeout) is a normal result with isError: true, so the model can read the reason and try something else.

      Transports

      MCP can run over two transports. stdio is for servers that run as a local program next to the host; messages travel over the program’s standard input and output. Streamable HTTP is for remote servers: the client POSTs each message, and the server answers with JSON or, for long operations, a stream of events.

      Our servers are remote and only ever answer with plain JSON: every tool finishes within its time limit, so there is nothing to stream. Only POST is routed on the MCP path; a GET there gets 405.

      Protocol versions: two eras

      MCP versions are named by their release date. Up to 2025-11-25, a connection began with an initialize handshake: the client and server agreed on a version and capabilities, and a remote server could hand out a session id that every later request carried.

      The 2026-07-28 revision, published as final on 28 July 2026, removed the handshake and the session. Every request now describes itself. Its _meta carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo and clientCapabilities, and the MCP-Protocol-Version header must match. A new server/discover method lets a client fetch a server’s capabilities up front when it wants them. The revision also adds caching hints to results and deprecates roots, sampling and logging. (Sources: the 2026-07-28 release and an SDK’s summary of the changes.)

      The servers speak both eras. They advertise 2026-07-28 and still answer the old initialize handshake for clients that use it. The code comment mentions one such case: Claude Code falls back to initialize when its server/discover probe times out. After a handshake, the version the client negotiated is accepted on every later request.

      The version check runs on every request except server/discover and initialize. It reads the version from _meta; if the client sent only the header, server/app.py copies the header’s value into _meta first. A request that names no version at all is let through, to stay friendly to old clients. A version outside the accepted list gets -32022 with the list of supported versions. tools/list answers say they can be cached for 5 minutes (ttlMs: 300000).

      In the code

      The servers are deliberately lenient. They don’t require the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name routing headers the 2026-07-28 revision introduced, and they don’t reject a request whose header and _meta versions disagree. That keeps every client working, old and new; Part 7 notes it as something to tighten when all clients speak the new revision.

      Statelessness fits this design

      The servers kept no per-conversation memory even before the protocol required it. When a tool finds a screen, it doesn’t remember it; it returns the screen’s id in a STATE UPDATES block, and the model passes it back on the next call. Any request can be answered by the instance without knowing what came before.

      There is one exception: when an answer is too large, the rest is kept in the server’s memory behind a one-time cursor for get_more_results (chapter 6.3). That works because each client is served by exactly one process. If you ever ran several processes for one client behind a load balancer, a cursor could land on the wrong one.

      Key takeaways

      • The host (Claude, ChatGPT…) talks to the server for the model; the model only sees tool descriptions and answers.
      • Our servers offer tools only, over Streamable HTTP, always answering with plain JSON.
      • They implement the stateless 2026-07-28 revision and still accept the older initialize handshake.
      • State lives in tool arguments, not on the server; the only exception is the paging cursor.

      1.6 OAuth 2.1, JWT and Entra ID

      The servers expose nGenue’s source code and read client databases, so they must know who is calling. This chapter explains the standard pieces that make that work. Part 4 then walks through our exact flow, line by line.

      Tokens instead of passwords

      People never type a password into Claude or into our server. They sign in on Microsoft’s own page; Microsoft then gives the AI client a short-lived access token that says “this is user X, and this token is meant for the nGenue MCP server.” The client sends that token with every request. Because the token is digitally signed, the server can check it on its own, without asking Microsoft each time.

      The four roles in OAuth

      OAuth roleIn our system
      Resource ownerThe person using Claude or ChatGPT
      ClientThe AI app’s connector (Claude, Claude Code, Cowork, ChatGPT)
      Authorization serverMicrosoft Entra ID, reached through our small proxy
      Resource serverOur MCP server, which checks tokens and serves tools

      The authorization code flow with PKCE

      OAuth 2.1 recommends one flow for apps acting for a person: the authorization code flow, protected with PKCE.

      1. The client makes a secret. It creates a random code_verifier and a code_challenge, which is the SHA-256 hash of the verifier.
      2. The browser goes to the sign-in page. The request carries the client id, where to return (redirect_uri), the scopes wanted, a random state, and the challenge.
      3. The person signs in. Microsoft redirects the browser back to the client with a one-time authorization code.
      4. The client swaps the code for tokens. It POSTs the code plus the original code_verifier to the token endpoint. Microsoft hashes the verifier, checks it matches the challenge, and returns an access token (and a refresh token, if offline_access was asked for).

      Someone who intercepts the code can’t use it, because they don’t have the verifier. OAuth 2.1 makes PKCE mandatory for this flow and drops older, weaker flows such as the “implicit” flow.

      Scopes, refresh tokens and client secrets

      • A scope names what access is requested. For our servers it is the API scope defined in the Entra app (OAUTH_SCOPE). offline_access asks for a refresh token; our proxy adds it automatically for code exchanges.
      • A refresh token lets the client get a new access token when the old one expires (typically after about an hour) without making the person sign in again.
      • A confidential client also proves its own identity with a client secret. Our proxy announces client_secret_post, which means the client puts its id and secret in the body of the token request. That is why the Entra app’s client id and secret are entered in each connector’s settings in Claude and ChatGPT.

      JWT: what’s inside a token

      Entra ID’s access tokens are JWTs: three parts separated by dots, each base64url-encoded. The first two are just JSON, readable by anyone; the third is the signature.

      RS256 means an RSA signature over a SHA-256 hash. Microsoft signs with a private key that never leaves Microsoft, and publishes the matching public keys at a JWKS address. The kid in the header says which key signed this token. Checking a token means checking, in order:

      1. the signature, with the public key whose id is kid;
      2. the algorithm is the one expected (RS256);
      3. the token isn’t expired (exp) or not yet valid (nbf);
      4. it was issued by the expected tenant (iss);
      5. it was issued for this server (aud), so a token meant for some other app can’t be replayed here.

      Microsoft Entra ID vocabulary

      • A tenant is an organisation’s directory in Entra ID, identified by a GUID (OAUTH_TENANT_ID).
      • An app registration describes one application. It gives it a client id (OAUTH_CLIENT_ID), allowed redirect addresses, client secrets, and under “Expose an API” an Application ID URI (often api://<client id>) with scopes. Today, one app registration covers all eleven server instances; one per client is planned.
      • Token versions. Entra issues v1.0 or v2.0 access tokens, depending on a setting in the API app’s manifest. They carry different issuers: https://sts.windows.net/<tenant>/ for v1.0 and https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0 for v2.0. In v2.0 tokens the audience is the API’s client id; in v1.0 tokens it is usually the Application ID URI. The server accepts both issuers and both audiences, so either setting works.
      • Endpoints: /oauth2/v2.0/authorize (sign-in), /oauth2/v2.0/token (tokens) and /discovery/v2.0/keys (the public keys), all under https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>.

      How an MCP client finds the sign-in page

      An MCP client starts with nothing but the server’s address. Three published standards lead it from there to Microsoft’s sign-in page:

      1. Its first request has no token, so the server answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="…/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource" (RFC 9728).
      2. That protected resource metadata names the server’s authorization_servers. Ours names itself, because of the proxy.
      3. The client reads the authorization server metadata (RFC 8414, or its OpenID Connect equivalent /.well-known/openid-configuration). It lists where to sign in, where to get tokens and where the public keys are.

      MCP also asks clients to send a resource parameter naming the server (RFC 8707). Entra ID’s v2 endpoints reject that combination with error AADSTS9010010, and they don’t know the mcp:* scopes some clients add. Our server therefore points clients at itself: /oauth/authorize and /oauth/token remove what Entra would reject, then pass everything on. It never issues or changes tokens. Chapter 4.3 shows the code.

      There is no dynamic client registration endpoint, the standard that lets a client register itself automatically. That is the other reason the client id and secret are typed into each connector by hand.

      API keys: the simpler alternative

      With AUTH_MODE=apikey, a client sends a fixed secret as Authorization: Bearer <key>, checked against the comma-separated list in API_KEYS. There is no sign-in, no expiry and no per-person identity. For logs, a key shaped key-<n>-<random> is recorded as n; any other key as a short hash, never the key itself. AUTH_MODE=none switches checking off, which is meant only for local testing on 127.0.0.1.

      Key takeaways

      • People sign in at Microsoft; the AI client receives a signed, short-lived JWT and sends it with every call.
      • The server checks the signature against Entra’s public keys, plus the expiry, issuer and audience, on every request.
      • Discovery documents lead any MCP client to the sign-in page; our proxy removes the two things Entra ID rejects.

      1.7 Tokens, parsers and syntax trees

      A builder has to understand Delphi source the way a compiler does: which text is a class, which is a method, what a method calls, which SQL it runs. That means parsing. This chapter explains how parsing works and the three parsers the builders use.

      From text to structure

      Parsing happens in two steps. A tokenizer (or lexer) cuts the text into tokens: keywords, names, strings, numbers, punctuation. A parser then arranges the tokens into a syntax tree that shows how they nest. The builders add a third step of their own: translating the tree into graph nodes and edges.

      Tokenized, the first line is: procedure (keyword), TEndUserForm (name), ., btnSaveClick (name), (, Sender, :, TObject, ), ;. Parsed, the whole snippet becomes a tree like this:

      From that tree the builder can write graph facts: a METHOD node …::btnSaveClick::METHOD, a call to ValidateInput, and a call through the data module dmEndUser to SaveEndUser.

      Why not regular expressions

      It is tempting to find methods with a pattern like procedure\s+(\w+)\.(\w+). It breaks quickly. Regular expressions can’t count nesting (a begin … end inside another), they don’t know that a word inside a string or a comment isn’t code, and every unusual layout needs another special case. The design document makes it the first rule: no regex for structural parsing. The DFM tokenizer’s first line says it too: “generator-based, character-by-character. No regex.”

      There is one deliberate exception. When the ScriptDOM service can’t be used, a lexical fallback reads SQL with simple token rules to find likely table names. Its results are marked "parser": "lexical-fallback", so every later step treats them as hints rather than facts.

      A hand-written parser: DFM files

      A .dfm file stores a form’s design: every control, its properties and its event handlers, as nested object … end blocks.

      The builder reads these with a recursive-descent parser: one function per grammar rule, calling each other the way the grammar nests. The rule for an object is “keyword, name, colon, class, then properties and child objects until end”, so _parse_object calls _parse_property for properties and itself for children.

      Its tokenizer is a generator: a function that uses yield to hand out one token at a time instead of building a full list in memory. That matters for DFM files of several megabytes. A pre-pass first strips the hex-encoded binary blobs (images, icons) that make up much of their size.

      tree-sitter: a ready-made parser for Pascal

      Writing a full Pascal parser by hand would take months, so the builders use tree-sitter, a parser generator. Someone writes the language’s grammar once. tree-sitter turns it into a fast C parser, and Python loads it as a compiled library. It is also error-tolerant: code it doesn’t understand becomes an ERROR node instead of stopping the parse, which matters on nearly a thousand real-world units.

      Both builders use the Pascal grammar from github.com/Isopod/tree-sitter-pascal. On first use they fetch it with Git, compile it into a shared library with tree-sitter 0.21’s Language.build_library(), and cache the result. That function was removed in tree-sitter 0.22, which is one reason the version is held at 0.21. The legacy builder pins the grammar to one commit, recorded in delphi_kg/data/tree_sitter_pascal.lock.json. The new-UI builder clones whatever the grammar repository holds at that moment; chapter 2.8 explains why that difference matters.

      Why it’s built this way

      The legacy builder’s lock file says it: “a different grammar can change the graph.” Pinning the grammar means a graph changes only when the code or the source changes, never because someone’s machine fetched a newer grammar. Compiling needs a C toolchain, but loading an already-built library doesn’t, so the cached library keeps working on machines without a compiler.

      Walking a tree-sitter tree means visiting nodes and reading their type, their children and their position. The builder stores start_point[0] + 1 as each node’s source line (tree-sitter counts rows from 0).

      Before tree-sitter sees a unit, a pre-parser deals with things the grammar can’t, such as conditional compilation ({$IFDEF …}) and include files. Part 2 covers it.

      The visitor pattern, in C#

      For T-SQL the builders use Microsoft’s own parser, ScriptDOM, inside the small .NET service (chapter 2.6). It parses SQL into a tree of “fragments” and offers the visitor pattern for walking it. You write a class with one Visit method per node type you care about, and the walker calls the right one as it passes each node. Everything you don’t override is simply walked through.

      Key takeaways

      • Parsing is tokenize, then build a tree; the builders then translate the tree into graph nodes.
      • DFM files use a hand-written recursive-descent parser; Pascal uses tree-sitter (with a pinned grammar in the legacy builder); T-SQL uses Microsoft ScriptDOM.
      • No regular expressions for structure. The only lexical shortcut, the SQL fallback, labels its results as hints.

      1.8 Knowledge graphs

      A knowledge graph stores facts as things and the relationships between them. For code, that turns questions like “what runs when Save is clicked?” into walks along relationships, instead of searches through text.

      Nodes, edges and properties

      A node is a thing: a unit, a form, a method, a button, a SQL statement, a table. An edge is a directed, typed relationship from one node to another: a form HAS_COMPONENT a button; a method REFERENCES (calls) another method. Both can carry properties: a method’s source file and lines, an edge’s confidence. The list of allowed node and edge types is the graph’s ontology. The legacy builder defines 40 node types and 91 edge types.

      Answering “what happens when Save is clicked” is now a walk along those arrows. That is, in essence, what get_action_chain does, with care for inherited forms, overrides, vendor code and limits.

      Ids you can read

      Every node has an id built from names, not from a counter: EndUserUnit::TEndUserForm::btnSaveClick::METHOD. Such ids are deterministic: rebuilding the graph from the same source gives the same ids, so an id the AI saw yesterday still works today. The last part says what kind of node it is. Delphi ids use :: because Delphi unit names may contain dots. SQL ids use dots (dbo.ENDUSER.TABLE), and the two sets of suffixes never overlap; a test checks that.

      When an id has to change between graph versions, the node keeps its old one in previous_id for one version, so stored references can be mapped across.

      How the graph is stored

      Both graphs share one envelope: _metadata (version, build time, counts, source details), nodes grouped by type, and edges grouped by edge type. Each edge records both directions’ names.

      A graph database, or JSON in memory?

      Graphs are often stored in a graph database such as Neo4j, which has its own query language, persistence and concurrent writers. These servers do something simpler: each loads its graph files into Python dictionaries at start-up and answers from memory.

      Graph databaseJSON files in memory (our choice)
      WritesMany writers, transactionsNone: the graph is rebuilt and replaced as a file
      SpeedNetwork hop and query planning per callDictionary lookups in the same process
      OperationsAnother service to install, secure and back upA file per client; copy it and restart
      CostDisk-backed; memory as configuredAbout 5 times the file size in RAM per instance, and 15–60 s to load

      Likely reason

      The graphs are read-only between builds, and each client needs its own. Loading a file per instance is the simplest thing that works on one Windows VM: there is no database to run, a build is deployed by copying files, and every answer is a lookup in local memory.

      Indexes: adjacency lists

      A list of edges is slow to search. So at start-up DelphiIndex builds adjacency lists: for every node, the edges leaving it and the edges arriving at it, so any neighbour is one dictionary lookup away.

      The real index builds dozens more lookup tables (forms by caption, methods by class, tables to SQL statements, frames to the forms that embed them), so most tools never scan the whole graph.

      Walking the graph, with limits

      Most tools walk outwards from a starting node. A breadth-first search visits neighbours first, then their neighbours, and so on. Two guards are essential: a visited set, because call graphs have cycles (A calls B calls A), and a depth limit, because some methods are reachable from half the codebase.

      The real tools use the same two guards with published numbers. For example, get_action_chain follows calls to a depth of 4 and lists at most 200 methods, saying so in chain_truncated when it stops. These limits are half of the answer to “how does it decide where to stop?” (chapter 6.4).

      Two graphs, one seam

      Every piece of SQL the builder finds becomes a SQL_PLACEHOLDER node with the raw text and what ScriptDOM parsed from it. The builder never draws edges into the SQL graph; it stays independent. When a server starts, it resolves the names in every placeholder against that client’s SQL graph and keeps the links in memory. A name that isn’t found is reported as not_in_sql_graph, and the playbook tells the model to say its SQL side is unknown, never that it doesn’t exist.

      Key takeaways

      • Nodes are things, edges are typed relationships, and readable ids stay stable across builds.
      • The servers load JSON graphs into dictionaries and adjacency lists, trading RAM for speed and simplicity.
      • Every walk has a visited set and a depth or size limit, and tools report when they stop early.

      1.9 Embeddings, Qdrant and reranking

      The graphs answer questions about code. Questions about the product (“how does a nomination flow work?”) are answered from nGenue’s documentation, through six documentation tools such as search_docs. Those tools search by meaning, not by exact words.

      Search by meaning

      A keyword search for “cancel a deal” misses a page that says “void a trade”. An embedding model turns a piece of text into a long list of numbers (a vector), placed so that texts with similar meaning end up close together. Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity: 1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated.

      Chunks and vectors

      Long documents are split into chunks (roughly a section each), and each chunk is embedded once, when the documentation is loaded into the vector database. That loading pipeline isn’t part of these repositories. Each stored chunk is a point: an id, its vector, and a payload with the text, the file name and section ids.

      The collection is called adaptive_chunks because long sections were split adaptively into several sibling chunks. After a search, the server stitches siblings back together (merge_adaptive_siblings) so the AI reads a whole section rather than a fragment.

      Qdrant

      Qdrant is a vector database: it stores points and finds the nearest ones to a query vector quickly, using an approximate index, with optional filters on the payload. Here it runs on the same Windows VM as the MCP servers, as its own NSSM service. All eleven instances share one collection, adaptive_chunks.

      Two-stage retrieval: find fast, then rank carefully

      An embedding model looks at the question and each chunk separately, which is what makes it fast, but also rough. A cross-encoder reads the question and one chunk together and scores how well the chunk answers it. That is far more accurate, but too slow to run on every chunk. So the search runs in two stages:

      The reranker is cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2, loaded once at start-up through the sentence-transformers library (which uses torch), running on the CPU. It runs under a lock, one rerank at a time, so concurrent searches can’t overload the processor.

      Who writes the answer?

      This pattern is called RAG: retrieve relevant text, then generate an answer from it. Here the two halves live in different places. The MCP server only retrieves. The only AI model it calls is the embedding model, and it calls no chat model. Claude or ChatGPT does the generating, using the chunks the tool returned.

      When something is down

      • All or nothing at start-up. Documentation search starts only if all four settings exist: QDRANT_URL, AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY and AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DEPLOYMENT. With only some of them, the server logs a warning and runs without it; the documentation tools then answer “not available” and every graph tool keeps working.
      • Temporary failures are retried. Embedding, Qdrant and reranker calls get up to three attempts, 1 s and then 2 s apart. A request Qdrant rejects (a 4xx error, a malformed id) fails at once, because retrying can’t fix it.
      • A broken reranker isn’t fatal. If reranking still fails after its retries, the chunks are returned in Qdrant’s order instead.
      • Their own pool. Documentation search runs on a dedicated pool of four threads (DOCS_MAX_CONCURRENT), so slow network calls can’t use up the threads that graph tools need.

      Key takeaways

      • Embeddings place similar meanings close together; Qdrant finds the nearest chunks fast.
      • A cross-encoder then reranks a small candidate set carefully, and split sections are stitched back together.
      • The server retrieves; the AI client writes the answer. Documentation search is optional and fails softly.

      1.10 SQL Server from Python

      Two tools, sql_query and get_menu_path, read a client’s QA database live. This chapter covers how Python talks to SQL Server, and the safety ideas the live-SQL code relies on.

      ODBC and pyodbc

      ODBC is a long-standing standard way for programs to talk to databases through a driver. Microsoft’s driver for SQL Server is “ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server”, installed on the VM. pyodbc is the Python package that speaks ODBC, following Python’s standard database API: connect, get a cursor, execute, fetch, close.

      Driver 18 encrypts connections by default. A SQL Server using a self-signed certificate, which is common when the database runs on the same machine, then needs TrustServerCertificate=yes in the connection string. The real string for each instance is NGENUE_SQL_CONN_STRING in its .env.

      Logins, users and roles

      SQL Server separates a login (who may connect to the server) from a database user (what that login may do in one database). Permissions usually come from roles. db_datareader can read every table and view and nothing else; db_datawriter, db_ddladmin and db_owner can change things. Each MCP instance connects with a login that should be in db_datareader only.

      The server doesn’t take that on trust. Shortly after start-up, it asks SQL Server what the login can actually do. If the login could change data, live SQL switches itself off and /health says why.

      Timeouts, pooling and session settings

      • A login timeout (15 s) limits how long connecting may take; a query timeout (conn.timeout, 30 s by default) limits each statement.
      • Connection pooling (pyodbc.pooling = True) keeps physical connections open and resets them between uses, so “a fresh connection per query” stays cheap.
      • Session settings make every query behave the same, whoever set up the connection before:

      In plain words: don’t send row-count messages; abort the whole statement on an error; never open a transaction silently; read only committed data; and wait at most 30 seconds for a lock instead of forever.

      Parameters and SQL injection

      Never paste user text into SQL. A value like ' ; DROP TABLE … would become part of the command. Values go in as parameters (? in pyodbc), which the driver sends separately from the SQL text. Names of tables and columns can’t be parameters, so they are wrapped in brackets, [ENDUSER], with any ] inside doubled.

      sql_query has four operations. describe, sample and distinct build their own SQL with parameters and bracketed names. query accepts the AI’s own SELECT, so it must pass a strict check first: exactly one read-only SELECT. The check tokenizes the SQL properly, so LIKE '%update%' inside a string is fine. It rejects words such as INSERT, UPDATE, EXEC, INTO or OPENQUERY, and locking hints such as TABLOCKX. Results stop at 1,000 rows. Chapter 3.8 walks through it.

      Errors that are safe to show

      Driver errors often contain server names and driver details. The live-SQL code translates them using their SQLSTATE, a standard five-character error class, before anything reaches the AI:

      Key takeaways

      • pyodbc talks to SQL Server through ODBC Driver 18, with a 15 s login limit and a 30 s query limit.
      • The login should be db_datareader only, and the server verifies that itself before running any query.
      • Values are parameters, names are bracketed, free-form SQL must be a single SELECT, and errors are cleaned before the AI sees them.

      1.11 Windows services, NSSM, IIS and ARR

      Everything on the server side runs on one Windows Server VM in nGenue’s office server room: eleven Python MCP processes, Qdrant, and SQL Server, with IIS in front. This chapter explains the Windows pieces that keep them running and reachable. Part 5 covers operating them.

      Windows services

      A Windows service is a program the operating system starts and supervises, without anyone being logged in. The Service Control Manager starts it at boot, runs it under a chosen account, restarts it according to its recovery settings, and lets administrators control it with services.msc or sc.exe. A Python script can’t become a service on its own, because a service must answer the Service Control Manager’s start and stop messages.

      NSSM: any program as a service

      NSSM, the Non-Sucking Service Manager, fills that gap. It registers itself as the service and runs your program as a child process: it starts it, restarts it if it exits, writes its output to log files, and stops it cleanly. Each MCP instance and Qdrant runs this way.

      In the code

      The start-up directory (AppDirectory) matters. The .env template uses relative paths such as ./graphs/graph_old.json, which resolve from the working directory, so each service must start inside its own instance folder. Its logs are whatever the server writes to standard error: start-up progress, warnings and one tool_call line per call (chapter 1.1).

      IIS

      IIS (Internet Information Services) is Windows’ built-in web server. It hosts sites, each with bindings: which address, port and host name it answers, and for HTTPS which certificate it presents. Here IIS doesn’t run any Python. It is the front door: it accepts HTTPS for mcp.ngenue.net and forwards each request to the right local process.

      ARR and URL Rewrite: one address, eleven servers

      Two IIS extensions do the forwarding. URL Rewrite matches incoming paths against rules. Application Request Routing (ARR), with its proxy switched on, lets a rule send a request to another server: here, to a Python process on the same machine. One rule per client, with the prefix stripped, gives eleven servers one public address:

      Because the prefix is stripped, every path an instance serves sits under its prefix publicly: /aep/v1/mcp, /aep/v1/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, /aep/v1/oauth/token. That is why each instance’s PUBLIC_URL includes its prefix (chapter 1.4). A few ARR settings affect this setup directly: the proxy timeout (tools may run for up to 90 seconds), response buffering, and the forwarded-header settings. Chapter 5.3 lists them with how to check each one.

      Where HTTPS ends

      In this kind of set-up, HTTPS ends at IIS: the certificate for mcp.ngenue.net is bound to the IIS site, and IIS talks plain HTTP to the Python processes on 127.0.0.1. That traffic never leaves the machine. The .env template’s HOST=127.0.0.1 keeps the Python servers unreachable from the network directly, so IIS stays the only way in.

      Python on Windows

      • The asyncio event-loop fix from chapter 1.2.
      • The memory check at start-up reads free RAM through the Windows API (GlobalMemoryStatusEx via ctypes) when psutil isn’t installed.
      • pyodbc needs the Microsoft ODBC driver installed on the machine; it is a separate download from the Python package.
      • Paths in .env may use forward slashes (./graphs/…); Python accepts them on Windows.

      Key takeaways

      • NSSM turns each Python server and Qdrant into a Windows service, with restarts and log files.
      • IIS with ARR and URL Rewrite gives eleven local servers one public HTTPS address, one path prefix each.
      • The Python processes listen only on 127.0.0.1; IIS is the only way in.

      Part 2

      Build the graphs

      How Delphi source becomes a knowledge graph: what the builders read, the rules they follow, every phase of a build with real timings, the ScriptDOM service, and the checks that keep each graph honest.

        Two builders do this work. delphi-kg_old_UI (distributed as delphi-kg-legacy 0.6.0) builds graph_old.json for each of the ten legacy clients. delphi-kg (0.5.2) builds graph_full.json for the new UI. They share most of their code; chapter 2.8 covers where they differ. Unless a passage says otherwise, the code shown comes from the legacy builder.

        2.1 Delphi for non-Delphi developers

        You can’t judge a graph of Delphi code without knowing what Delphi code looks like. This chapter is a short tour for someone who has never opened the Delphi IDE: the files, the language, and how a screen is put together.

        What Delphi is

        Delphi is a development environment from Embarcadero for building native Windows applications. Its language is Object Pascal: Pascal with classes, properties and exceptions. Its user-interface library is the VCL (Visual Component Library). Both nGenue front ends, the legacy nTrack UI and the new UI, are Delphi applications. For each client the source lives in three folders under nGenue <CLIENT>\:

        • Ntrack: the application itself, in about 46–48 module folders;
        • NtrackLibrary: shared nGenue units and base forms;
        • NtrackDevEx: vendored third-party component code (DevExpress-based), which the builders treat as “vendor” code.

        The files

        ExtensionWhat it isBecomes in the graph
        .pasA unit: one source file of Pascal codeUNIT, plus its classes, methods, fields…
        .dfmThe design of a form, frame or data module: controls, their properties, their event handlersFORM / FRAME / DATA_MODULE, COMPONENT, EVENT_BINDING, SQL_PLACEHOLDER
        .dprThe program file: the main unit, listing units and the forms created at start-upPROJECT, with HAS_UNIT and PROJECT_AUTO_CREATES edges
        .dprojThe MSBuild project: configurations (Debug, Release), conditional symbols, search pathsRead for build settings, such as which {$IFDEF} symbols are on
        .dpkA package: a group of units compiled togetherPACKAGE, with HAS_UNIT and REQUIRES_PACKAGE edges
        .incInclude files pulled into a unit with {$I file.inc}Expanded before parsing

        Some files are skipped on purpose: *_TLB.pas files (generated COM type libraries), Delphi’s __recovery folders, and backups such as Foo.pas.~3~.

        A unit, a class and a form

        Here is a simplified screen, written the way the nTrack code is. The unit has an interface section, which other units can see, and an implementation section, which holds the method bodies. Its uses clauses list the units it depends on; names such as System.SysUtils contain dots.

        The form’s design lives next to it in EndUserUnit.dfm. When the program runs, Delphi reads that file and creates every control it lists, sets its properties, and connects each event to the method with that name. That “by name” wiring is why the builders can link a button to its handler without running anything.

        The first word, inherited, is visual form inheritance: this form starts from everything its ancestor (TBaseForm) already has and adds to it. The shared base forms live in a library module. Inheritance chains are one reason a screen’s behaviour can’t be read from its own files alone.

        Data modules, datasets and data-aware controls

        A data module (TDataModule) is a non-visual container for database objects shared by several forms. By the naming convention, data module classes start with Tdm and form classes with Tfrm. Inside data modules and forms you find:

        • Datasets such as TADOQuery and TADOStoredProc, or nGenue’s own TntpADOQuery. Their SQL property holds the statement, with parameters written :NAME.
        • Data sources (TDataSource), which connect a dataset to controls.
        • Data-aware controls such as TDBEdit or grid columns, whose DataSource and DataField properties say which column they show and edit.

        Code changes data through dataset operations: Open, Edit, Insert, Post, Delete and ExecSQL. Events such as BeforePost or OnValidate run code around them. These are exactly the things the behavioural walkers record (chapter 2.5).

        Other things you will see in the graph

        • Frames (TFrame): reusable panels embedded in several forms (CONTAINS_FRAME edges).
        • Properties: property Name: string read FName write SetName; looks like a field to callers, but runs methods.
        • Overloads: several methods with one name and different parameters; their ids get a short hash suffix (chapter 2.4).
        • with blocks: with dmEndUser.qrySave do SQL.Add(…) makes names inside the block refer to that object. The builders track this “with scope” so SQL.Add lands on the right query.
        • Conditional compilation: {$IFDEF DEBUG} … {$ENDIF} keeps or drops code depending on symbols defined in the .dproj configuration.
        • Interposer classes: a unit that redeclares a library class under the same name (TADOQuery = class(Data.Win.ADODB.TADOQuery)), so every unit that uses it silently gets the subclass. The legacy builder resolves these (InterposerScopeResolver).

        From Delphi to the graph

        In the codeIn the graph
        TEndUserForm = class(TBaseForm)CLASS TEndUserForm -INHERITS_FROM→ CLASS TBaseForm
        uses EndUserDM in the implementation sectionUNIT -USES_IMPLEMENTATION→ UNIT EndUserDM
        object btnSave: TButton … OnClick = btnSaveClickCOMPONENT -HAS_EVENT_BINDING→ EVENT_BINDING -BINDS_EVENT→ METHOD
        dmEndUser.SaveEndUser(FEndUserID)METHOD -REFERENCES→ METHOD SaveEndUser
        qrySave.SQL.Text := 'UPDATE …'METHOD -HAS_SQL→ SQL_PLACEHOLDER (raw text plus what ScriptDOM parsed)
        qrySave.ExecSQLMETHOD -HAS_OPERATION→ DATASET_OPERATION -OPERATION_TARGETS→ the query
        ShowMessage('Name is required') after a checkMETHOD -HAS_VALIDATION→ VALIDATION (with the message text)

        Key takeaways

        • A screen is a unit (.pas) plus its design (.dfm), often inheriting from a base form, usually calling into a data module.
        • Events and controls are wired by name, so the builders can link them by reading files alone.
        • Data flows through datasets, data sources and data-aware controls; code changes data through dataset operations.

        2.2 Setting up and running a build

        Builds run on a developer’s Windows laptop, not on the server VM. The real build logs show it: their source and output paths sit under a user’s Desktop folder. This chapter lists what that laptop needs, the command, and what comes out.

        What the laptop needs

        NeedWhy
        Python 3.11 exactlytree-sitter-languages 1.10 has no wheels for 3.12 or later; the package refuses to install there
        Git, and network access the first timeThe Pascal grammar is fetched from GitHub on first use
        A C compiler (on Windows, Microsoft’s C++ Build Tools)tree-sitter 0.21 compiles the grammar into a library on first use; later builds reuse the cached library
        .NET 9 SDK, and NuGet access the first timeTo run the ScriptDOM service (start.bat checks for dotnet)
        The client’s source treeNtrack, NtrackLibrary and NtrackDevEx for one client
        Memory and timeA legacy client builds in about 5–6 minutes; the new UI took 11½ minutes (chapter 2.5)

        Install

        Watch out

        Both builders contain a Python package called delphi_kg. If both are installed into one Python, whichever was installed last wins, and python -m delphi_kg.cli may run the wrong one. The legacy builder was renamed delphi-kg-legacy and now stamps every graph with its own name, version and code hash (chapter 2.8) for exactly this reason. Give each builder its own virtual environment.

        Run a build

        1. Start ScriptDOM. In the delphi-scriptdom folder, run start.bat. It restores packages and starts the service on http://127.0.0.1:5235. Check it with curl http://127.0.0.1:5235/health.
        2. Run the builder with the client’s three source roots, the output file, and the ScriptDOM address.
        3. Read the end of the console output: the parse census result, the diagnostics summary and the final BUILD COMPLETE line.

        Watch out

        If you leave out --scriptdom-url, neither builder complains: every SQL statement is parsed by the lexical fallback, which finds fewer tables and columns. When the address is given and the service doesn’t answer, the legacy builder stops with an error unless you add --allow-sql-fallback. The new-UI builder falls back to the lexical parser for each request that fails, and records a diagnostic.

        The options that matter

        OptionBuildersWhat it does
        --source (repeatable)bothA source root; a client normally has three
        --outputbothThe graph file; sidecar files are named after it
        --scriptdom-urlbothThe ScriptDOM service; without it, SQL is parsed lexically
        --parallel, --workers NbothProcess-pool parallelism; --workers defaults to the number of cores, at most 8
        --bundle-sourcebothAlso writes source.zip and source_manifest.json, which the servers use to show source lines
        --baselinebothA diagnostics baseline: expected diagnostics to suppress
        --coverage-baseline, --coverage-drop-thresholdbothCompare node and edge counts with the last accepted build
        --census-fail-threshold, --census-excludebothHow many method bodies may go missing (default 0), and which roots to skip (default NtrackDevEx)
        --incrementalbothRe-parse only files whose hash changed; resolvers still run on the whole graph
        --shard-by-type, --no-schema-validation, --skip-pas, --notesbothSplit output by node type; skip the slow schema check; DFM-only build; free-text notes
        --client, --source-revisionlegacyRecord which client this is (default: from the folder name) and which commit each root was at
        --build-config, --strict-includeslegacyWhich .dproj configuration’s symbols to compile with; fail on a missing {$I} file
        --allow-structural-fallback, --allow-sql-fallback, --allow-unclaimedlegacyBuild anyway when the grammar, ScriptDOM or some source units are missing
        --compare-with, --prettylegacyCompare the new graph with an older one; write indented JSON

        What comes out

        FileContents
        graph_old.json (or graph_full.json)The graph: _metadata, nodes, edges
        graph_old.diag.jsonEvery diagnostic: severity, code, message, file, node (chapter 2.7)
        graph_old.coverage.jsonNode and edge counts per type, and the coverage checks
        graph_old.logThe console log, with a timing line per phase
        graph_old.manifest.jsonPer-file hashes, with --incremental
        source.zip, source_manifest.jsonThe source tree and its hashes, with --bundle-source

        To deploy, these are copied into an instance’s graphs/ folder on the VM and the instance is restarted (chapter 5.4). The server needs the graph, and the source bundle if it should show code; the other files are for people.

        Other commands

        Besides build, both builders offer validate (check a graph file), export-schema, accept-baseline and diff-baseline (manage the diagnostics baseline), accept-coverage-baseline, census, shard, and two debugging commands, parse-dfm and parse-pas, which parse a single file and print what they found. The legacy builder adds compare-graphs (node-by-node comparison of two graphs) and readme-stats.

        Key takeaways

        • Builds run on a laptop with Python 3.11, Git, a C compiler, the .NET 9 SDK and the client’s three source roots.
        • Start ScriptDOM first and always pass --scriptdom-url; without it, SQL is parsed lexically and silently.
