        • A build writes the graph plus sidecars for diagnostics, coverage and the log; only the graph and the source bundle go to the server.

        2.3 Design principles

        The builder’s design document, DESIGN_v2.md, opens with rules it calls “non-negotiable”. Later rounds of work added more, written as comments and tests. Knowing them explains most of the code’s shape, and they are worth reusing in any graph builder.

        The rules, and how each is enforced

        RuleWhat it meansHow the code holds to it
        No regex for structureStructure comes from a grammar: tree-sitter or recursive descent. Regex is allowed only for small lexical jobsCode review: a new regex must be justified as lexical
        Conventions are configurationnGenue’s naming habits (Tfrm, Tdm, nTP) live in one typed Conventions object, not scattered through the codeconventions.py; the legacy builder also fails if a module has no business domain mapped
        Deterministic idsAn id is a pure function of names: same source, same idAll ids come from ids.py; tests check that the same arguments give the same string
        Deterministic outputSame source, byte-identical graphSorted keys, compact JSON, parallel results merged in submission order
        Plug-in extractorsEach concern (PAS, DFM, SQL, each resolver) is its own module with typed inputs and outputsAdding a node type touches the model, one extractor and the schema export
        Schema derived, never writtenThe JSON Schema is generated from the pydantic modelsexport-schema; a test fails if the committed schema drifts
        Diagnostics, not exceptionsBad data (an unparsable file, an unresolved name) becomes a diagnostic; the build carries onA DiagnosticCollector passed everywhere; only error-severity problems change the exit code
        No count decreasesA change may not make any node or edge type smaller unless that drop is declared in advanceexpected_deltas.py and the coverage baseline
        Say what you areEvery graph records who built it, from what, and how_metadata: builder, code hash, grammar commit, client, source revision, build config, features

        One rule that changed: degrade, or fail loudly?

        The original design says that when ScriptDOM is unreachable, the build should not fail but fall back to lexical SQL hints and flag every affected statement. The new-UI builder still works this way.

        The legacy builder later turned this around. Before parsing anything, it checks that the pinned grammar loads, that ScriptDOM answers, and that every source unit is accounted for. If any check fails, it stops with an explanation, unless you pass the matching --allow-… flag. Its comments give the reason: a degraded graph looks complete, so a missing service should be a decision someone makes, not something that happens quietly.

        Key takeaways

        • Grammar-based parsing, deterministic ids and output, and a derived schema are the foundation.
        • Data problems become diagnostics; only structural errors fail a build.
        • The legacy builder refuses to build a quietly degraded graph unless told to.

        2.4 Nodes, edges and ids

        Every tool answer is built from the node and edge types defined in delphi_kg/model/. This chapter is the map: what kinds of nodes exist, how they connect, how ids are formed, and how each node remembers where it came from.

        The 40 node types

        GroupNode typesFound by
        ContainersPROJECT, PACKAGE, MODULE, UNIT, EXTERNAL_UNITDiscovery, the PAS parser, the uses resolver
        TypesCLASS, INTERFACE, RECORD, ENUM, TYPE_ALIAS, CLASS_HELPERThe PAS parser
        MembersMETHOD, PROPERTY, FIELD, CONSTANT, LOCAL_VARIABLE, GLOBAL_VARThe PAS parser and behavioural walkers
        ScreensFORM, FRAME, DATA_MODULE, COMPONENT, EVENT_BINDINGThe DFM extractor
        DataSQL_PLACEHOLDER, COLUMN_REFThe SQL extractor and the column resolver
        BehaviourDATASET_OPERATION, PROPERTY_WRITE, VALIDATION, FIELD_READ, FIELD_WRITE, DATASET_STATE_CHANGE, CONDITION, DIALOG_OPEN, PERMISSION_CHECK, EXCEPTION_BLOCK, DYNAMIC_OBJECT, RUNTIME_BINDING, BATCH_OPERATION, CASE_STATEMENT, TRANSACTION, EXTERNAL_CALLThe behavioural walkers, which read method bodies

        The behavioural types are what make the graph more than a code index. A VALIDATION node records a check and the message it shows; a DATASET_OPERATION records that a method posts, deletes or executes SQL on a particular dataset; a PERMISSION_CHECK records which security right guards an action. Tools like get_action_chain and get_form_behavior are mostly reports over these nodes.

        The 91 edge types, by family

        FamilyExamplesAnswers questions like
        ContainmentHAS_MODULE, HAS_UNIT, HAS_CLASS, HAS_FORM, HAS_METHOD, HAS_COMPONENT, HAS_EVENT_BINDING, HAS_SQLWhat is inside this?
        TypesINHERITS_FROM, IMPLEMENTS, OVERRIDES, HELPER_FOR, FORM_BACKED_BY_CLASS, COMPONENT_INSTANCE_OFWhat does this form inherit? Which override runs?
        DependenciesUSES_INTERFACE, USES_IMPLEMENTATION, MODULE_DEPENDS_ON, REQUIRES_PACKAGEWhich modules depend on this one?
        CallsREFERENCES, INSTANTIATES, REGISTERS_CLASSWho calls this method? What creates this form?
        Screen wiringBINDS_EVENT, BINDS_RUNTIME_HANDLER, ACTION_TRIGGERS_METHOD, CONTAINS_FRAME, LABELS_CONTROL, ENABLED_BY, OPENS_ON_TAB, DIALOG_OPENS_FORMWhat runs when this is clicked? Which label names this field?
        Data wiringDATASOURCE_BINDS_DATASET, CONTROL_BOUND_TO_DATASOURCE, COMPONENT_BINDS_FIELD, CONTROL_BINDS_DATASET_FIELD, MASTER_DETAIL_OF, LOOKUP_FROM, EXECUTES_SQL, MAPS_COLUMNWhich column does this control show? Where does a lookup get its values?
        BehaviourHAS_OPERATION, OPERATION_TARGETS, HAS_VALIDATION, HAS_CONDITION, GUARDS_DELETE, CHECKS_PERMISSION_CONSTANT, READS_GLOBAL_VAR, WRITES_GLOBAL_VAR, BATCH_ITERATESWhat does Save write? What stops a delete?

        Each edge stores two labels, one for each direction: forward_label (HAS_SQL) and reverse_label (SQL_OF). Tools can then describe a relationship naturally from either end.

        How ids are formed

        Every id is built by one module, ids.py, from names alone:

        • Parts are joined with :: because Delphi unit names contain dots (Data.Win.ADODB); a dot can’t tell you where a unit name ends.
        • The type suffix is always last, in capitals, so you can tell a node’s type from its id.
        • Overloaded methods (same name, different parameters) get a short hash of their signature after #.
        • Characters that would break parsing (spaces, tabs, line breaks, /, \, :, #) are replaced with _ using a fixed table; dots stay.
        NodeId
        Module ProspectsProspects::MODULE
        Unit Data.Win.ADODBData.Win.ADODB::UNIT
        Class TfrmProspect in unit fProspectfProspect::TfrmProspect::CLASS
        Method LoadCustomerfProspect::TfrmProspect::LoadCustomer::METHOD
        Two overloads of Save…::Save::METHOD#a1b2c3d4 and …::Save::METHOD#e5f6g7h8
        Form frmProspect: TfrmProspectfProspect::TfrmProspect::FORM
        Component btnSave on that formfProspect::frmProspect::btnSave::COMPONENT
        Its OnClick bindingfProspect::frmProspect::btnSave::OnClick::EVENT_BINDING
        The first SQL statement in LoadCustomerfProspect::TfrmProspect::LoadCustomer::stmt-1::SQL_PLACEHOLDER

        Notice that components are keyed by the form’s instance name (frmProspect), the way the DFM names them, while the form and class use the class name. When a later graph version must change an id, the node keeps its previous one in previous_id for one version.

        Where each node came from

        Most nodes carry a provenance object: the source_file as a path relative to its source root with forward slashes, plus line_start and line_end where they apply. Behavioural nodes add source_line, taken from tree-sitter’s position. These are what let a tool answer “where is this?” and fetch exactly those lines from source.zip.

        No duplicate edges, by rule

        Several extractors can discover the same relationship. Rather than one global rule for what counts as “the same edge”, each edge type declares which properties make two edges different. A call (REFERENCES) at two different places in a method is two edges; the same event bound twice is one.

        Key takeaways

        • 40 node types in six groups; the 16 behavioural types record what method bodies actually do.
        • 91 edge types, each stored with a forward and a reverse label.
        • Ids are readable, stable and built in one place; provenance points back to the exact file and lines.

        2.5 The pipeline, phase by phase

        A build runs as a fixed sequence of phases. The builder logs each one with its duration, so the real logs that ship with the two repositories give an honest picture of where the time goes.

        Real timings

        PhaseLegacy builder, V26 source (28 Oct 2026)New-UI builder, V27 source (4 Nov 2026)
        Discovery1 s: 966 PAS, 666 DFM, 46 modules6 s: 1,027 PAS, 721 DFM, 48 modules
        DFM extraction17 s53 s
        PAS parsing34 s: 966 parsed, 0 failed1 min 29 s: 1,027 parsed, 0 failed
        Parse censusPASS: 1 method body missingFAIL: 252 method bodies missing
        SQL extraction36 s: 5,629 SQL placeholders53 s: 5,882 SQL placeholders
        Resolvers19 s34 s
        Behavioural extractionabout 1 min 44 s2 min 58 s: 168,390 nodes
        Post-behavioural resolvers3 s11 s
        Enabling resolver2 s(legacy builder only)
        Coverage5 s6 s
        Validation and writing1 min 34 s and about 9 sabout 3 min 36 s together
        Source bundle6 s33 s
        Total5 min 34 s: 388,593 nodes, 817,286 edges11 min 25 s: 461,013 nodes, 1,023,575 edges

        Watch out

        The new-UI log shows the parse census failing: 252 method bodies are missing from the syntax trees, and nothing was built for them. The builder records this as an error diagnostic, which makes the exit code non-zero, but still writes the graph. Whether the graph in production came from this build, and which units lost bodies, is worth checking (Part 7).

        1 · Discovery

        Discovery walks each --source root. Every immediate subfolder becomes a MODULE; library folders such as baseforms and ntracklibrary are flagged as libraries. Every .pas becomes a candidate unit, paired with its .dfm. When .dpr, .dproj or .dpk files exist, they add PROJECT and PACKAGE nodes and cross-checks: a unit listed in the project but missing on disk gets a warning. The step also computes a source fingerprint over every file it read, so two graphs can be compared by what they were built from.

        The legacy builder adds two checks here. It works out the client id from the folder name (nGenue TEXICAN-RETAIL becomes TEXICAN-RETAIL). And it refuses to continue if some source units would be left out of every module, unless you pass --allow-unclaimed.

        2 · DFM extraction

        Every form, frame and data module file goes through four steps:

        1. A pre-pass strips the hex-encoded binary blobs (images, icons) that make up much of a DFM’s size. The few forms saved in Delphi’s binary format (the converter’s docstring names three) are converted to text first.
        2. The generator-based tokenizer and the recursive-descent parser from chapter 1.7 build a tree of frozen ObjectIR records.
        3. A translator turns that tree into FORM, FRAME or DATA_MODULE nodes, a COMPONENT per control, an EVENT_BINDING per On… property, and a SQL_PLACEHOLDER for every dataset’s SQL text.
        4. The DFM SQL is left unparsed for now (parsed = None); phase 5 fills it in.

        Frame classes are collected first, so a frame embedded in a form can be recognised as one. With --parallel, files are processed in a worker pool.

        3 · PAS parsing

        Each unit is prepared, parsed and translated:

        • A pre-parser handles what the grammar can’t: it evaluates {$IFDEF} blocks against the project’s conditional symbols (the legacy builder lets you pick the .dproj configuration with --build-config; Debug by default), expands {$I} include files, and patches a few constructs the grammar trips on, such as a bare raise.
        • tree-sitter parses the result into a syntax tree. In a sequential build the trees are kept in memory for the SQL and behavioural phases. In a parallel build each worker process re-parses its unit, because syntax trees can’t be sent between processes.
        • A translator walks the tree and emits UNIT, CLASS, INTERFACE, RECORD, ENUM, METHOD, PROPERTY, FIELD and CONSTANT nodes, plus the uses clauses. It also records with scopes, so later phases know which object a bare name refers to.

        4 · Parse census

        tree-sitter is error-tolerant, which has a hidden cost: after a parse error, the declarations that follow can be swallowed into an ERROR node. The unit still “parses”, but some method bodies silently vanish. The census counts method headers against the method bodies actually found in each tree. By default the build allows zero missing bodies (--census-fail-threshold 0) outside the vendored NtrackDevEx root; above that it records the error census_threshold_exceeded, naming the worst units.

        5 · SQL extraction

        First, a walker finds SQL in method bodies. It recognises five patterns:

        SQL that is built at runtime from variables can’t be known exactly. It is still recorded, with is_dynamic: true and __DYNAMIC__ markers where the unknown parts go, and parsed lexically.

        Then every placeholder, from Pascal and from DFMs, is parsed. With ScriptDOM, statements go in batches of 50. Delphi’s :NAME parameters are sent as @NAME, because T-SQL doesn’t accept the colon form, and are reported back as :NAME. A statement ScriptDOM can’t classify is re-parsed lexically on its own. The result is stored in each node’s parsed field: statement kind, tables, columns, parameters, procedures, the write target and the columns written.

        6 · Resolvers

        Extractors look at one file at a time. Resolvers connect things across files, by name, once everything has been read. The orchestrator runs them in a fixed order, because later ones depend on earlier ones:

        GroupResolvers, in order
        FoundationsVclStub (placeholders for VCL classes), Inheritance, Uses
        FormsDfmMerge (inherited DFMs), InheritedSql, Event, PasDfmLink, ComponentClassLink, InterposerScope (legacy)
        DataDataBinding, MasterDetail, FrameEmbedding, ComponentMetadata
        Labels and gridsLabelLink, TFieldDecode, GridColumnDecode, CaptionFallback, ComponentCollection, ColumnRef, ControlField, Lookup, ServiceUnit
        Calls and messagesCallGraph, WMMessageRouting, DocComment

        A resolver that can’t decide never guesses silently. When an ancestor class matches several candidates, the resolver picks one, lists all of them, and records multi_candidate_ancestor. A class whose ancestor lies outside the source (most VCL classes) gets an unresolved_ancestor diagnostic at info level, because that is expected.

        7 · Behavioural extraction

        Eighteen walkers read every method body’s syntax tree and record what the code does: DatasetOperation, PropertyWrite, Validation, FieldRead, FieldWrite, InheritedCall, DatasetStateChange, Condition, DialogOpen, PermissionCheck, ExceptionBlock, DynamicObject, RuntimeBinding, LocalVariable, Case, BatchOperation, Transaction and ExternalCall. This is the longest phase: in the new-UI build it produced 168,390 nodes, over a third of the graph. With --parallel it runs unit by unit in worker processes, and results are merged in submission order to stay deterministic (chapter 1.2).

        8 · Post-behavioural and enabling resolvers

        A second round of resolvers works on what the walkers found. Examples: SaveChain (what a save path writes), TabLoadChain (datasets opened when a tab is shown), NavigationLink and, in the legacy builder, DialogTarget (which screen opens which), PermissionConstant (which security right a check uses), GlobalVarAccess, ModuleCoupling, SqlLinkage and CodeSqlLink, ParamResolution, DeadCode and BatchIterates. The legacy builder then runs the enabling resolver, which works out which checkbox enables which input. On legacy screens a filter is often drawn as [x] Filter by Date [start] to [end], so only the checkbox carries the words a user would search for.

        9 · Coverage

        Coverage is the build checking itself for silent losses. It runs three checks against the finished graph:

        1. Population diff: every node and edge type’s count is compared with the last accepted build (the coverage baseline). A drop to zero is an error; a drop beyond the threshold is a warning.
        2. Classifier fall-through audit: for each classifier with a default bucket, the most common labels that landed in that bucket are listed. The docstring’s example: 3,695 TntpADOQuery components classed as plain UI controls.
        3. Zero-instance report: every node and edge type with no instances at all is listed.

        10 · Validation

        Two kinds of check run before anything is written. Structural checks are mechanical: every edge’s ends exist, no two nodes share an id, there are no inheritance cycles, and no Delphi id suffix overlaps a SQL one. Semantic checks look for things that are probably wrong: an override with no method to override, an event handler whose signature doesn’t match its event, an event bound to a handler that can’t be found. Then the whole graph is validated against graph.schema.json. That step is thorough and slow, 1 min 34 s for V26, and can be skipped with --no-schema-validation.

        11 · Writing

        The graph is written as compact, key-sorted JSON (about a quarter smaller than indented JSON), followed by the diagnostics and coverage sidecars and, with --bundle-source, source.zip. The zip’s entry names are exactly the graph’s source_file values, so the server can open any node’s file with no path translation.

        Key takeaways

        • Read (discovery, DFM, PAS, SQL), connect (resolvers), observe behaviour (walkers), then check (census, coverage, validation) and write.
        • Behavioural extraction and validation take most of the time; a legacy client builds in under six minutes.
        • The build reports its own silent losses: missing method bodies, count drops, things that fell into a default bucket.

        2.6 The ScriptDOM service

        Every SQL statement found in Delphi code is parsed by Microsoft’s own T-SQL parser, ScriptDOM, the parser SQL Server’s tools are built on. ScriptDOM is a .NET library, and Python can’t load it directly, so delphi-scriptdom wraps it in a small local web service that the builders call over HTTP.

        What it is

        • An ASP.NET Core application for .NET 9, using the NuGet package Microsoft.SqlServer.TransactSql.ScriptDom (version 161.*).
        • It listens on http://127.0.0.1:5235, the local machine only, and is started by start.bat, which checks for the .NET SDK, restores packages and runs the project.
        • It runs on the developer’s laptop, only while a build runs. The MCP servers never call it.

        Its two endpoints

        EndpointPurpose
        GET /healthLiveness: the service name, its status and its parser version. The legacy builder calls it before a build starts.
        POST /parseParse a list of statements and return one result per statement, in the same order

        Inside the service

        1. Split on GO. GO isn’t T-SQL; it is a batch separator understood by tools. The text is split into batches first, remembering each batch’s starting line.
        2. Parse each batch with TSql150Parser (SQL Server 2019 syntax), with quoted identifiers on. Syntax errors are counted into parse_errors; above zero, the result may be partial.
        3. Walk the tree with the DmlVisitor from chapter 1.7. It records the statement kind (the outermost one wins), table references with their aliases, column references, variables and parameters, executed procedures, and for writes the target table and the columns assigned.
        4. Resolve aliases at the end, so that in UPDATE e SET … FROM ENDUSER e the write target is reported as ENDUSER, not e.

        How the builders call it

        • Each request carries up to 50 statements and waits at most 5 seconds.
        • A failed request is retried after a pause. If it still fails, those statements are parsed lexically and a diagnostic says so.
        • The backend counts what it did (statements sent, parameters rewritten, unknown statements re-parsed, requests retried and failed) and the counts go into the build diagnostics, so a weak SQL parse is visible after the fact.

        Why it’s built this way

        T-SQL is large and full of special cases; a home-made parser would quietly miss tables in complex statements. Calling Microsoft’s parser makes table and column extraction as reliable as SQL Server’s own tools, at the cost of one small service to start before each build. The lexical fallback keeps a build possible without it, clearly labelled as hints.

        Key takeaways

        • ScriptDOM is Microsoft’s T-SQL parser, wrapped in a .NET 9 service on 127.0.0.1:5235, used only at build time.
        • It splits on GO, parses with SQL Server 2019 syntax and reports kind, tables, columns, parameters, procedures and write targets.
        • The builders send batches of 50, rewrite Delphi parameters, retry, and fall back visibly.

        2.7 Diagnostics, baselines and tests

        A graph that is quietly wrong is worse than no graph, because the AI will repeat its mistakes confidently. The builders therefore spend a lot of effort reporting on themselves. This chapter covers the reports and how to use them.

        The diagnostics sidecar

        Everything worth knowing about a build’s data quality goes into <output>.diag.json: a summary and a list.

        SeverityMeaningExamples
        infoExpected; recorded for completenessunresolved_ancestor for a VCL class, external_uses for a VCL unit
        warnProbably worth a lookmulti_candidate_ancestor, unresolved_event_handler, scriptdom_unreachable
        errorThe graph is structurally wrong, or a gate failedorphan_edge_target, an id collision, census_threshold_exceeded

        The exit code is 0 when there are no error-severity diagnostics and 1 when there is at least one; warnings and infos never change it. A real codebase produces thousands of diagnostics, so each code is capped at 50 listed instances per build, with the rest counted in the summary.

        Baselines: only show what’s new

        Two kinds of baseline keep the noise down, so a reviewer only has to look at what changed:

        • The diagnostics baseline (diagnostics_baseline.json). After reviewing a build, an engineer accepts its expected diagnostics with accept-baseline. Later builds given --baseline suppress those and surface only new ones; diff-baseline shows the difference. The baseline is meant to be committed, so accepting one is reviewed like code.
        • The coverage baseline: per-type node and edge counts from the last accepted build (accept-coverage-baseline). The coverage phase compares against it (chapter 2.5). The legacy builder keeps one entry per client, keyed by the client id.

        A third mechanism makes “no count decreases” workable: expected_deltas.py, where a change declares in advance which counts it will move and why. A drop that isn’t declared is treated as a regression.

        Comparing two graphs

        The legacy builder’s compare-graphs command (and build --compare-with) compares two graphs node by node and edge by edge. Each node becomes a fingerprint of all its fields, keyed by collection and id; edges are compared as counted fingerprints. It reads one graph at a time to save memory, and ignores _metadata, because build times always differ. It is the quickest way to answer “what did this change actually change?”.

        Tests

        RepositoryTest filesTests
        delphi-kg_old_UI (legacy builder)1542,160 test functions
        delphi-kg (new-UI builder)971,784 test functions
        ngenue_mcp_legacy (server)1012,377 tests collected by pytest
        ngenue_mcp (server)17588 tests collected by pytest

        Run them from a repository folder with python -m pytest -q (the builders set testpaths = ["tests"]). The builder tests use small fixture files, including real DFMs under tests/fixtures/, and check things like id determinism, schema drift, census behaviour and each resolver. The builder figures count test functions; parametrised tests run more cases. Chapter 3.13 covers the server tests, including a real run.

        Key takeaways

        • Every build writes a diagnostics sidecar; only error-severity items make the exit code non-zero.
        • Diagnostics and coverage baselines, plus declared expected deltas, mean a reviewer looks only at what changed.
        • About 3,900 builder test functions and almost 3,000 server tests guard the code.

        2.8 The legacy fork

        There are two builders because there are two products: the legacy nTrack UI, which each of ten clients runs in its own version, and the new UI. delphi-kg_old_UI began as a copy of delphi-kg and was then hardened for building many client graphs. Most of the code is still shared, and the differences are mostly about safety and record-keeping.

        What differs

        Legacy builder (delphi-kg_old_UI)New-UI builder (delphi-kg)
        Distributed asdelphi-kg-legacy 0.6.0delphi-kg 0.5.2
        Outputgraph_old.json, one per clientgraph_full.json
        Pascal grammarPinned to one commit by a lock fileCloned at its latest commit on first use, then cached
        Missing grammar, ScriptDOM or unitsStops, unless an --allow-… flag is givenDegrades and records diagnostics
        Stamps in _metadataBuilder name, version and code hash; client; source revisions; build config; features; allowed valuesFewer
        Extra build options--client, --source-revision, --build-config, --strict-includes, --compare-with, --pretty, three --allow-… flagsnone
        Modules only herebuilder_info, client_id, compare_graphs, conventions_checks, grammar_pin, with_rekey; resolvers dialog_target, interposer_scope, source_textresolver registered_classes
        Tests2,1601,784

        Why the legacy differences exist

        Each legacy-only piece fixes a problem an audit found, and the docstrings name it:

        • Which builder made this graph? Both builders install a package named delphi_kg and both used to be called delphi-kg 0.5.2, so a legacy client could be built with the new UI’s code and nothing in the graph would show it. builder_info now stamps the builder’s identity and a hash of its code into every graph.
        • Which client is this? The client used to live only in free-text --notes, copy-pasted between builds. client_id derives it from the source folder and stores it in _metadata.source.client, where it also keys the coverage baseline.
        • Can the server rely on it? contract.py ships the values the builder may write into certain fields (_metadata.allowed_values) and a list of features the graph carries. The legacy server checks them at start-up and refuses to start on a value it doesn’t handle, instead of letting a feature go quietly empty.
        • Same source, same graph. Pinning the grammar (grammar_pin) means a graph changes only when code or source changes. with_rekey makes a parallel build produce exactly what a sequential one does.
        • Commented-out code isn’t code. source_text removes comments and string contents before pattern-based resolvers read a body. Its example is a line in V26 that reads //gridBadInvoices.DataSource := dsGenInvoices; one line above the assignment that actually runs.

        Watch out

        The new-UI builder clones the Pascal grammar’s latest commit the first time it runs on a machine. Two laptops that first built on different dates can therefore parse the same source differently, and nothing in the graph records which grammar was used. The census failure in the new-UI log (chapter 2.5) is the kind of symptom that drift can cause. Porting the grammar pin from the legacy builder is a small, valuable change (Part 7).

        Key takeaways

        • The legacy builder is the hardened fork: pinned grammar, fail-loudly guards, identity and client stamps, a contract with the server.
        • The new-UI builder is simpler and degrades quietly; its unpinned grammar is the most important gap.

        2.9 The other graph files

        A server instance reads more than the Delphi graph. Each file below sits in the instance’s graphs/ folder and is named in its .env. The sizes are those of the copies shipped with the legacy server repository, in decimal megabytes as /health reports them.

        FileSizeWhat it holdsRead by
        graph_old.json / graph_full.json471 MBThe Delphi graph (this Part)Most tools, through DelphiIndex
        database_graph.json172 MBThe SQL graph: the database’s objects and their relationshipsSQL tools, through SqlIndex
        code_flows/2,100 files, 194 MBOne file per procedure, function or trigger: its step-by-step flowFlow tools, through CodeFlowIndex
        data_dictionary.json6.4 MB12,135 plain-English descriptions of tables and columnsDescription and dictionary tools
        retail_graph.json0.1 MBThe business workflow: 20 workflow steps and which documents describe eachWorkflow and documentation tools
        source.zip, source_manifest.json15 MBThe Delphi source, entry names matching the graph’s source_file valuesget_source_slice and source previews

        The SQL graph, code flows, data dictionary and workflow graph are produced outside the four repositories in this handbook. This handbook describes their contents and how the servers use them, not how they are built.

        The SQL graph

        database_graph.json uses the same envelope as the Delphi graph (_metadata, nodes, edges), plus join_cliques. Its metadata records the source database and builder. The shipped copy holds:

        NodesEdges
        tables 683, views 1, procedures 1,617, functions 193, triggers 289, columns 9,382, temp_columns 12,441, indexes 965, users 40, roles 13has_column, has_index, index_covers, foreign_key, fk_column_link, uses_table (12,021), calls (4,611), triggers_on, fires_into, references_column (62,383), column_fires_trigger, trigger_reads_column, view_column_source, member_of, has_permission, mined_join

        Its ids use dots (dbo.ENDUSER.TABLE), so they can never collide with Delphi ids (chapter 1.8). Procedure nodes carry their data flows (tables read and written, temp tables, parameters), which tools such as get_data_flow_summary and trace_table_write_chain report on.

        Code flows

        Each file in code_flows/, named <schema>.<name>.json, breaks one database object into ordered blocks.

        Each block knows its parent, its branch, the conditions it runs under, and whether it sits in a TRY, a CATCH, a transaction or a loop. Tools such as get_procedure_flow, get_conditional_branches and get_error_handling_surface read these.

        The data dictionary

        data_dictionary.json is one flat object with 12,135 entries keyed table:dbo.ENDUSER or column:ENDUSER|ACCOUNTINGGROUP. Each entry has a kind and a plain-English desc, such as: “A retail gas customer account that holds the contract with a local distribution company (LDC)…”. These descriptions are what let the AI explain a table in business terms instead of guessing from its name.

        The workflow graph

        retail_graph.json describes the business process the software supports: 20 workflow nodes with ids such as wholesale::pre-workflow, each with a title, type and summary, plus file_to_node_map, which says which documentation file belongs to which step. The documentation tools use it to search “the step before or after this one” (search_adjacent_docs) and to place an answer in the overall workflow (get_workflow_context).

        And one store that isn’t a file

        The documentation chunks live in Qdrant, in the shared collection adaptive_chunks (chapter 1.9). Each point’s payload carries the chunk text, its file_name, and for split sections is_adaptive_split and original_section_id.

        The legacy server repository also ships database_schema.json (140 MB), a raw export of the database’s schema whose header names the database nGenueMainlineQA_UX. No server code reads it; it looks like an input to the SQL graph builder that was copied along with the graphs.

        Key takeaways

        • Each instance reads six kinds of data: Delphi graph, SQL graph, code flows, data dictionary, workflow graph and source bundle, plus Qdrant for documents.
        • The SQL graph and code flows describe the database side; the dictionary and workflow graph add business meaning.
        • Only the Delphi graph and the source bundle are produced by the repositories this handbook covers.

        Part 3

        Serving the graphs

        Inside the two MCP servers: start-up, the hand-written protocol layer, the tool contract, the in-memory indexes, documentation search, live SQL and every tool family, with real calls.

          How the examples in this Part were made

          To show real behaviour, not just code, I ran the legacy server locally against the graphs shipped in its repository: AEP’s Delphi graph (version 2.5, 471 MB) and the SQL graph beside it. The test machine was a 4 GB Linux container, with sign-in switched off, no documentation search, no live SQL and no code flows. Every start-up line, answer, size and timing quoted below comes from that run. Timings on the VM will differ.

          3.1 Repository tour

          The two server repositories, ngenue_mcp_legacy and ngenue_mcp, share one architecture and most of their core code. This tour follows the legacy repository; chapter 3.12 lists where the new-UI server differs.

          The layout

          Four layers

          It helps to read the code as four layers, each knowing as little as possible about the others:

          1. Transport (server/app.py, auth/): HTTP, sign-in, JSON-RPC envelopes, status codes. Knows nothing about Delphi.
          2. Protocol (server/handler.py, server/registry.py): MCP methods, protocol versions, tool definitions, threads and timeouts, structured answers. Knows nothing about Delphi either. The same core could serve any tool set.
          3. Loader (loaders/ngenue.py): the nGenue-specific start-up. It loads the graphs, connects the optional services, discovers the tools and builds the instructions.
          4. Tools and indexes (tools/): everything that knows what a form, a dataset or a stored procedure is.

          The seam between layers 2 and 3 is one setting, LOADER_MODULE. server/app.py imports whatever module it names and calls its load_and_register(registry).

          The 24 tool categories

          CategoryToolsCategoryTools
          discovery16sql5
          code13object_detail5
          form12maintenance5
          cross_unit12impact_tracing5
          diagnostic9cross_boundary5
          sql_schema7sql_behavior4
          code_flow7data_binding4
          behavioral7sql_search, sql_discovery, data_dictionary3 each
          docs6sql_bridge, meta2 each
          cross_graph, corpus_scan6 eachsql_live1

          That is 148 tools. Two are asynchronous on purpose (sql_query and get_menu_path, which run live SQL). Four documentation tools run on their own thread pool. Fourteen declare an output schema and so also send a structured copy of their answer. Chapter 3.9 walks through what each family is for.

          Files worth knowing early

          • loaders/tool_manifest.txt: the list of tools this server must serve. Start-up fails if a listed tool is missing, which almost always means a tool file failed to import.
          • scripts/mcp_harness.py: calls tools in-process, without HTTP, the same way the server does. It is the fastest way to try a tool against a graph.
          • mcp-inspector.json: point MCP Inspector, the protocol’s official debugging client, at a local server.
          • README.md: the operator’s notes: how to update code on an instance, how to replace a graph, what to check after a deployment. Part 5 builds on it.

          Key takeaways

          • Transport and protocol code know nothing about Delphi; one loader setting connects them to the nGenue tools.
          • 148 tools in 24 categories, one folder each, checked against a manifest at start-up.
          • Indexes (the graphs in memory) and tools (questions over them) live together under tools/.

          3.2 Start-up, step by step

          A server spends most of its life answering in milliseconds, because it does all its heavy work once, at start-up. This chapter follows one start-up from the command to the first request, using the real log of the test run.

          The sequence

          1. The process starts. NSSM runs python -m server.app in the instance folder. Importing server/app.py builds ServerConfig, which reads .env through python-dotenv, and configures logging.
          2. uvicorn starts and runs the FastAPI lifespan (chapter 1.1) before it opens the port. Until start-up finishes, connections are refused; in the test run, /health began answering after about 20 seconds.
          3. The configuration is validated. An invalid one ends the process at once with an exact exit code (_fatal_exit). AUTH_MODE=none is allowed but logged as a warning.
          4. The loader is imported by name (LOADER_MODULE=loaders.ngenue) and its load_and_register(registry) is awaited.
          5. Required paths are checked. A missing Delphi graph, SQL graph or tools folder stops start-up with a clear message.
          6. Memory is checked. Free memory is compared with an estimate based on the graph file sizes. A shortfall is logged, not fatal.
          7. The Delphi graph is loaded on a worker thread: json.load, version and contract checks, then the lookup indexes (chapter 3.6).
          8. A self-check runs on a sample of label-to-control links, comparing the graph’s answer with the vendored scorer.
          9. The SQL graph, data dictionary and workflow graph are loaded. The code-flow index is opened lazily: it reads a procedure’s file only when asked.
          10. Documentation search is connected only if all four of its settings are present (chapter 1.9). Otherwise its tools will answer “not available”.
          11. The source bundle is opened and a sample of files is checked against the manifest’s hashes.
          12. The instance works out who it is: the client, the graph versions and a hash of its own code, reported in one line and in /health.
          13. Cross-graph links are built: every SQL object named in Delphi code is resolved against the SQL graph (chapter 3.6).
          14. Tools are discovered and registered, then checked against tool_manifest.txt. A listed tool that no file provides is fatal.
          15. The instructions are loaded and prefixed with the identity line, and a drift check compares them with the served tools.
          16. Live SQL’s permission self-check starts in the background, when a connection string is configured (chapter 3.8).
          17. The handler is created with the instructions, and uvicorn starts accepting connections.

          The real log

          Three things stand out. Loading the Delphi graph is most of the start-up: about 9 seconds to parse the JSON and 5 more to build the caption and label indexes. Everything else together takes under 5 seconds. And the process settled at about 1.8 GB of memory, well under the start-up estimate of about 3 GB, which is deliberately cautious.

          Watch out

          In the copy shipped with the repository, the AEP instance’s SQL graph was built from the database nGenueMainlineQA_UX, not from an AEP database, and the Delphi graph (version 2.5) predates the builder’s identity stamps. The cross-graph code says each client should pair its Delphi graph with its own SQL graph. The production instances may well be different. /health shows each instance’s pairing, and it is worth checking all eleven (Part 7).

          What /health reports

          After start-up, GET /health answers with what is actually loaded: the tool count, the client, a code build id and a hash of the tool manifest; the graph’s file, size, version, build date and counts, and the scorer self-check result; the SQL graph’s version and source database; the cross-graph link statistics; and the state of live SQL. Its status is healthy when everything is in order and degraded when a problem was found after start-up, such as a source file whose hash doesn’t match. The code also has a starting answer (HTTP 503) for a request that arrives before the loader is done, though uvicorn normally keeps the port closed until then. Chapter 5.6 shows how to use it when something goes wrong.

          When start-up fails

          ProblemWhat happens
          Invalid configuration, missing graph or tools folderFatal: the process exits with a message (and NSSM, if set to restart, tries again)
          A graph from another product line, or an unreadable versionFatal, with a message naming the builder to use
          A tool in the manifest that no file providesFatal: a tool file probably failed to import (look for tool_load_failed)
          Source bundle doesn’t match the graphFatal with SOURCE_BUNDLE_STRICT=on; otherwise a warning, served anyway
          Only some documentation-search settings presentWarning; documentation search is switched off
          Less free memory than estimatedWarning only
          A served tool missing from the manifest, instructions out of step with the toolsWarning

          Key takeaways

          • All the heavy work happens once: about 19 seconds for AEP in the test run, mostly loading the Delphi graph.
          • Each step logs one clear line, and /health reports what was actually loaded.
          • Anything that would make answers wrong stops start-up; anything optional degrades with a warning.

          3.3 The protocol layer

          The servers implement MCP themselves, without an SDK. That makes the protocol code short enough to read in an afternoon. This chapter follows a request through it and shows real exchanges with the test server.

          The MCP endpoint

          Every MCP message arrives at POST /mcp, the function mcp_endpoint in server/app.py. It does five things, in order:

          1. Refuses to work before start-up has finished (-32603, “Server not initialized”).
          2. Requires Content-Type: application/json and parseable JSON (-32700 otherwise).
          3. Reads the MCP-Protocol-Version header, so it can be copied into the message’s _meta if the client only sent it there.
          4. Handles a single message, or a JSON array of them concurrently with asyncio.gather.
          5. Sends the answer with the HTTP status from the table in chapter 1.4 and the header MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28. A request made only of notifications gets 204.

          Each message goes through _process_one. A message with no id is a notification and gets no answer. Otherwise it must say "jsonrpc": "2.0" and name a method. The method is then routed to the handler, and the handler’s result is wrapped in a JSON-RPC response.

          The handler’s method table

          MCPHandler in server/handler.py maps each method name to one function. It keeps no per-client state: every call stands alone.

          MethodWhat it returns here
          server/discoverSupported versions, capabilities, server info, the instructions; cacheable for an hour
          initializeThe older handshake: the negotiated version, capabilities, server info, the instructions
          tools/listAll 148 tool definitions; cacheable for 5 minutes
          tools/callOne tool’s answer (chapters 3.4 and 3.5)
          resources/list, resources/read, resources/templates/listSupported by the core, but the nGenue loader registers none
          prompts/list, prompts/getLikewise: none registered

          Before any method except server/discover and initialize, the handler checks the protocol version in _meta (chapter 1.5) and logs the client’s name and version if the client sent them.

          Real exchanges

          These are the test server’s actual answers, cut where long:

          Protocol errors, as they really come back

          RequestHTTPAnswer
          Body that isn’t JSON400-32700 “Parse error: invalid JSON”
          Method tools/explode400-32601 “Method not found: tools/explode”
          Tool get_frm_overview (misspelt)400-32602 “Unknown tool: get_frm_overview”, with the 148 valid names in data.available
          _meta version 2023-01-01400-32022 “UnsupportedProtocolVersionError”, with the five supported versions
          Only a notification (notifications/initialized)204No body
          GET /mcp405“Method Not Allowed”
          ping400-32601 “Method not found: ping”

          Watch out

          The last row is a gap. MCP defines ping as a basic method that any side may send to check that the other is alive, and the answer should be an empty result. These servers don’t implement it. The clients in use today don’t appear to depend on it, but a client or monitor that pings would see an error. Adding a one-line handler is a quick fix (Part 7).

          Key takeaways

          • One endpoint, one function per method, no session: the whole protocol layer is a few hundred readable lines.
          • Version handling, batches and notifications follow the published protocol; the servers answer both the stateless and the handshake era.
          • Errors come back with JSON-RPC codes and fitting HTTP statuses; ping is the one standard method missing.

          3.4 The registry and the tool contract

          Between the protocol and the tools sits a small contract: what a tool must declare, what it receives, what it returns, and what happens around it on every call. Knowing this contract is enough to read any of the 148 tools, or to write a new one.

          The registry

          Registry in server/registry.py holds MCP’s three kinds of things: tools, resources and prompts. Each tool is wrapped in a ToolEntry, which turns the tool’s class attributes into its tools/list definition (to_mcp()), runs it on the right thread within the time limit, and builds the structured copy of the answer. The registry also reports the server’s capabilities: here only {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}, because no resources or prompts are registered.

          What a tool declares

          AttributePurpose
          name, descriptionWhat the model sees. The description says what the tool returns, what it needs, and which state it sets
          input_schemaThe tool’s own arguments, as JSON Schema
          required_state, optional_stateState fields it needs or reads (active_form, sql_context…); their schemas are added to the published input schema automatically
          output_stateState fields it sets in its STATE UPDATES trailer
          output_schemaOptional: the answer’s shape; when set, the answer is also sent as checked structuredContent
          annotations, titleFilled in by BaseTool (read-only, idempotent, closed-world, not destructive) unless the tool sets its own
          response_token_budgetOptional: a different size budget for this tool’s answers
          run_in_thread, thread_poolOptional: run on a dedicated pool (the documentation tools use one)
          deprecatedMarks an old tool kept for compatibility

          And one method, execute(args, deps), which gets checked arguments plus the shared ToolDeps (the indexes and services from chapter 1.1) and returns a ToolResult. A tool may also override validate() for extra argument rules.

          What a tool returns

          ToolResult in tools/models.py has three fields that matter: content (the answer, usually a dict), state_updates (values the model should pass back on later calls) and error (a message, or None). Its to_mcp_text() builds the text the model reads:

          1. The content as indented JSON, or, for an error, {"error": …} plus any partial content, such as “did you mean” candidates.
          2. A trailer headed ─── STATE UPDATES (pass these as parameters to subsequent tool calls) ───, one line per value, with list counts in _counts.
          3. The hard size cap: text over 80,000 characters is cut at a line break, with a notice and a cursor for get_more_results.

          What happens around every call

          Two details make this robust. Every path, the HTTP server and in-process callers such as tests and scripts/mcp_harness.py alike, goes through mcp_execute, so the checks can’t be skipped. And argument checking is generous where it is safe: "25" becomes 25 for an integer argument, and a screen may be named by its node id, class name, unit name or caption. Where it isn’t safe, it is strict: a misspelt parameter or an empty search term is an error that says what to do next, never an empty result the model could report as fact.

          Key takeaways

          • A tool is a class: a name, a description, schemas, state declarations and one execute method.
          • Every call runs the same pipeline: validate, resolve names, execute on a thread within 90 s, trim, add the state trailer, cap.
          • Failures become readable error answers; the model is never handed a silent empty result.

          3.5 Anatomy of a tool, with real calls

          This chapter reads one real tool and then follows the calls a model would make to answer “what happens when I click Save on the End User screen?”, against the AEP graph in the test run.

          One tool, start to finish

          get_form_overview lives in tools/tools/form/get_form_overview/tool.py (176 lines):

          The pattern is typical: no database, no network, only dictionary lookups and short walks over the indexes. Almost every tool (145 of 148) also has a build_section() method that renders the same result as Markdown, for reports built outside MCP.

          Following a question through real calls

          1. Find the screen. The model doesn’t know ids, so it searches by words.

          The best match is an exact caption match. The trailer hands the model the id it needs next. This tool has an output schema, so the answer also carried a checked structuredContent copy.

          1. Get the shape of the screen. The model passes active_form back.

          One screen: 571 components, 208 methods, 153 event bindings, 48 of them inherited from the base add/edit form, and 20 SQL statements. This is why the answers are built from a graph and not by reading files.

          1. Trace the action.

          In 51 milliseconds the tool found that Save is an action (actSave in the action list actBaseAddEdit) wired to sbtnSaveClick. It followed the calls without hitting its limits (chain_truncated: false) and collected 19 dataset operations, 16 validations and 2 permission checks. The SQL statements reached travel on in sql_context, so a later call doesn’t repeat them (chapter 6.2).

          Three ways an answer is kept small, seen live

          • Paging, built into tools with long lists. get_form_components on this screen (4 ms) returned "total": 571, "shown": 50, "truncated": true, "next_offset": 50: the first page of 50, with complete counts and a way to read on.
          • The token budget (first pass, about 16,000 tokens). find_dead_methods across the whole graph (57 ms, 59,398 characters) came back trimmed, and its note said: “Answer trimmed to fit the size limit (about 16,000 tokens; it was about 30,839): dead_methods shows 97 of 200. To see more: ask for the next page with offset (next_offset where shown); pass limit to choose the page size; narrow the question with module_filter, category.”
          • The hard cap (second pass, 80,000 characters, state trailer included). The rest of the text is kept in memory behind a one-time cursor valid for 30 minutes, and get_more_results(cursor) returns the next part. None of the test calls was large enough to trigger it.

          Chapter 6.3 explains why there are two passes and what each guarantees.

          Tool errors, seen live

          CallWhat came back (HTTP 200, isError: true)
          get_form_overview with no argumentsValidation failed: Tool 'get_form_overview' requires 'active_form'. Call the appropriate discovery tool first to obtain it.
          get_form_overview with active_form: "Customer Maintenance"Screen 'Customer Maintenance' was not found in the graph. Did you mean: CustomerUnit::TCustomerForm::FORM; fServiceScreen::TfrmServiceScreen::FORM; …?

          Both tell the model exactly what to do next: call a discovery tool, or pick one of the candidates. Chapter 6.5 follows what the model does with them.

          One log line per call

          Key takeaways

          • A tool is a short class that walks the in-memory indexes; real calls take a few to a few dozen milliseconds.
          • The STATE UPDATES trailer carries ids from one call to the next; the model passes them back as arguments.
          • Paging, the token budget and the hard cap keep answers readable, and each one says how to get the rest.

          3.6 The in-memory indexes

          The answers in chapter 3.5 took milliseconds because every question is a lookup in structures built at start-up. This chapter describes those structures, in tools/tools/indexes/.

          The indexes

          IndexReadsIn the test run
          DelphiIndexgraph_old.json14.2 s; 357,297 nodes, 746,237 edges; most of the 1.8 GB process
          SqlIndexdatabase_graph.json4.1 s; 683 tables, 1,616 procedures, 289 triggers, 193 functions
          CodeFlowIndexcode_flows/Lazy: reads one procedure’s file when a tool asks for it
          DataDictionaryIndexdata_dictionary.json0.1 s; 12,134 entries (one malformed entry skipped)
          WorkflowIndexretail_graph.json20 workflow nodes, 140 document mappings
          SourceBundlesource.zip + manifest1,544 files; opened once, each file hash-checked on first read
          Cross-graph linksboth graphsBuilt at start-up; 97.2 % of 7,208 references resolved

          DelphiIndex

          DelphiIndex (2,388 lines) loads the graph with one json.load and then fills 69 attributes, most of them lookup structures, served through 101 methods. They fall into a few groups:

          GroupStructuresUsed for
          The graphnodes_by_id, nodes_by_type, adj_out, adj_in, edges_by_typeEvery lookup and walk (chapter 1.8)
          Structureform_registry, unit_registry, module_registry, class_registry, unit_to_module, form_to_unit, method_to_class, class_to_form, frame_embeds“Which unit is this form in?”, “which form does this class back?”
          Searchmethod_name_index, validation_text_index, method_body_nodes, caption_registry, caption_words, display_label_registry, hint_registry, snippetsFinding things by the words people use
          Datatable_to_placeholders, column_to_fields, component_binds_field_index, dataset_field_col_index, permission_check_by_name“Which screens use this table or column?”
          Screen meaninglabel_links, labeled_by, enabled_by, enables, paired_with, component_root, derived names“Which field is ‘Filter by Date’?”
          Quality flagsdead_methods, unreferenced_methods, memory_leak_candidates, unreachable_componentsMaintenance and diagnostic tools

          The start-up log gives the size of the screen-meaning indexes for AEP: 73,046 snippets, 72,421 component roots, 8,965 captions, 2,435 caption words, 3,739 label links and 3,834 labelled controls. Building them is the five seconds after the JSON is parsed.

          Which graphs the server accepts

          Before building anything, DelphiIndex checks the graph’s _metadata:

          • Version. The legacy server knows versions 2.3 to 2.11 and 3.0. A newer minor version of a known major loads with a warning; an unreadable version is refused.
          • Line. A graph stamped for another product line is refused with a message naming the right builder. Versions 2.3 to 2.5 predate the line stamp and are accepted unstamped.
          • Contract. The values the graph declares in allowed_values are compared with the values the server handles. Anything unknown becomes a logged contract warning rather than a feature that silently returns nothing.

          Tools then adapt to what a graph carries. In the test run, find_dead_methods added this note, because AEP’s graph is version 2.5: “This graph is older than 2.11: is_dead_code and has_no_resolved_callers are the same set…”. Older graphs still work, with answers that say what they can’t tell apart.

          SqlIndex and the smaller indexes

          • SqlIndex reads SQL graphs of major version 5 (the test graph is 5.2) and refuses others. Its 37 public methods find tables, procedures, triggers and functions by name, and answer about columns, indexes, foreign keys in both directions, callers and callees, triggers fired by a column, permissions, join cliques and mined join paths.
          • CodeFlowIndex is lazy: get_flow() opens one procedure’s JSON when a code-flow tool asks for it. That is why 194 MB of flows cost nothing at start-up.
          • DataDictionaryIndex looks up a table, column or object description and searches them by words.
          • WorkflowIndex knows each workflow step, which documents belong to it, and the steps before and after it.

          Cross-graph links

          Delphi code names SQL objects every way T-SQL allows: ENDUSER, dbo.ENDUSER, [dbo].[EndUser], "EndUser", nGenue.dbo.ENDUSER, LSP_X;1. At start-up, every table, view, procedure and function named in a SQL placeholder is normalised to its bare upper-case name and looked up in the SQL graph. Each reference ends up with a status: resolved, not_in_sql_graph, system_object, cte or a temporary table.

          In the test run: 4,924 placeholders named SQL objects; 7,208 references, of which 6,999 (97.2 %) resolved to 973 distinct objects; 115 names weren’t in the SQL graph, the most common being the procedure LSP_PRICING_FILL_DROPDOWN, named by 28 placeholders. Tools report these honestly. The playbook tells the model to say such an object’s SQL side is unknown, never that it doesn’t exist.

          Memory, and why many threads can share it

          The test process settled at 1.8 GB of memory with a 471 MB Delphi graph and a 172 MB SQL graph, and the whole machine showed about 2.4 GB in use at the busiest moment sampled during loading. Part 5 turns this into a sizing rule for the VM. The indexes are built once and only read afterwards. Tools never change them, which is what lets many tools run at once on different threads without locks (chapter 1.2).

          Key takeaways

          • One graph file becomes dozens of dictionaries, so tools answer with lookups instead of searches.
          • The server checks each graph’s version, line and contract before trusting it, and tools adapt to older graphs.
          • Indexes are read-only after start-up: safe to share between threads, and replaced only by a restart with new files.

          3.7 Documentation search

          The graph knows what the code does; the documentation knows why, and how people use it. Six tools search nGenue’s product documentation. Chapter 1.9 explained the techniques (embeddings, Qdrant, reranking); this chapter is about the tools, their data and how they behave.

          The six tools

          ToolWhat it doesKey arguments
          search_docsSearch by meaning: embed the question, fetch candidates from Qdrant, rerank, return the best chunks with source file, heading and scorequery, top_k (default 10)
          get_adaptive_siblingsThe full text of chunks by id. A chunk that is one part of a split section comes back as the whole section, its parts merged in orderchunk_ids, max_chars, offset
          expand_contextNeighbouring chunks (parent, child or sibling) of chunks already found, using the chunks’ hierarchy metadatachunk_ids, direction
          get_overviewA full walkthrough of the business workflow, from entry points to end, by following before/after links. No search involvednone
          get_workflow_contextOne workflow step’s prerequisites, next steps and documentsnode_id or workflow_node
          search_adjacent_docsA search limited to the documents of the steps before or after a given onequery, direction, before_node_ids, after_node_ids

          Previews, then full text

          Search results could easily fill the model’s context, so the search tools return each chunk’s content as a 500-character preview. A chunk that was cut is marked truncated: true with its full_length, and the answer lists truncated_chunk_ids with a full_text_hint. The model then asks get_adaptive_siblings for exactly those chunks. The tool descriptions spell out the rule: field tables and long sections are often past the preview, so text beyond a preview must not be treated as missing.

          search_docs also tries to place its results in the business workflow: from the files the chunks came from, it derives the workflow step they belong to, so the model can follow up with get_workflow_context.

          What it needs

          PieceSettingWhere it runs
          Qdrant, collection adaptive_chunksQDRANT_URL, QDRANT_API_KEY, COLLECTION_DOCSOn the VM, as an NSSM service; one collection shared by all instances
          EmbeddingsAZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DEPLOYMENT, AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION (2024-10-21)Azure OpenAI; one call per search
          Reranker cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2RERANKER_MODEL, RERANKER_DEVICE (cpu)Inside each server process, loaded at start-up

          The four connection settings are all-or-nothing (chapter 1.9). The documentation tools run on their own pool of four threads, and reranking runs one at a time under a lock, so heavy searching can’t slow down graph tools. Each search costs one embedding call to Azure OpenAI, billed by the token. The documents themselves are chunked, embedded and loaded into Qdrant by a separate ingestion pipeline that isn’t part of these repositories. Updating the documentation means re-running that pipeline, not touching the servers.

          When it isn’t there

          The answer is an error the model can read and pass on, and every graph tool keeps working. Temporary failures while running are retried (three attempts, 1 s and 2 s apart). A reranker that still fails leaves the results in Qdrant’s order rather than failing the search.

          Key takeaways

          • Search returns previews; the model fetches full text only for the chunks it needs.
          • Three workflow tools add the business process around a document: what comes before and after.
          • Documentation search is optional per instance, shares one Qdrant collection, and fails softly.

          3.8 Live SQL, safely

          Two legacy tools read the client’s QA database while a conversation runs: sql_query, for any read-only question, and get_menu_path, which reads the menu tables. Letting an AI write SQL against a real database needs care. The legacy server’s answer, in tools/tools/sql_live/_live_sql.py, is several independent layers, so that no single mistake can do harm.

          The sql_query tool

          OperationWhat it runs
          describeA table’s columns, types, nullability and primary key, from INFORMATION_SCHEMA
          sampleSELECT TOP n * FROM [table] (default 10 rows)
          distinctA column’s distinct values with counts (top 100)
          queryThe model’s own SELECT, after the checks below

          The first three build their SQL themselves, with table and column names bracket-quoted. The description tells the model to prefer them for quick lookups. Every result reports its columns with their types, the rows, a row_count, whether it was truncated at 1,000 rows, and elapsed_ms. An empty result reads (no rows).

          Seven layers of protection

          LayerWhat it does
          1. A read-only loginThe connection string’s login should be db_datareader only (chapter 1.10)
          2. A permission self-checkAfter start-up the server asks SQL Server what the login can do. If it could write, or the check can’t run, live SQL switches itself off and /health says why
          3. One plain SELECTA real tokenizer (strings, comments, [names]) checks for exactly one statement starting with SELECT or WITH, at most 20,000 characters
          4. Blocked words and hintsStatement keywords such as INSERT, EXEC, INTO, OPENQUERY, WAITFOR; locking hints such as TABLOCKX; four-part names that reach linked servers
          5. Fixed session settingsNOCOUNT, XACT_ABORT, no implicit transactions, READ COMMITTED, a 30 s lock timeout
          6. LimitsA 30 s query timeout on the connection, 1,000 rows, at most 4 queries at once plus 20 waiting, and a 10 s queue wait
          7. A safety netIf a query outlives its limits by 5 seconds, the server cancels it itself, in case the driver’s own timeout failed

          Because the check works on tokens, it is precise in both directions. WHERE NOTE LIKE '%update%' passes, because update is inside a string. MERGE JOIN, OPTION (USE HINT …) and OFFSET … FETCH NEXT pass, because those words are part of a SELECT there. SELECT … INTO is refused with its own explanation. A column that happens to be called OPEN gets a hint to write [OPEN]. Each refusal is a sentence the model can act on.

          Busy, timeout and connection problems each become a message that says what to do: “Live SQL is busy (all 4 query slots are in use). Try again shortly, or answer from the graph tools if they cover the question.” “The query was stopped after 30 seconds. Narrow it — add a WHERE clause or TOP, or join fewer tables — and try again.”

          get_menu_path, and what happens without live SQL

          get_menu_path answers “how do I get to this screen?” It combines the live menu tables (MNU_FORM and related) with facts from the graph: whether the home screen registers the form class so the menu can open it by name, and which screens open it in code. On the test server, with no database configured, it still answered from the graph and marked the menu part unavailable:

          sql_query in the same situation answered with an error naming the missing setting: “Live SQL is not configured on this server (NGENUE_SQL_CONN_STRING is not set).” Chapter 6.7 follows what the model does when live SQL is off, finds nothing, or fails.

          Settings

          SettingDefaultMeaning
          NGENUE_SQL_CONN_STRING(none)The ODBC connection string; without it live SQL is off
          SQL_QUERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS30Per-query limit, also used for the lock timeout
          SQL_QUERY_MAX_CONCURRENT4Queries running at once
          SQL_QUERY_QUEUE_WAIT_SECONDS10How long a query may wait for a slot
          SQL_QUERY_PERMISSION_CHECKonThe read-only self-check; turn off only for a login verified read-only by hand

          Key takeaways

          • Read-only login, self-check, tokenized single-SELECT check, fixed session, limits and a cancelling safety net: seven layers, each enough to stop a different mistake.
          • Every refusal and failure is a sentence that tells the model what to do next.
          • Without live SQL, the graph-based parts of an answer still come back. (The new-UI server’s live SQL is simpler and lacks several of these layers; see chapter 3.12.)

          How the model picks a tool

          The model chooses from three sources of guidance: each tool’s description, which states what it returns and what it needs; the input schema, whose required fields tell it what to find first; and the playbook’s query patterns (chapter 3.10), such as “What does [screen] do?” → find_form_by_name → get_form_overview → get_action_chain. Typical answers combine families: a discovery tool to get an id, a form or behavioural tool for the screen, then a cross-graph or SQL tool to reach the database.

          Key takeaways

          • Eight categories cover Delphi code and screens, eleven the database, and five bridge the two or add meaning, documents and server facts.
          • Discovery tools come first: they turn words into the ids every other tool needs.
          • Descriptions, required fields and the playbook’s patterns together steer the model’s choice.

          3.10 The instructions playbook

          Tool descriptions say what each tool does. The instructions say how to use 148 of them well together: which to call first, what the state fields mean, how to page, and what never to claim. They are the closest thing this system has to an agent’s logic, and they live in a text file.

          How they reach the model

          MCP lets a server send instructions with server/discover or initialize (chapter 1.5). Each instance loads its file at start-up (INSTRUCTIONS_FILE), puts one identity line in front, naming the client, the graph versions and the code build, and sends the result. The host gives it to the model as guidance for using this server. Both servers keep the playbook in the repository, so it is reviewed and versioned like code.

          LegacyNew UI
          Filengenue_old_ui_instructions.mdngenue_instructions.md
          Size74,925 characters, 1,352 lines28,726 characters, 628 lines

          What’s in the legacy playbook

          SectionLinesPurpose
          Opening1–9What this server is: the legacy nTrack UI of a natural-gas ETRM and retail platform, three analysis domains
          Knowledge graphs and data sources10–57The seven sources (Delphi graph, SQL graph, code flows, data dictionary, workflow graph, documentation vectors, live QA database), what each holds and its limits
          State tracking: critical58–137Every state field, what its values look like, how sql_context accumulates
          Answer size and paging138–156Pages, the token budget, the hard cap and get_more_results
          Domain 1: Delphi source analysis157–935Tool-by-tool guidance; the bulk of the file
          Domain 2: SQL analysis936–1020Database tools
          Domain 3: documentation and workflow1021–1054Documentation tools and the workflow graph
          Common query patterns1055–1221Recipes: question → tool sequence
          Cross-domain workflows1222–1256Questions that need code, database and documents together
          Important behaviours1257–1352Rules about what to say and never say

          In its own words

          These rules encode lessons that are hard to see from code alone. Inherited buttons are real buttons. An object missing from the SQL graph is unknown, not absent. Several matching screens mean the model should ask the user, not pick one silently. Each rule turns a known failure into instructions.

          Keeping playbook and tools in step

          At start-up the loader compares the tool names mentioned in the instructions with the tools actually served, and logs a warning for any drift, such as a renamed tool the playbook still recommends (instruction_drift in loaders/ngenue.py). The test suite checks other parts, such as the documented settings matching the gates in code.

          Likely trade-off

          At about 75,000 characters (very roughly 19,000 tokens), the legacy playbook is large. Hosts usually keep server instructions in the model’s context for the whole conversation, so it costs context and tokens on every turn. In return, the model gets detailed, tested guidance. The new-UI playbook is less than half the size. Measuring answer quality with a shorter legacy playbook would show whether all of it earns its place.

          Key takeaways

          • The playbook is the system’s “agent logic”: tool order, state rules, paging and honesty rules, in plain text.
          • It is sent with server/discover or initialize, prefixed with the instance’s identity.
          • A start-up check and tests keep it in step with the tools; its size is a cost worth measuring.

          3.11 One tool call, end to end

          This chapter puts the previous ten together by following one call, get_action_chain for Save on the End User screen, from the user’s question to the answer.

          The journey

          1. The model decides. From the question, the tool descriptions and the playbook, it chooses get_action_chain with action_filter: "save" and the active_form an earlier call returned.
          2. The host sends it. The client POSTs a JSON-RPC tools/call to https://mcp.ngenue.net/aep/v1/mcp with its Entra ID token. Depending on its settings, the host may first ask the person to approve the call (chapter 6.6).
          3. IIS forwards it. HTTPS ends at IIS; the URL Rewrite rule strips /aep/v1 and ARR proxies the request to the AEP process on 127.0.0.1.
          4. The token is checked. OAuthMiddleware verifies the signature, expiry, issuer and audience (chapter 4.4); a bad token gets 401 here.
          5. The protocol layer reads it. mcp_endpoint checks the content type and parses the JSON; _process_one validates the envelope; MCPHandler.route checks the protocol version and calls _tools_call.
          6. The tool is found and checked. An unknown name is a -32602 error; bad arguments are an isError answer.
          7. It runs on a thread. ToolEntry.run sends mcp_execute to a worker thread, limited to 90 seconds; the event loop keeps serving other requests.
          8. The pipeline runs. Arguments are checked again; the form name resolves to its node id; execute walks the indexes (51 ms for this call in the test run); the answer is trimmed to the token budget.
          9. The text is built. JSON, then the STATE UPDATES trailer (active_method, the new sql_context entries), then the 80,000-character cap. This answer was 30,763 characters, so nothing was cut.
          10. The answer is sent. _tools_call logs tool_call name=get_action_chain ms=51 chars=30763 cut=no and returns {"resultType": "complete", "content": [{"type": "text", …}]} (with structuredContent for tools that declare an output schema). It goes back through FastAPI, IIS and the internet.
          11. The model reads it and either answers the person or calls another tool, passing the state values back (chapter 6.1).

          On this path the server’s own work was about 51 milliseconds. Everything else is network, IIS, and above all the model’s thinking between calls. That is why the speed of an answer is dominated by how many calls the model makes, not by the server.

          Key takeaways

          • One call crosses the client, the network, IIS, auth, the protocol layer, the registry, a worker thread, the tool and the indexes, and back.
          • Each layer can stop the call with a clear answer: 401, a JSON-RPC error, or an isError result.
          • Server time is tens of milliseconds; the number of calls the model makes decides how long an answer takes.

          The two servers share their design, and most of what this Part says applies to both. The legacy server has since been hardened for ten clients, through many rounds of work the code calls “batches”, and the new-UI server hasn’t caught up in several places. This chapter is the honest comparison.
