          Answer sizeToken budget (first pass) plus the 80,000-character cap with cursorThe character cap with cursor only (tools/tools/_budget.py doesn’t exist here)
          Live SQLThe seven layers of chapter 3.8A simpler tool (see below)
          Start-up loader828 lines: memory check, scorer self-check, source-bundle checks, identity, cross-graph links, manifest, drift check431 lines
          DelphiIndex2,388 lines1,236 lines
          Sign-in codeIdentical middlewares; the OAuth proxy differs in 28 lines
          Tests2,377588

          The new-UI server’s live SQL

          The new UI’s sql_query lives in one file. It checks queries in three layers: a keyword blocklist, structural checks (must start with SELECT or WITH; no semicolons outside strings), and, if the sqlglot library is installed, a parse. Reading it next to the legacy module shows four gaps:

          • No per-query timeout. pyodbc.connect(timeout=30) sets the login timeout, and SET LOCK_TIMEOUT only limits waiting for locks. Nothing stops a slow query, although the file’s header says “query timeout (30 s)”. The 90-second tool limit stops waiting for it, but the query keeps running on SQL Server.
          • One shared connection, no lock. A single pyodbc connection is reused by every call, and the tool runs on the shared thread pool. pyodbc connections must not be used by two threads at once, so concurrent calls can interfere.
          • No read-only self-check. Safety rests entirely on the login being read-only.
          • A coarser check. The blocklist scans the raw text, strings included, so LIKE '%update%' is refused. The sqlglot layer isn’t a declared dependency, so it may not be active.

          Watch out

          The legacy live-SQL module could be ported to the new-UI server almost unchanged; it is self-contained. Until then, make sure the new UI’s database login is db_datareader only (Part 7).

          Which version is deployed?

          The repositories are a snapshot. The tool list this Claude workspace received from the production AEP server has 135 tools, against 148 in the repository. Some of its descriptions are older too: find_dialog_users has no paging arguments there, and find_forms_using_external_call doesn’t mention its units_without_form list. Either production runs an older build than the repository, or the client is holding an older copy of the list. Each instance’s /health reports its code_build_id and tool_manifest_hash; comparing them across the eleven instances, and with the repository, settles it (chapter 5.4).

          Key takeaways

          • Same architecture; the legacy server is the hardened one: budget, live-SQL safety, start-up checks and four times the tests.
          • The new UI’s live SQL lacks a query timeout, connection safety and the read-only self-check.
          • What is deployed may differ from the repository; /health tells you which build each instance runs.

          3.13 Tests and local tools

          You can try nearly everything in this Part on a laptop, without IIS or Entra ID. This chapter covers the test suites, with a real run of both, and the scripts that let you call tools directly.

          Running the tests

          From a server repository folder: python -m pytest -q. Both suites ran on the test machine (Python 3.12 on Linux; the project targets 3.11 on Windows):

          SuiteTestsResultTime
          ngenue_mcp_legacy (tests/ and tools/tests_mcp/)2,3772,376 passed, 1 failed28 s
          ngenue_mcp588584 passed, 4 skipped2.6 s

          The one failure is a real finding about the repository copy, not about the code. A test checks that tool folders retired long ago are gone, and the copy still has them (for example tools/tools/behavioral/get_all_conditions). The loader skips retired folders, so they do no harm, but they should be deleted.

          Watch out

          Both server archives shared for this handbook contain a real .env file next to .env.example. I didn’t open them, but a .env normally holds API keys, an Entra client secret and a database password. Keep .env out of archives and source control. If these archives have travelled beyond the people who already hold those secrets, rotate the secrets (Part 7).

          What the tests cover

          • Protocol and server: test_server.py, test_server_error_paths.py, test_server_main.py, structured answers, async tools and thread use.
          • Sign-in: test_oauth_middleware.py and test_oauth_proxy.py.
          • Start-up: loader behaviour, registration of every tool, the manifest, and the loader’s contract.
          • Tools: 86 files in tools/tests_mcp/, many running on small real slices of the AEP graph cut by scripts/make_slice.py.
          • Graph contract: tests/contract/ holds a small legacy 3.0 graph and its golden counts. Every tool must answer it without crashing, and must also answer versions of it with newer features removed, so tools keep working on older client graphs.

          tests/conftest.py raises both size limits to very large values so tests see whole answers; the limits themselves have their own tests.

          Calling tools without a server

          Values after key= are read as JSON when they parse; --tokens estimates how many tokens the model would read. Other useful scripts:

          ScriptUse
          local_check.pyRuns calls through the real path (loader → registry → handler), with sweeps, a manual sample to eyeball, and an optional byte-for-byte comparison with another copy of the code
          check_output_schemas_live.pyChecks every tool with an output schema on the real graphs, through tools/call
          make_slice.pyCuts a small, real slice of a graph around one screen, for tests
          check_sheets.pyRuns QA workbooks row by row through the tools and writes annotated copies
          review_links.pyBuilds an evidence pack for checking label-to-control links without the Delphi IDE

          Running a server locally

          This is how the examples in this Part were made. Create a .env next to the code, pointing at a graph folder, with AUTH_MODE=none and HOST=127.0.0.1, then run python -m server.app and call it with any HTTP client. For a visual client, MCP Inspector can use the bundled mcp-inspector.json.

          Watch out

          AUTH_MODE=none is for a laptop only, with HOST=127.0.0.1. Never use it on a machine other people can reach.

          Key takeaways

          • Both suites run in seconds; the legacy suite’s one failure points at stale folders in the repository copy.
          • The harness and local scripts call tools exactly as the server does, without HTTP or sign-in.
          • Keep real .env files out of archives; rotate secrets that may have travelled.

          Part 4

          Secure: sign-in and secrets

          How a person in Claude or ChatGPT gets a Microsoft Entra ID token, why the server runs its own small OAuth proxy, how every token is checked, and how secrets move from .env files to Azure Key Vault.

            How the examples in this Part were made

            The responses quoted here come from a second local instance started in OAuth mode with a made-up tenant and app id (00000000-… and 11111111-…), a made-up public URL (https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1) and the small contract graphs from the test suite. Only the token request was forwarded to the real Microsoft Entra ID, which rejected it, as it should.

            4.1 Three ways to authenticate

            Each instance runs in one of three modes, chosen by AUTH_MODE in its .env. The production instances use Entra ID (OAuth); the other two modes exist for scripts and local work.

            AUTH_MODEClient sendsServer checksIdentity in the logsUse for
            oauthAuthorization: Bearer <Entra ID access token>Signature, expiry, issuer and audience (chapter 4.4)The person’s preferred_usernameClaude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cowork
            apikeyAuthorization: Bearer <key>Exact match against API_KEYSThe <name> in key-<name>-<random>, or a short hashScripts, monitoring, trusted automation
            noneNothingNothingNoneA laptop, with HOST=127.0.0.1 only

            Start-up refuses a mode that is incompletely configured. apikey needs at least one key. oauth needs OAUTH_TENANT_ID, OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AUDIENCE, OAUTH_SCOPE and PUBLIC_URL, because the discovery documents must contain reachable addresses.

            What is protected, and what is public

            The auth middleware protects only the MCP endpoint. Everything a client must read before it has a token stays public: /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, /.well-known/openid-configuration, /oauth/authorize and /oauth/token. /health and / are public too.

            Watch out

            /health answers without a token, and its answer names the client, the graph versions and build dates, the source database name and a code build id (chapter 3.2). Behind IIS’s per-client rule, https://mcp.ngenue.net/<client>/v1/health is most likely reachable from the internet. That isn’t a secret leak, but it is more than outsiders need. Restricting /health to the VM and your monitoring, with an IIS rule, is cheap (Part 7).

            Key takeaways

            • One mode per instance: Entra ID tokens in production, API keys for automation, none only on a laptop.
            • Only the MCP endpoint is protected; discovery, the OAuth proxy and /health are public by design.
            • An incomplete configuration stops start-up instead of running half-protected.

            4.2 The sign-in flow, step by step

            Chapter 1.6 explained OAuth in general. Here is the exact sequence for these servers, with the real requests and answers from the demo instance.

            The sequence

            1. The connector is set up once. In Claude or ChatGPT, someone adds a custom connector with the instance’s address (for AEP, https://mcp.ngenue.net/aep/v1/mcp) and the Entra app’s client id and client secret.
            2. The first call has no token. The server answers 401 and says where to learn more:
            HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="mcp", resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"

Bearer token required
            1. The client reads the protected resource metadata. It names the server itself as the authorization server, because of the proxy:
            {
  "resource": "https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1/mcp",
  "scopes_supported": ["mcp:tools", "api://11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/mcp.access"],
  "resource_name": "Handbook OAuth demo",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1"]
}
            1. The client reads the authorization server metadata. The sign-in and token addresses point at the server’s proxy; the keys and issuer are Entra ID’s:
            {
  "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/v2.0",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1/oauth/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1/oauth/token",
  "jwks_uri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/discovery/v2.0/keys",
  "scopes_supported": ["openid", "offline_access"],
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_post"]
}
            1. The browser goes to the proxy’s sign-in address with the client id, its callback address, the scopes it chose (here mcp:tools and the API scope), a state, a PKCE challenge, and the resource parameter that MCP requires.
            2. The proxy cleans the request and redirects to Entra ID. The real Location header: resource is gone, mcp:tools is gone, offline_access was added, everything else is untouched.
            HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://login.microsoftonline.com/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/oauth2/v2.0/authorize
  ?response_type=code&client_id=11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
  &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclaude.ai%2Fapi%2Fmcp%2Fauth_callback
  &scope=api%3A%2F%2F11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555%2Fmcp.access+offline_access
  &state=abc123&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM&code_challenge_method=S256
            1. The person signs in at Microsoft. Multi-factor authentication and any Conditional Access policies apply here; the first time, the person may be asked to consent. Entra ID then sends the browser back to the client’s callback with a one-time code.
            2. The client exchanges the code through the proxy. It POSTs the code, the PKCE verifier, its client id and secret (and resource again) to /oauth/token. The proxy removes what Entra would reject, forwards the rest, and returns Entra’s answer exactly as it came. In the demo, Entra rejected the made-up code; that rejection is what the client received:
            HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"AADSTS9002313: Invalid request. Request is malformed or invalid. …"}
            1. The client calls MCP with its token, and the middleware checks it on every request (chapter 4.4).
            2. When the token expires (after about an hour), the client uses its refresh token through the same /oauth/token proxy, with no new sign-in.

            Key takeaways

            • Discovery documents lead any MCP client from the server’s address to Microsoft’s sign-in page.
            • The proxy rewrites two things on the way to Entra ID and passes Entra’s answers back unchanged.
            • MFA, Conditional Access and consent all happen at Microsoft; the server only checks the resulting token.

            4.3 Why the OAuth proxy exists

            In an ideal world, the server’s metadata would point clients straight at Entra ID. Two incompatibilities prevent that, and auth/oauth_proxy.py exists only to bridge them.

            The two problems

            • The resource parameter. MCP asks clients to say which server a token is for, using the standard resource parameter (RFC 8707). Entra ID’s v2 endpoints reject a request that combines resource with v2 scopes, with error AADSTS9010010.
            • MCP scopes. Clients pick scopes from the protected resource metadata, and the server lists mcp:tools there next to the real API scope. Entra ID knows nothing about mcp:* scopes.

            So the metadata names the server as its own authorization server, and two small endpoints sit in front of Entra ID.

            What it does not do

            • It never issues, changes or stores tokens. Entra ID issues them, and the answer is passed through byte for byte.
            • It never logs secrets. It logs only the grant type and Entra’s status code. The client secret passes through in the request body, which is unavoidable for client_secret_post.
            • It doesn’t decide who may sign in or where codes are sent. Entra ID checks the client id, the secret and the registered redirect addresses.
            • It offers no dynamic client registration, which is why each connector needs the client id and secret typed in.

            Trade-offs to know

            • The issuer. The authorization server metadata is served from the server’s address but declares Entra ID’s issuer, because tokens carry Entra’s iss. The OAuth metadata standard (RFC 8414) expects the issuer to match the address the metadata came from. Today’s clients accept this; a stricter client could refuse it.
            • Availability. If Entra ID can’t be reached, /oauth/token answers 502 server_error, “Authorization server unreachable”. Existing tokens keep working until they expire, because checking a token needs only the cached public keys.

            Key takeaways

            • The proxy exists for two reasons: Entra ID rejects MCP’s resource parameter and doesn’t know mcp:* scopes.
            • It strips those, adds offline_access, and otherwise forwards; it issues nothing and stores nothing.
            • Its one standards wrinkle, a borrowed issuer, works with today’s clients.

            4.4 Checking a token

            OAuthMiddleware in auth/oauth_middleware.py checks the token on every MCP request. It is a resource server only: it keeps no sessions or cookies. Its only state is a cache of Entra ID’s public keys.

            What happens on each request

            1. Find the token in Authorization: Bearer …. None: 401 with the plain challenge from chapter 4.2, which starts sign-in.
            2. Read the token’s header without trusting it, to get kid, the id of the key that signed it. No kid: rejected.
            3. Find that public key. Keys are cached by id. An unknown id triggers a fresh fetch of Entra ID’s key list, at most once every five minutes and by one request at a time (an asyncio.Lock). Microsoft rotates its signing keys, so new ids appear from time to time.
            4. Verify with PyJWT: the signature with that key, the algorithm (RS256 only), expiry and not-before, the issuer (Entra’s v2 or v1 issuer for the tenant) and the audience (OAUTH_AUDIENCE or OAUTH_CLIENT_ID).
            5. On any failure: 401 with error="invalid_token", which tells the client to sign in again rather than retry. The log says why: expired, wrong audience, wrong issuer, or the library’s own message.
            6. On success: the person’s preferred_username (or upn, or sub) is recorded on the request and logged as Authenticated: …, and the request continues.

            In the demo, a request with Authorization: Bearer not-a-real-token got this answer, and the log recorded Token rejected: Not enough segments:

            HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="mcp", resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.test/demo/v1/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", error="invalid_token"

Invalid or expired token

            What it does not check

            The check proves that a token was issued by your tenant for this app. It doesn’t look at the token’s scopes (scp), app roles (roles) or group memberships, and it doesn’t care which client application asked for the token. In practice, who can use the server is decided entirely in Entra ID: whoever can obtain a token for the app’s audience gets in. Chapter 4.5 shows how to use that.

            Watch out

            The middleware writes three “Token debug” lines at INFO level for every request (token length, key id, issuer, audience, version), plus the user name. None of them contain the token itself, but at INFO level they make the logs noisy and full of personal identifiers. Moving the debug lines to DEBUG level is a one-word change per line (Part 7).

            No clock leeway is configured, so expiry is checked to the second. Keep the VM’s clock synchronised.

            Key takeaways

            • Every request: key by kid from a cache, then signature, algorithm, time, issuer and audience.
            • Failures get 401 with invalid_token and a logged reason; success logs who it was.
            • No scope, role or group checks: access control lives in Entra ID.

            4.5 Entra ID: one app today, one per client next

            Today one Entra ID app registration serves all eleven instances. That is simple, but it has a consequence that follows directly from chapter 4.4.

            One app: what it means

            • Every instance has the same audience, so a token obtained through the AEP connector is equally valid on PEP, Snyder or any other instance.
            • Anyone who can sign in to that one app can reach every client’s source code and QA database through any instance, given its address.
            • Per-client access control can’t be expressed at the token level at all.

            One app per client: the plan

            Giving each client instance its own app registration fixes all three, with no code change. Each instance’s .env gets that app’s OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AUDIENCE and OAUTH_SCOPE. The audience check then rejects another client’s token automatically.

            1. Register the app for the client, for example “nGenue MCP – AEP”, single tenant.
            2. Add redirect addresses: the callback address each AI client documents for custom connectors.
            3. Expose an API: set the Application ID URI (api://<client id>) and add a scope such as mcp.access. OAUTH_SCOPE is the full scope string; OAUTH_AUDIENCE is the Application ID URI.
            4. Choose the token version. Setting the manifest to issue v2.0 access tokens is the cleaner choice; the server accepts both versions either way.
            5. Create a client secret for the connectors and note its expiry date. Eleven apps mean eleven secrets to renew on a calendar.
            6. Require assignment. In the app’s Enterprise application properties, turn on “Assignment required”, then assign the people or groups who work on that client. Others can’t obtain a token at all.
            7. Update the connectors for that client with the new client id and secret.

            Defence in depth

            Per-client apps plus assignment give isolation without touching the code. Two small code additions would make it stricter: check that scp contains the configured scope, and optionally require an app role in roles. Then even a misconfigured audience can’t let a wrong token through.

            Key takeaways

            • With one shared app, any valid token works on every instance.
            • One app per client, with assignment required, makes each instance accept only its own client’s people.
            • The cost is eleven secrets and eleven connector configurations to maintain.

            4.6 Secrets: .env today, Azure Key Vault next

            Every instance reads its settings from the .env file beside its code. Most settings are harmless; a few are secrets.

            Which settings are secret

            SettingSecret?Why
            NGENUE_SQL_CONN_STRINGYesContains the database login’s password
            AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEYYesLets anyone use the embedding deployment, billed to nGenue
            QDRANT_API_KEYYesAccess to the documentation vectors
            API_KEYSYes, when usedEach key is a full credential to the instance
            OAUTH_TENANT_ID, OAUTH_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AUDIENCE, OAUTH_SCOPE, URLs, pathsNoIdentifiers, not credentials

            Notably, the Entra client secret is not on the server at all. It lives in each AI client’s connector settings and only passes through the token proxy.

            The risks of .env files

            • Eleven copies of the shared secrets (the Azure OpenAI key, the Qdrant key, perhaps the same database login) sit in eleven files, readable by anyone with access to the folder.
            • Files travel. The server archives shared for this handbook each contained a real .env (chapter 3.13).
            • There is no rotation workflow and no record of who read a secret.

            Right away: restrict each instance folder’s NTFS permissions to the service account and administrators, keep .env out of source control and archives, and rotate any secret that may have left the VM.

            Azure Key Vault from an on-premises VM

            An on-premises server can use Key Vault without storing any credential, through Azure Arc. An Arc-enabled server gets a system-assigned managed identity, and processes on it obtain tokens from a local endpoint (Microsoft’s guide). The Azure SDK for Python supports this directly. The steps:

            1. Connect the VM to Azure Arc and enable its managed identity.
            2. Create a Key Vault and give the VM’s identity read access to secrets (for example the “Key Vault Secrets User” role).
            3. Let the service account use the identity. On Windows, the account running the services must be a local administrator or a member of the “Hybrid Agent Extension Applications” group.
            4. Store secrets per client, for example aep-sql-conn or shared-azure-openai-key.
            5. Load them at start-up, before ServerConfig is built. Because python-dotenv never overwrites a variable that is already set, values placed in the environment first simply win over the .env file.

            Rotation then becomes: update the secret in the vault, restart the instance. Key Vault can log every read for audit.

            Key takeaways

            • Four settings are secrets; the Entra client secret is not on the server at all.
            • Today: lock down the folders, keep .env out of archives, rotate what may have leaked.
            • Next: Azure Arc gives the on-premises VM a managed identity, so a few lines at start-up can read secrets from Key Vault with nothing stored on disk.

            Part 5

            Host and operate

            What runs where, on-prem and in the cloud; the Windows Server VM with IIS, ARR, NSSM, Qdrant and SQL Server; deploying code and graphs safely; capacity, health and logs; the planned Jenkins pipeline; and how the same system could run on Azure or AWS.

              What is known, and what is suggested

              The repositories don’t contain the VM’s configuration: no IIS rules, NSSM settings or port list. This Part combines what the code and README require, what you have described about the set-up, and common practice for this kind of host. Where it shows a folder layout, port number or command, treat it as an example to compare with the real VM, not as a record of it.

              5.1 What runs where: on-prem and cloud

              ComponentWhereStarted by
              IIS with ARR and URL RewriteWindows Server VM, nGenue’s office server roomWindows
              10 legacy MCP instances + 1 new-UI instanceSame VM, each on its own 127.0.0.1 portNSSM, one service each
              Qdrant (documentation vectors)Same VMNSSM
              SQL Server with each client’s QA databaseSame VMSQL Server service
              Microsoft Entra ID (sign-in, signing keys)Microsoft cloud—
              Azure OpenAI (embeddings)Azure—
              Graph builders and ScriptDOMA developer’s laptop, during buildsBy hand
              SQL graph builder, documentation ingestionSeparate projectsBy hand
              Azure Key Vault, Jenkins, one Entra app per clientPlanned—

              What leaves the VM

              • To the AI clients: every tool answer, which can include source code, SQL text and, through live SQL, QA data. From there it becomes part of a conversation with Anthropic’s or OpenAI’s models, under those services’ terms.
              • To Azure OpenAI: the text of each documentation search query, to be embedded.
              • To Entra ID: sign-in redirects and token requests through the proxy, and periodic downloads of public signing keys.

              Nothing else calls out. Graphs are read from local disk, and the QA databases and Qdrant are on the same machine.

              Key takeaways

              • One on-premises Windows VM hosts IIS, eleven MCP processes, Qdrant and the QA databases.
              • The cloud provides identity (Entra ID) and embeddings (Azure OpenAI); builds happen on a laptop.
              • Tool answers, which can contain code and data, are what leave the VM.

              5.2 The Windows Server VM

              Everything server-side shares one machine. This chapter lists what an operator should know about it, and the settings worth checking.

              One folder per instance

              The code expects each instance to have its own .env and graphs/ folder, with relative paths resolved from the instance folder (chapter 1.11). A layout like this keeps instances independent:

              NSSM settings worth checking

              SettingRecommendedWhy
              AppDirectoryThe instance folderRelative paths in .env resolve from here
              AppStdout, AppStderr, AppRotateFiles, AppRotateBytesA log file per instance, rotated by sizeThe server logs to standard error; unrotated files grow without limit
              AppExit Default Restart, AppRestartDelayRestart, after a short delayA crashed instance comes back on its own
              ObjectNameA dedicated low-privilege accountNot LocalSystem; the account needs to read its folder, write its logs, and nothing more
              StartSERVICE_DELAYED_AUTO_START, or staggered startsSee below

              Watch out

              After a reboot, eleven instances starting at once all parse their graphs at the same moment. That is the memory peak of the whole system, at the same time as SQL Server and Qdrant start. The README advises restarting instances one at a time; at boot, delayed or staggered starts do the same. Each instance needs 20–60 seconds before it accepts connections (chapter 3.2).

              The neighbours: SQL Server and Qdrant

              • SQL Server by default will use most of the machine’s memory for its cache, and doesn’t give it back quickly. On a VM shared with eleven memory-heavy processes, set its maximum server memory explicitly (chapter 5.5).
              • Qdrant holds the documentation vectors, shared by all instances. Its storage should be backed up (Qdrant can take snapshots), or rebuilt by re-running the documentation ingestion.

              Routine care

              • Windows updates and reboots: plan them; afterwards, check every instance’s /health (chapter 5.6).
              • Backups: the graphs can be rebuilt but are slow to rebuild, so keep the last good set per client. The .env files hold secrets until Key Vault replaces them; back them up securely or not at all.
              • Clock: keep it synchronised; token expiry is checked to the second (chapter 4.4).

              Key takeaways

              • One folder, one .env, one port and one NSSM service per instance.
              • Rotate logs, restart on failure, run as a low-privilege account, and stagger starts.
              • SQL Server and Qdrant share the machine; cap SQL Server’s memory.

              5.3 IIS and ARR routing

              IIS gives the eleven local processes one public HTTPS address. Chapter 1.11 explained the mechanism; this chapter covers what the rules must achieve, and the settings that matter for this system.

              What the rules must do

              • For each legacy client, send everything under /<client>/v1/ to that instance with the prefix removed. That covers the MCP endpoint, its discovery documents and its OAuth proxy, and each instance’s PUBLIC_URL must include the same prefix.
              • For the new UI, whose PUBLIC_URL is the bare host, send /mcp, /.well-known/… and /oauth/… at the root to its instance.

              Settings that matter here

              SettingWhereWhat to check
              Proxy time-outARR Server Proxy SettingsLonger than the 90-second tool limit plus a margin, so IIS doesn’t cut off a long but legitimate call
              HTTPS binding and certificateThe IIS sitemcp.ngenue.net on 443, with a certificate renewed before it expires
              Reverse rewrite of host in response headersARR Server Proxy SettingsHarmless here: the only redirect, from /oauth/authorize, points at Microsoft
              A rule for /healthURL RewriteConsider answering outside callers with 404, leaving /health to the VM and monitoring (chapter 4.1)

              What clients see during a restart

              While an instance loads its graphs, its port is closed (chapter 3.2), so IIS can’t connect and answers 502 Bad Gateway for that client, typically for 20–60 seconds. Other clients aren’t affected. Restart outside working hours, or use the two-port switch in chapter 5.4 for zero downtime.

              Testing a route

              A 401 means IIS reached the AEP instance and its auth middleware answered. The resource_metadata address shows that the instance’s PUBLIC_URL carries the right prefix. A 502 means the instance is down or still loading; a 404 means no rule matched.

              Key takeaways

              • One rewrite rule per client prefix, plus root paths for the new UI; each PUBLIC_URL must match its prefix.
              • Set the proxy time-out above the tool limit; consider hiding /health from outside.
              • A restart means 20–60 seconds of 502s for that one client.

              5.4 Deploying code and graphs

              Both code and graphs are read once at start-up, so every change is copy, restart, check. The legacy README gives the order: code first, everywhere; then graphs, one client at a time.

              Deploying code

              1. Test first. Run the test suite (chapter 3.13) on the new code.
              2. Copy the whole code over each instance’s old copy: server/, auth/, loaders/ (including tool_manifest.txt), tools/ and the instructions file. Never copy .env or graphs/.
              3. Restart the instance’s service, one at a time.
              4. Check /health. code_build_id, a hash of the code’s .py files, and tool_manifest_hash must be identical on every instance running the same code.

              Tool folders removed from the repository may stay behind on an instance. Discovery skips retired folders, but deleting them keeps instances clean, and it is what the failing test in chapter 3.13 asks for.

              Deploying a new graph

              1. Keep the previous files (graph_old.json, and source.zip with its manifest if bundled) until the new ones are proven.
              2. Copy the builder’s outputs over the paths in .env (DELPHI_GRAPH_PATH and the source bundle).
              3. Restart that instance.
              4. Check /health. graph.nodes, graph.edges and graph.built_at must match the builder’s log; client.id must name this instance’s client; the status should be healthy, not degraded.
              5. Ask the flagship question, as the README puts it: “What happens when a user clicks Save on the End User screen?” (get_action_chain with action_filter=save). Compare with the previous graph’s answer.
              6. Only then delete the previous files, or keep them as the rollback copy.

              Rolling back is the same in reverse: put the previous files back and restart.

              Knowing what is deployed

              Chapter 3.12 found that the production tool list may be older than the repository. A small script that reads every instance’s /health and prints client.id, code_build_id, tool_manifest_hash, graph.version and graph.built_at answers “what is running where?” in one table.

              Zero-downtime option

              A suggestion

              Because restarts cost 20–60 seconds per client, a blue-green switch is worth considering for busy clients. Run the new copy on a second port, wait for its /health, point the client’s IIS rule at the new port, then stop the old copy. It needs twice the memory for that client for a few minutes.

              Key takeaways

              • Code first everywhere, then graphs one client at a time; always copy, restart, check.
              • /health proves what is running: code build, manifest, graph counts and dates, client.
              • Keep the previous graph until the new one answers the flagship question.

              5.5 Memory and capacity

              Memory is the resource that decides how many instances one VM can hold. CPU matters much less.

              The rule of thumb, and a measurement

              The code estimates each instance’s need as 5 × the Delphi graph file + 3 × the SQL graph file + 300 MB (_DELPHI_MEMORY_FACTOR, _SQL_MEMORY_FACTOR and _BASE_MEMORY_MB in loaders/ngenue.py). It compares that with free memory at start-up and warns if it is short. For AEP that gives 5 × 471 + 3 × 172 + 300 ≈ 3,000 MB.

              In the test run, AEP’s process settled at about 1.8 GB once loaded, and the machine showed about 2.4 GB in use at the busiest moment sampled during loading. The estimate is deliberately cautious, and covers the parsing peak. Use it for planning.

              • Documentation search adds more. The reranker loads torch and a small model in every instance that has documentation search configured. Measure an instance with it on before sizing, and expect several hundred MB more.
              • Code flows cost little: they are read on first use.
              • The new-UI graph is about 1 GB, so by the same rule its instance needs about 5 GB plus its SQL graph.

              Sizing the whole VM

              To that total add SQL Server’s cap, Qdrant’s working set, IIS, Windows itself and a margin for restarts. Then set SQL Server’s maximum memory so it can’t take what the instances need:

              CPU and concurrency

              • Most tool calls take milliseconds (chapter 3.5), so CPU is rarely the limit. The heavy moments are start-up parsing, corpus-wide scans and reranking.
              • Each instance is its own process with its own thread pools: Python’s default pool for graph tools, four threads for documentation search, four live-SQL slots with up to 20 queued. A burst at one client can’t starve another.
              • One process per client is also one point of failure per client. A crash or restart affects only that client, for 20–60 seconds.

              Key takeaways

              • Plan 5× the Delphi graph + 3× the SQL graph + 300 MB per instance; AEP measured 1.8 GB after loading against a 3 GB estimate.
              • Add documentation search, SQL Server (capped), Qdrant and Windows to get the VM total.
              • CPU is rarely the limit; memory and start-up time are.

              5.6 Health, logs and troubleshooting

              Watching /health

              Poll each instance’s /health from the VM every minute or so, with the script in chapter 5.4 or any monitoring tool, and alert when an instance doesn’t answer, answers other than 200, reports degraded, or reports a code_build_id different from the others. degraded comes with a list of problems. Typical ones: a graph newer than the code, values the code doesn’t handle, or a source bundle that doesn’t match its graph. A memory shortfall at start-up and the live-SQL self-check result have their own fields; read them too.

              Log lines worth knowing

              LineMeans
              tool_call name=… ms=… chars=… cut=…One per call: the busiest tools, slow calls, big answers
              tool_call … error=…A tool failed or timed out; the reason follows
              tool_response_cut tool=… chars=… cap=…An answer hit the 80,000-character cap
              Authenticated: <user>, Token rejected: …Sign-in successes and failures, with the reason
              OAuth proxy: Entra ID /token responded …Token exchanges and Entra’s status
              tool_load_failedA tool file failed to import; start-up will stop if it is in the manifest
              live_sql_disabled_login_can_write, live_sql_permission_check_passedThe live-SQL self-check result
              Memory at start-up: …, nGenue ready: … tools in …sStart-up memory and duration

              Troubleshooting

              SymptomLikely cause and fix
              Clients get 502 from IISThe instance is down or still loading. Check its service and log; wait 20–60 s after a restart
              Sign-in loops, or 401 invalid_token right after sign-inAudience or issuer mismatch. Compare the token’s aud, iss and ver (logged by the token-debug lines) with OAUTH_AUDIENCE, OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and the tenant
              Microsoft shows AADSTS9010010The client went to Entra ID directly instead of through the proxy. Check the protected resource metadata names the instance’s own URL
              Start-up stops: unsupported graph version, or not the legacy lineThe graph came from the wrong builder or is unreadable (chapter 3.6)
              Start-up stops: a tool in the manifest that no file providesA tool file failed to import; read the tool_load_failed warning
              MemoryError, or the process killed during start-upNot enough RAM (chapter 5.5); stagger starts
              sql_query says “not configured” or “switched off”No connection string, or the self-check found a login that can write
              Documentation tools say “not available”Not all four documentation-search settings are present, or Qdrant or Azure OpenAI was unreachable at start-up
              Answers trimmed, or ending in next_cursorWorking as designed (chapter 6.3)
              “Did not finish within 90 s”The call hit MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS; narrow the question

              Key takeaways

              • Poll /health on every instance; alert on no answer, degraded or a differing code build.
              • The tool_call line is the most useful one in the logs: tool, time, size and cut, per call.
              • Most incidents are a restart in progress, a wrong audience, a wrong graph, or not enough memory.

              5.7 The planned Jenkins pipeline

              Today a person builds each graph on a laptop and copies it to the VM. The plan is to automate this with Jenkins. Nothing of it exists yet, so this chapter is a proposal, built on the gates the builders and servers already have.

              The stages

              1. Agent. A Windows build agent with Python 3.11, Git, the C++ build tools (for the grammar), the .NET 9 SDK (for ScriptDOM), and read access to each client’s source.
              2. Build. Start ScriptDOM; run the builder with --scriptdom-url, --bundle-source, --baseline, --coverage-baseline and --client. The legacy builder fails loudly if anything it needs is missing, which suits automation.
              3. Gates. Pass only if the exit code is 0 (no error-severity diagnostics), the census passed, coverage reports no dropped types, and diff-baseline shows no unreviewed diagnostics.
              4. Smoke test. Run scripts/mcp_harness.py with the new graph: the flagship get_action_chain question and a few per-client questions with expected answers.
              5. Archive every output with the build number, so any deployed graph can be traced to its build.
              6. Deploy to the VM over WinRM or SSH: copy to the instance’s graphs\ folder (keeping the previous files), restart that one service.
              7. Verify with /health: client id, node and edge counts, built_at, status. On failure, restore the previous files and restart.
              8. Repeat per client, one at a time. A separate code pipeline runs the tests, copies the code to all instances and checks that every code_build_id matches.

              Why it’s worth it

              Most of the risks found in this handbook disappear when builds and deployments are automated and logged: a missing --scriptdom-url, a failed census that still shipped, an unpinned grammar, drift between the repository and the VM, a stray .env in an archive. The gates already exist in the code. The pipeline only has to refuse to continue when they fail.

              Key takeaways

              • Build, gate, smoke-test, archive, deploy, verify, roll back: per client, one at a time.
              • The builders’ exit codes, census, coverage and baselines are ready-made gates.
              • /health is the deployment check; keeping the previous files makes rollback trivial.

              5.8 Hosting on Azure or AWS

              The servers are ordinary Python web applications. The test run in Part 3 ran them on Linux unchanged, so they can move to the cloud. What they need from any platform follows from earlier chapters.

              What any platform must provide

              • Memory per instance of 2–6 GB, by the rule in chapter 5.5, and plenty of headroom at start-up.
              • Always on, with a readiness check. Start-up takes 20–60 seconds, so no scale-to-zero, and traffic only after /health answers.
              • One running copy per client, or a shared store for get_more_results cursors. They live in process memory (chapter 1.5), so two copies behind a load balancer could lose them.
              • Path-based routing and HTTPS, replacing IIS and ARR.
              • Network access to the QA databases, Qdrant, Entra ID and Azure OpenAI.
              • Secret storage and log collection.

              How today’s pieces map

              TodayOn AzureOn AWS
              IIS + ARR + URL RewriteApplication Gateway or Front Door, path rulesApplication Load Balancer, path rules
              NSSM servicesContainer Apps, App Service or AKS (or a VM with services)ECS (Fargate or EC2), EKS (or EC2 with services)
              .env secretsKey Vault with managed identitySecrets Manager with an IAM role
              Graphs on local diskBaked into a per-client image, or mounted from Azure Files or BlobBaked into an image, or EFS / S3
              Qdrant on the VMA Qdrant container, or Qdrant’s managed cloudSame
              QA databases on the VMSQL Server on a VM, Azure SQL, or kept on-prem over VPNRDS for SQL Server, SQL Server on EC2, or on-prem over VPN
              Log filesAzure Monitor / Application InsightsCloudWatch
              Entra ID sign-inUnchanged: Entra ID works the same wherever the server runs

              Three realistic paths

              PathEffortGood forWatch
              Lift and shift: the same Windows set-up on an Azure VM or EC2LowestMoving quickly, keeping every procedure in this PartSame single-VM limits; you still run IIS and NSSM
              One container per client on a managed container platformMediumIndependent deploys, health-checked restarts, per-client sizingLarge images if graphs are baked in; set minimum one replica; check memory limits of the plan you choose
              Kubernetes (AKS or EKS)HighestMany clients, many environments, an existing platform teamOperational overhead for eleven fairly static services

              The deciding question

              The hardest part of moving isn’t the MCP servers; it is the QA databases they read live. If those stay on-premises, any cloud host needs a private network path to them (VPN or ExpressRoute or Direct Connect), and live SQL latency grows. Deciding where the QA databases live usually decides the rest.

              Key takeaways

              • Any platform must give each client an always-on, memory-heavy, single-copy service with a readiness check.
              • Every on-prem piece has a direct Azure and AWS equivalent; Entra ID stays as it is.
              • Where the QA databases live decides more than which compute service you pick.

              Part 6

              How it behaves in a conversation

              Your design questions, answered with evidence: who decides what, how context is managed and trimmed, how stopping works, what happens when a tool fails or isn’t approved, what live SQL does when it finds nothing, and why there’s no agent framework.

                6.1 Who decides what

                Most of the questions in this Part have the same first answer: the server doesn’t decide that. An MCP server is a toolbox. The reasoning loop, the context and the approvals all live in the AI application. Four parties share the work:

                PartyDecidesDoesn’t decide
                The personThe question, approvals (when asked), follow-ups, which connector is onWhich tools run or in what order
                The model (Claude, GPT)Which tool to call next, with which arguments; when it has enough; what the answer saysWhat a tool returns; whether a call is allowed
                The host (Claude app, Claude Code, Cowork, ChatGPT)Runs the loop: sends tool calls, enforces permissions and approvals, manages the context windowWhat the tools mean
                The MCP serverWhether a call is valid; what each tool returns; how big an answer may be; what state to suggest nextAnything about the conversation: it never sees it

                The server still shapes the conversation strongly through what it sends: tool descriptions, the instructions playbook (chapter 3.10), state suggestions, error messages that say what to do, and size limits. It steers by information, not by control.

                Key takeaways

                • The model chooses and stops; the host runs the loop and the approvals; the server answers calls.
                • The server never sees the conversation, only one tool call at a time.
                • It steers the model through descriptions, the playbook, state, error messages and size limits.

                6.2 How is context managed?

                There are two kinds of context, kept in two different places on purpose.

                The conversation: in the host

                Everything the model has seen (the question, tool descriptions, the instructions, every tool answer) lives in the model’s context window, which the host manages. The server keeps no copy and no memory of earlier calls. That is why it scales simply and why any call can be retried.

                Working state: passed explicitly

                Multi-step questions need some continuity: which screen we are on, which method, which SQL statements have been seen. Instead of storing that per conversation, each tool returns it in a STATE UPDATES trailer, and the model passes it back as ordinary arguments on later calls. The playbook says it plainly: “State fields are explicit tool arguments — there is no hidden pipeline state.”

                State fieldHoldsExample
                active_formThe screen in focusEndUserUnit::TEndUserForm::FORM (a class, unit or caption works too)
                active_unit, active_class, active_methodThe code in focusEndUserUnit::TEndUserForm::sbtnSaveClick::METHOD
                active_table, active_column, active_procedure, active_view, active_indexThe database object in focusdbo.ENDUSER.TABLE
                sql_contextThe SQL statements collected so farA list of statements, each with tables, columns, parameters and text

                Required state shows up in each tool’s published schema (chapter 3.4), so the model can see it must find a screen before asking about one. A tool that needs active_form and doesn’t get it answers: Validation failed: Tool 'get_form_overview' requires 'active_form'. Call the appropriate discovery tool first to obtain it.

                sql_context: a delta, not a pile

                sql_context grows across a conversation, so it is handled with care. The model passes back what it already has; tools return only the statements it doesn’t have yet; and each statement’s text is cut to 600 characters (SQL_CONTEXT_TEXT_CHARS in tools/tools/_helpers.py). The same SQL never comes back twice, and one long statement can’t fill the context.

                Key takeaways

                • The conversation lives in the host; the server keeps nothing between calls.
                • Working state travels as tool arguments, suggested by each answer’s STATE UPDATES trailer.
                • sql_context is passed as a delta, with each statement capped at 600 characters.

                6.3 Does it drop information it doesn’t need?

                Yes, deliberately and in layers, because a model’s context is finite and every token costs. The rule throughout is that nothing is cut silently: every cut says what was left out and how to get it.

                LayerWhat it doesHow the model gets more
                Focused toolsAnswer one question (counts, a chain, a list) instead of returning filesCall a more detailed tool, or get_source_slice for source lines
                Scope rulesVendor methods skipped unless include_vendor; call chains to depth 4 and at most 200 methods; name-only matches kept apart from real stepsPass the flag; follow a method with its own tool; chain_truncated says when it stopped
                PagingLong lists come 50 rows at a time, with full countsCall again with offset = next_offset, or pass limit
                Token budget (first pass)An answer over about 16,000 tokens has its longest lists and strings trimmed, and a note addedThe note names the paging and narrowing arguments of that tool
                Hard cap (second pass)Text over 80,000 characters, state trailer included, is cut at a line with a noticeget_more_results(cursor), once, within 30 minutes
                PreviewsDocumentation chunks come as 500-character previewsget_adaptive_siblings for the full text
                State deltasql_context returns only new statements, capped at 600 characters eachThe full SQL via get_method_sql or get_form_sql

                Why two size passes?

                The first pass (tools/tools/_budget.py) works on the data: it trims lists inside the JSON so the answer stays valid, paging fields stay right, and the note can name the tool’s own arguments. The second pass (tools/budget.py) works on the final text, including the state trailer, which the first pass leaves whole, and guarantees an absolute ceiling with a way to continue. One keeps answers useful; the other keeps them bounded. In the test run, find_dead_methods showed the first pass working: about 30,839 tokens trimmed to fit, with “dead_methods shows 97 of 200” and how to see more (chapter 3.5).

                The host may also drop or summarise older parts of a long conversation to fit its context window. That is outside the server’s control. Because the server’s state lives in arguments, not in the server, the model can always re-establish it by calling a discovery tool again.

                Key takeaways

                • Seven layers keep answers small: focused tools, scope rules, paging, a token budget, a hard cap, previews and a state delta.
                • Every cut is announced, with the exact way to get the rest.
                • The host’s own context management is separate; explicit state makes it recoverable.

                6.4 How does it decide where to stop?

                Stopping happens at two levels, decided by different parties.

                Inside a tool: fixed, published limits

                Every walk through the graph has a visited set and a limit (chapter 1.8), and the limits are part of each tool’s description, so the model knows them before calling. get_action_chain, for example, follows calls to depth 4, lists at most 200 methods, and reports chain_truncated: true if it stopped early. Lists stop at a page; every call stops at 90 seconds. These limits are deterministic: the same question on the same graph always stops in the same place.

                Across tools: the model decides

                Whether to make another call or answer is the model’s judgement, guided by:

                • The question. “Which table does Save write?” ends sooner than “explain the whole save process”.
                • The playbook’s recipes, which show where a typical investigation ends, for example find_form_by_name → get_form_overview → get_action_chain for “What does [screen] do?”.
                • The answers’ own signals: truncated, next_offset, chain_truncated, not_in_sql_graph, found_in_sql_graph: false. The playbook tells the model what each means and what to say about it.
                • The host’s limits on how long a single turn may run.

                The server never says “done”. There is no completion signal in MCP for that, and the server can’t know what the person needs. What it guarantees is that each answer states whether it is complete.

                Key takeaways

                • Tools stop at fixed, documented limits and say so when they do.
                • The model decides when the whole question is answered, guided by the question, the playbook and the answers’ completeness flags.
                • Answer time grows with the number of calls the model chooses to make, not with server work (chapter 3.11).

                6.5 What if a tool fails?

                Failures are designed as instructions. Each kind comes back as something the model can read and act on, and the conversation continues.

                FailureWhat the model receivesWhat it typically does next
                Missing or wrong argumentsisError with what is wrong, e.g. Tool 'sql_query' does not take 'limit', 'table_name' (did you mean 'table'?). Its parameters are: column, operation, query, rows, table.Retries with corrected arguments
                Required state missing… requires 'active_form'. Call the appropriate discovery tool first …Calls a discovery tool, then retries
                Name not foundScreen 'Customer Maintenance' was not found … Did you mean: …?Picks a candidate, or asks the person
                Too slowTool '…' did not finish within 90 s …Narrows the question (filters, a smaller scope)
                A bug inside a toolInternal error in tool '…' (…). This is a fault in the server, not an empty result: do not conclude that the item does not exist. Try a different tool or rephrase the request. (the full traceback goes to the log)Tries another tool, or tells the person
                An unknown tool nameJSON-RPC error -32602 with the list of valid namesCorrects the name
                Token expired or invalidHTTP 401 to the host, not the modelThe host signs in again or refreshes the token
                Instance down or restartingHTTP 502 from IIS to the hostThe host reports a connector error; retrying a minute later works

                In the code

                The first row is a real example worth knowing. The playbook’s own sql_query recipes write table_name=, column_name= and limit=, but the tool’s parameters are table, column and rows. A model that follows the playbook is corrected by this error message and succeeds on the second try. It works, but it costs a round trip each time (Part 7).

                A tool failure doesn’t end the conversation or affect other calls. Each call is independent, and a failing tool can’t corrupt the shared indexes, which are read-only.

                Key takeaways

                • Every failure becomes a readable message with a next step: fix arguments, discover first, pick a candidate, narrow down.
                • Protocol and sign-in failures go to the host, which handles them without the model.
                • Failures are isolated: one bad call can’t affect another.

                6.6 What if a tool isn’t approved?

                Approval happens entirely in the host, before anything is sent. If a call isn’t approved, the server never receives it; there is nothing in the server’s logs.

                How Claude handles it

                In Claude, each connector’s tools have a permission setting: Always allow, Needs approval or Blocked, grouped into read-only tools and write or delete tools (Claude Help Center). In organisations that use custom roles, admins can set a ceiling per role, and a blocked tool is hidden: Claude can’t see or call it. For Claude Code, its own managed settings combine with these, and the most restrictive wins. With Needs approval, the person sees each call and can typically allow it once, allow it always (unless an admin has removed that option) or deny it.

                What happens after a denial

                • The host tells the model the call wasn’t run.
                • The model continues without it: it may try another tool that covers the question, answer from what it already has (saying what is missing), or ask the person.
                • Since state lives in arguments, nothing on the server side is left half-done.

                A sensible policy for these servers

                Every tool on these servers is read-only and says so in its annotations (readOnlyHint: true, chapter 3.4). Always allow for the graph and documentation tools avoids an approval click on every one of the several calls a typical question needs. sql_query is the one worth considering for Needs approval. It is read-only and heavily guarded (chapter 3.8), but it runs model-written SQL against a real database, and a person glancing at each query is cheap insurance.

                Key takeaways

                • Approval is the host’s job; a denied call never reaches the server.
                • The model carries on without the call: another tool, a partial answer, or a question back.
                • For these read-only servers, allow the graph tools; consider approval for sql_query.

                6.7 What if live SQL finds nothing or fails?

                “Found nothing” and “failed” are different, and the answers keep them apart.

                SituationWhat comes backSensible next step
                The query ran and matched no rowsA normal result: (no rows), row_count: 0. Not an errorCheck the filter: distinct shows real values, and a case or spelling mismatch is common. Then report “none found”, which is a real answer
                The query was refusedisError naming the rule, e.g. “SELECT … INTO creates a table; only plain SELECTs can run.”Rewrite as a plain SELECT
                Busy (all four slots in use)“Live SQL is busy … Try again shortly, or answer from the graph tools if they cover the question.”Wait, or use the graph
                Too slow“The query was stopped after 30 seconds. Narrow it — add a WHERE clause or TOP, or join fewer tables — and try again.”Narrow the query
                Database unreachable“Live SQL is unavailable: … the database connection failed.”Answer from the graph, and say live data couldn’t be checked
                Not configured on this instance“Live SQL is not configured on this server (NGENUE_SQL_CONN_STRING is not set).”Same
                Switched off by the self-check“Live SQL is switched off: the server’s database login can change data …”Same; an operator must fix the login

                Much of what people ask live SQL for can also be answered from the graphs, without data: table structure (get_table_columns), what writes a table (find_writers), which screens use it (find_forms_using_table). get_menu_path shows the pattern. Without a database it still answered from the graph and marked its menu part "menu_source": "unavailable" (chapter 3.8).

                Key takeaways

                • No rows is a valid answer, not an error; refusals, busy, slow, unreachable and switched-off each have their own message.
                • Every failure message says what to do, including “answer from the graph tools”.
                • Structure and usage questions don’t need live SQL at all.

                6.8 Why plain Python, and when a framework would help

                The servers use FastAPI and a few libraries, but no agent framework (such as LangChain or LangGraph) and no MCP SDK. Both choices follow from what the server is.

                No agent framework: the server isn’t an agent

                Agent frameworks orchestrate a model: they call it, parse its tool choices, run tools, loop, keep memory. In this system that loop already exists, in Claude and ChatGPT. The server makes no chat-model calls at all; its only AI call is one embedding per documentation search (chapter 1.9). An agent framework would have nothing to orchestrate.

                No MCP SDK: control over a moving protocol

                Official MCP SDKs exist, and they would have saved writing the protocol layer. The hand-written layer is small (chapter 3.3), and it gave the team exact control:

                • serving the stateless 2026-07-28 revision and the older handshake at the same time, leniently;
                • mapping each error to the JSON-RPC code and HTTP status that keep every client working (-32601 as 400, not 404);
                • checking structured answers against their schema before sending, because one client rejects mismatches.

                The cost is that every protocol change is the team’s to implement. The missing ping is the visible example (chapter 3.3).

                When a framework would help

                If you want to…Consider
                Build your own assistant (an internal chat page, a nightly QA run) that uses these toolsAn agent framework, or a model API’s own tool-use and MCP support: they provide the loop the hosts provide today
                Stop maintaining the protocol layer as MCP evolvesThe official MCP Python SDK for transport and protocol. The tools are plain classes, so they can move over largely unchanged
                Evaluate answer quality systematicallyAn evaluation harness that replays question sets through a model with these tools; the existing QA workbooks are a starting set
                Answer the same multi-step questions oftenA composite tool on the server (one call instead of three), which plain Python makes easy

                Key takeaways

                • No agent framework, because the server isn’t an agent: the loop lives in the AI host.
                • No MCP SDK, for control over a changing protocol, at the price of maintaining it.
                • Frameworks earn their place if you build your own assistant or evaluation loop around these tools.

                Part 7

                Observations and risks

                Kept apart from the explanations on purpose: what could break, leak or mislead, how likely it is, and what to do about it.

                  Every item below was found while writing this handbook, and each points to the chapter with the evidence. Three labels say how sure each finding is: verified (read in the code, or seen in a run), observed in the shared copy (true of the archives provided; production may differ), and to check (likely, but only the VM can confirm). Severity combines impact and likelihood; effort is small (hours), medium (days) or large (weeks).

                  7.2 Security

                  #FindingWhy it mattersWhat to do
