Verified (4.4, 4.5).Any token from any connector is accepted by every instance; anyone who can sign in to the app can reach every client’s code and QA data.One app per client with “Assignment required” and per-client groups. Then add an scp check (and optionally roles) in OAuthMiddleware.
                  S2Real .env files inside both server archives. Observed in the shared copy (3.13); not opened.They normally hold the SQL password, the Azure OpenAI key and the Qdrant key. Archives get forwarded.Rotate those secrets if the archives travelled; exclude .env from archives and source control; restrict NTFS permissions; move to Key Vault (4.6).
                  S3The new-UI server’s live SQL lacks safeguards: no per-query timeout (its timeout=30 is the login timeout), one connection shared across threads without a lock, no read-only self-check, a keyword check that also scans strings. Verified (3.12).A slow query keeps running on SQL Server; concurrent calls can interfere; safety depends entirely on the login.Confirm the login is db_datareader only now; port tools/tools/sql_live/_live_sql.py, which is self-contained.
                  S4/health is public and names the client, the source database, graph versions and dates, and a code build id. Verified locally (4.1); external reachability is to check.Free reconnaissance for anyone who finds the address.An IIS rule answering 404 to outside callers for /<client>/v1/health; keep it for the VM and monitoring.
                  S5Three “Token debug” lines and the user name logged at INFO on every request. Verified (4.4).Noisy logs full of personal identifiers, kept as long as the logs.Change the debug lines to logger.debug; set a log retention period.
                  S6Tool answers leave the VM for the AI providers, including source code and, through live SQL, QA data. Verified (5.1).Fine for nGenue’s own code, but QA databases may hold client data that contracts cover.Confirm what the QA databases contain, and that the AI providers’ terms fit those contracts.
                  S7The authorization server metadata borrows Entra ID’s issuer while being served from the server’s address. Verified (4.3).Works with today’s clients; a strict client following RFC 8414 could refuse it.Keep an eye on client updates; nothing to change now.
                  S8Auth runs before CORS, so a browser’s preflight request to /mcp gets 401; ALLOWED_ORIGINS empty means any origin. Verified (1.4).Only browser-based clients are affected; the AI hosts are not.If a browser tool is ever needed, let OPTIONS through the auth middleware and list origins explicitly.
                  S9HOST defaults to 0.0.0.0 in the code, though the template sets 127.0.0.1. Verified (Appendix C).An instance whose .env lacks the line listens on every interface, reachable without IIS unless a firewall blocks its port.Set HOST=127.0.0.1 on every instance; change the code default to match the template.

                  7.3 Reliability and capacity

                  #FindingWhy it mattersWhat to do
                  R1Each restart closes the port for 20–60 s, and after a reboot all eleven instances parse their graphs at once. Verified (3.2, 5.2).Clients get IIS 502s during restarts; boot is the memory peak of the whole VM.Stagger or delay service starts; restart off-hours; consider the two-port switch (5.4) for busy clients.
                  R2SQL Server, Qdrant and eleven memory-heavy processes share one VM. To check: SQL Server’s memory cap and the ARR time-out.An uncapped SQL Server can squeeze the instances; an ARR time-out under 90 s cuts long calls.Cap SQL Server’s memory (5.5); set the ARR time-out above 90 s (5.3); size with the formula plus the reranker.
                  R3One VM, no fail-over. Verified (5.1).A VM, disk or network outage stops all clients at once.Decide the acceptable downtime; at minimum, keep a documented rebuild procedure and the last good graphs off the VM.
                  R4Timeouts stop waiting, not work (except legacy live SQL, which cancels). Verified (1.2).A pathological call keeps a thread busy after its answer was given up.Rare with millisecond tools; watch for tool_timeout in the logs.
                  R5ping isn’t implemented (answers -32601). Verified (3.3).A client or monitor that pings sees an error.Add "ping": lambda params: {} to the handler’s method table.
                  R6In the shared copy, AEP’s SQL graph came from nGenueMainlineQA_UX, not an AEP database. Observed in the shared copy (3.2).Cross-graph links and SQL tools would describe another database than the client’s.Check each instance’s /health sql_graph.source_database; build one SQL graph per client database.
                  R7get_more_results cursors live in process memory. Verified (1.5).Fine with one process per client; breaks with two copies behind a load balancer.Only matters for scale-out (5.8): move cursors to a shared store first.
                  R8Lenient protocol handling: the routing headers of 2026-07-28 aren’t required, header/_meta version mismatches aren’t rejected, and batches are still accepted. Verified (1.5).Good for compatibility today; it drifts from the specification over time.Tighten once all clients speak 2026-07-28; consider the official conformance tests.

                  7.4 Operations

                  #FindingWhy it mattersWhat to do
                  O1The deployed version may differ from the repository. This workspace’s tool list for production AEP has 135 tools with older descriptions; the repository has 148. To check (3.12).The handbook describes code that may not be running; fixes may not have shipped.Run the /health table script (5.4) on the VM. If builds differ, redeploy; if they match, refresh the connector’s tool list in Claude.
                  O2Builds and deployments are manual. Verified (2.2, 5.7).Easy mistakes: omitting --scriptdom-url silently weakens SQL parsing; a failed census can ship; nobody records what was deployed.The Jenkins pipeline in 5.7, using the builders’ existing gates.
                  O3The new-UI builder clones the latest grammar; its shipped log shows the census failing (252 method bodies missing) while the graph was still written. Verified (2.5, 2.8).Graphs can change with the build date, not the code; 252 methods may be missing from the new UI’s graph.Port grammar_pin from the legacy builder; rebuild; block deployment unless the census passes.
                  O4AEP’s graph (version 2.5) predates the builder’s identity stamps: builder, source_commit and source_fingerprint are empty. Observed in the shared copy (3.2).No way to tell which builder or source produced it; newer graph features are missing (tools note this).Rebuild each client with the current legacy builder, passing --client and --source-revision.
                  O5The archives look like copies of deployed folders: real .env files, graphs, logs and retired tool folders that make one test fail. Observed in the shared copy (3.13).Source and deployment are mixed, which is how secrets travel.Keep source in Git, without .env or graphs; deploy from Git; delete retired folders.
                  O6No automated health monitoring is visible. To check.A degraded or stopped instance is found by users.Poll every instance’s /health each minute; alert on failure, degraded or a differing code build (5.6).
                  O7Secrets will need a renewal calendar once each client has its own Entra app. Verified as a consequence (4.5).An expired connector secret silently breaks sign-in for that client.Track expiry dates; renew ahead; Key Vault can hold the server-side secrets.
                  O8A 140 MB database_schema.json is shipped but never read. Verified (2.9).Clutter and copy time.Leave it out of deployments.

                  7.5 Code health

                  #FindingWhy it mattersWhat to do
                  C1Two forks drifting apart: the servers differ in hundreds of lines (loader 828 vs 431, DelphiIndex 2,388 vs 1,236; the new UI lacks the token budget and the live-SQL module), and so do the builders. Verified (2.8, 3.12).Every fix must be made twice, and the new-UI line lags behind in safety.Extract one shared core package (protocol, registry, budget, live SQL, auth, index base) with product-specific tools and graph adapters on top.
                  C2A hand-written MCP layer on a protocol that changed fundamentally in 2026-07-28. Verified (6.8).Each protocol change is the team’s to implement; ping shows the cost of a missed detail.Follow the specification’s changelog; consider the official SDK for transport and protocol once it supports both eras; keep the tools as they are.
                  C3The playbook calls sql_query with wrong argument names (table_name, column_name, limit instead of table, column, rows). Verified (6.5).Every such call fails once and is retried: wasted time and tokens.Fix the recipes; extend the start-up drift check from tool names to argument names.
                  C4The legacy playbook is about 75,000 characters (roughly 19,000 tokens). Verified (3.10).Likely paid in context and cost on every conversation.Measure answer quality with a trimmed version on the QA question sets; keep what earns its place.
                  C5Very large modules: DelphiIndex (2,388 lines), the builder CLI (about 1,900 lines). Verified.Hard to review and to change safely.Split by concern when next touched (registries, search, screen meaning).
                  C6The new-UI live SQL relies on an optional sqlglot that isn’t a declared dependency. Verified (3.12).Its third check layer may be silently absent.Declare it, or replace the module as in S3.
                  C7The new-UI server’s dependency lists are incomplete: requirements.txt lacks pyodbc and jsonschema; pyproject.toml lists only four packages. Verified (Appendix B).A fresh install from either file gives a server whose live SQL can’t import its driver.Declare every import in both files; test a clean install in the pipeline.

                  For balance

                  These lists are long because this handbook looked hard, not because the system is weak. The legacy line in particular shows unusual discipline: deterministic builds, self-reporting diagnostics, a census for silent losses, a contract between builder and server, failures written as instructions, seven layers of live-SQL safety, and almost 2,400 server tests that pass. Most findings are about the new-UI line catching up, about operations around the code, and about identity, all fixable without redesign.

                  Part 8

                  Before you build something like this

                  The prerequisites, a learning path and a stage-by-stage blueprint for building your own code knowledge graph and MCP server.

                    8.1 Prerequisites

                    A system like this touches many fields, but each at a practical, learnable depth. Before starting, check you have, or can get, the following.

                    Skills

                    SkillDepth neededWhere this handbook covers it
                    PythonClasses, dataclasses, type hints, decorators, exceptions, packaging; comfortable reading 2,000-line modules1.1
                    ConcurrencyWhen to use processes, threads or asyncio; never blocking an event loop1.2
                    Data shapesJSON, pydantic models, JSON Schema1.3
                    Web basicsHTTP, JSON-RPC, FastAPI, middleware, reverse proxies1.4
                    MCPTools, schemas, the two protocol eras, errors versus tool errors1.5, 3.3
                    IdentityOAuth code flow with PKCE, JWT validation, an Entra ID app registration1.6, Part 4
                    ParsingTokenizers, recursive descent, tree-sitter trees, the visitor pattern1.7
                    Graph modellingChoosing node and edge types from the questions to answer; ids; traversal with limits1.8, 2.4
                    The target languageEnough Delphi (or whatever you analyse) to recognise its constructs2.1
                    SQL ServerLogins and roles, timeouts, parameters1.10, 3.8
                    HostingWindows services and IIS, or containers in the cloud1.11, Part 5
                    Testingpytest, fixtures, golden data, regression gates2.7, 3.13

                    Access and tools

                    • Source code for every product line and client, ideally in Git, with commit ids you can record in each graph.
                    • A database copy per client (QA or anonymised), and a login you can make read-only.
                    • An Entra ID administrator who can create app registrations and enterprise applications.
                    • A build machine with Python 3.11, Git, a C compiler and the .NET 9 SDK (for ScriptDOM).
                    • A host with enough memory (chapter 5.5), HTTPS, and somewhere for secrets.
                    • An AI client that supports remote MCP connectors, and MCP Inspector for debugging.

                    The mindset that makes it work

                    Three habits matter more than any technology choice. First, start from questions: collect the real questions people need answered before modelling anything. Second, be honest about uncertainty: a graph and tools that say “unknown” or “cut here” are worth more than ones that sound complete. Third, make quality measurable: golden counts, golden questions, gates that fail loudly.

                    Key takeaways

                    • About a dozen skills, each at a practical depth, all covered somewhere in this handbook.
                    • Secure the access early: source with commit ids, a read-only database login, Entra ID admin help.
                    • Start from real questions, report uncertainty, and measure quality.

                    8.2 A learning path

                    Eight steps, each ending in something small you build yourself. Done in order, each one makes the next easier. Allow roughly a week per step alongside other work.

                    StepLearnBuildRead
                    1Modern Python and asyncioA script that loads a large JSON file in a worker thread while an asyncio loop keeps answering a timer1.1, 1.2
                    2FastAPI, JSON-RPC, JSON SchemaA FastAPI app with one POST endpoint that dispatches JSON-RPC methods and validates arguments against a schema1.3, 1.4, 3.3
                    3MCPA two-tool MCP server (tools/list, tools/call); connect MCP Inspector and then Claude to it on a laptop1.5, 3.4, 3.13; modelcontextprotocol.io
                    4ParsingParse one Delphi unit with tree-sitter and print its methods with line numbers; write a tiny recursive-descent parser for DFM objects1.7; tree-sitter docs
                    5Graph modellingA graph of one screen: units, classes, methods, components, event bindings, calls; adjacency lists; a callers query with depth limits1.8, 2.4
                    6Tool designThree tools over that graph: find a screen, describe it, trace an action, passing ids through state; add paging and a size note3.5, 6.2, 6.3
                    7IdentityAn Entra ID app; a token-checking middleware with PyJWT; an end-to-end sign-in from Claude to your laptop server through a tunnel1.6, Part 4; Microsoft identity platform
                    8Quality and operationsGolden questions with expected answers run by pytest; a /health endpoint reporting what is loaded; a scripted deploy2.7, 3.13, 5.4, 5.6

                    Try it

                    Before step 4, run the real thing. Start the legacy server locally against a graph with AUTH_MODE=none (chapter 3.13), connect MCP Inspector, and replay the calls in chapter 3.5. Seeing real answers first makes every later step concrete.

                    Key takeaways

                    • Eight steps from Python to operations, each ending in a small working build.
                    • Connect a real AI client early (step 3); it changes how you design tools.
                    • Finish with quality and operations, not as an afterthought.

                    8.3 A blueprint, stage by stage

                    This is how to build a system like this one, for nGenue’s code or any other, in an order that delivers something useful early and avoids the problems found in Part 7. Each stage lists its output, its decisions and the trap to avoid.

                    Stage 0 · Questions before code

                    • Output: 30–50 real questions with expected answers, written by the people who will ask them (“What happens when I click Save on End User?”).
                    • Decisions: which questions need code structure, behaviour, the database, documentation or live data.
                    • Trap: modelling the whole language first. Model what the questions need.

                    Stage 1 · A graph model from the questions

                    • Output: node and edge types, an id scheme, provenance fields, as pydantic models with a generated schema.
                    • Decisions: deterministic, readable ids (chapter 2.4); one graph per product line and client; a _metadata block with builder identity, source revision, versions and features from day one.
                    • Trap: ids from counters. They make every rebuild a new world.

                    Stage 2 · A builder that reports on itself

                    • Output: discovery → parse → resolve → behaviours → validate → write, as in chapter 2.5.
                    • Decisions: grammar-based parsing, a pinned grammar, an authoritative SQL parser, diagnostics instead of exceptions, byte-identical output.
                    • Trap: silent loss. Add the census and coverage checks early; make the build fail loudly when a required service is missing.

                    Stage 3 · Five good tools before fifty

                    • Output: discovery, overview, trace, SQL for a screen, and table usage, over in-memory indexes.
                    • Decisions: explicit state in arguments, paging with counts, a size budget with notes, errors written as instructions, published limits.
                    • Trap: tools that return whole files. Answer the question asked; offer a path to more.

                    Stage 4 · The MCP server

                    • Output: an MCP endpoint with tools/list and tools/call, a registry, threads and timeouts, /health.
                    • Decisions: an official SDK for the protocol unless you have a specific reason not to; if you write it yourself, include ping and run the conformance tests.
                    • Trap: one code base per product line. Build one core with plug-in tool sets and graph adapters (C1 in Part 7).

                    Stage 5 · The playbook

                    • Output: instructions with state rules, query recipes and honesty rules, tested against the Stage 0 questions.
                    • Decisions: what the model must never claim (absence from a graph isn’t proof of absence); how long the playbook may be.
                    • Trap: recipes that drift from the tools. Check tool and argument names automatically (C3).

                    Stage 6 · Identity and secrets from the start

                    • Output: one Entra app per client with assignment required; a token check including scope; secrets in a vault.
                    • Decisions: who may see which client’s code and data; how connectors get their credentials.
                    • Trap: “one app for now”. Retrofitting isolation is harder than starting with it (S1).

                    Stage 7 · Hosting and a pipeline

                    • Output: a host sized by the memory rule, a reverse proxy, health monitoring, and a build-gate-deploy-verify pipeline.
                    • Decisions: on-premises or cloud, decided by where the databases live (chapter 5.8).
                    • Trap: manual deploys from archives. They are how versions drift and secrets travel (O1, O5).

                    Stage 8 · Measure, then grow

                    • Output: a scorecard on the Stage 0 questions per release: correct, partial, wrong, calls used, tokens used.
                    • Decisions: what to add next: behavioural walkers, documentation search, live SQL with its safety layers, more clients.
                    • Trap: adding tools without measuring. Every new tool is something the model might choose wrongly.

                    What this system teaches

                    The strongest ideas here are worth copying anywhere. Graphs built deterministically and checked for silent loss. Tools that answer one question, say what they left out and how to get more. State passed in the open. Errors written as next steps. Safety in layers where real data is touched. The weak points are mostly ones of growth: two product lines forked instead of sharing a core, identity and secrets set up for one tenant-wide app and plain files, manual operations. Starting with Stages 4, 6 and 7 done right avoids all of them.

                    Key takeaways

                    • Start from questions, model only what they need, and build a builder that reports its own losses.
                    • Five good tools, one shared core, a tested playbook, per-client identity and secrets from day one.
                    • Automate build and deploy, measure answers on real questions, and grow only what the measurements justify.

On graph 3.0 the field itself can be the target (a field that declares no component), code on other screens reaches the component by type (aForm.edName.Visible), and rows carry target_resolution and target_kind. On older graphs such control accesses are field reads and writes, marked ui_control_value; field_access_note says which applies. For a data-aware control, binding (datasource, dataset, the TField it shows); for a TField, shown_by (the controls showing it); instances lists the copies of the component the same field declares on other screens (an inline frame’s child on each host). Requires active_unit or active_class plus field_name.

                      sql_live · 1 tool · What is actually in the data?

                      Execute read-only operations against the live nGenue SQL Server database. Four operations available:

                      Use this tool whenever you need live database information instead of asking the user to run a query. Prefer ‘describe’, ‘sample’, and ‘distinct’ for quick lookups — use ‘query’ for anything more complex.

                      Only SELECT queries are accepted. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL, EXEC, and SELECT INTO are all blocked. Results capped at 1,000 rows.

                      operationstringyesWhich operation to run. ‘query’ for arbitrary SELECT, ‘describe’ to show table structure, ‘sample’ for sample rows, ‘distinct’ for distinct column values with counts.
                      querystringThe T-SQL SELECT statement to execute. Required when operation=‘query’. Ignored otherwise.

Scans sql_placeholder nodes whose columns_referenced list includes the column and whose tables_referenced list includes the table. Use this for column-change impact analysis to know which Delphi UI screens need their field definitions, MaxLength, or display widths updated. Each form entry also lists captions: the on-screen labels of the fields bound to the column on that screen. Pair with find_objects_referencing_column for complete SQL + Delphi coverage.

                      column_namestringyesColumn name (e.g. ‘ACCOUNTNUMBER’).
                      find_writersWhich Delphi screens and routines write a table, or one column of it.

                      Which Delphi screens and routines write a table, or one column of it. Three routes: a statement that writes it (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE: its written table and columns; basis says whether the graph’s parser or the statement’s text named the table), a call to a stored procedure that writes it — directly or through up to max_depth procedures calling it (SQL graph) — and a dataset write (Post, Delete, ApplyUpdates ... on a dataset whose own SQL reads the table; for a column, a field write such as FieldByName(‘X’).Value := ... or a Post of a dataset with a stored field for it). A DELETE removes the row, so it counts for every column. Each row gives the route, owners, the methods running it, screens (or units outside any screen) and line; by_form summarises. operation narrows to INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE (a statement writing several tables: the write this table gets). Design-time SQL that the code replaces before every call running it is listed apart (replaced_design_time_sql). Paged.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      table_namestringyesSQL table name in any spelling, e.g. ENDUSER.
                      column_namestringOnly writers of this column. Optional.
                      operationstringOnly this kind of write. Optional.
                      max_depthintegerLevels of procedures calling a writer procedure. Default 2.
                      limitintegerHow many writers to return (default 50). Totals always count everything.
                      offsetintegerSkip this many first — pass next_offset from the previous answer for the next page.
                      get_cross_graph_contextGet a unified view of a SQL table from both the Delphi application graph and the SQL database graph simultaneously.

                      Get a unified view of a SQL table from both the Delphi application graph and the SQL database graph simultaneously. Shows which Delphi forms reference the table via SQL, and which SQL procedures/triggers/functions operate on it. sql_graph says whether the table is in the SQL graph this instance serves (when it is not, its SQL side cannot be shown). Delphi SQL in units without a screen is listed by unit. Each kind of SQL object lists up to limit_per_kind (default 25, writers first) with its total, and up to 100 Delphi forms with their total. The ideal starting point for cross-graph questions about a table.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      table_namestringyesSQL table name to analyse from both graphs.
                      limit_per_kindintegerSQL objects listed per kind (procedures, triggers, functions). Default 25.
                      get_procedure_usageIs a stored procedure still called, and from where?

                      Is a stored procedure still called, and from where? With procedure_name (any spelling): the Delphi statements that run it — SQL text or a stored-procedure component’s ProcedureName — with the methods running each (run_by), the screens or units, the line and the screens inheriting a base form that runs it; its SQL-graph callers up to max_depth levels, each flagged when Delphi calls it; and a verdict: called_from_delphi, called_through_procedures, called_by_trigger, called_only_from_sql or no_callers_found. Without procedure_name: every procedure in the SQL graph that no Delphi statement names and nothing calls (candidates for removal; needs the SQL graph). Paged.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      procedure_namestringProcedure name, e.g. ‘LSP_SAVE_ENDUSER’. Omit to list unused procedures.
                      max_depthintegerLevels of SQL callers to follow. Default 3.
                      limitintegerHow many rows to return (default 100). Totals always count everything.
                      offsetintegerSkip this many first — pass next_offset from the previous answer for the next page.
                      trace_procedure_to_uiWhich button, menu item, action or screen event runs a stored procedure, end to end: the Delphi statements that name…

                      Which button, menu item, action or screen event runs a stored procedure, end to end: the Delphi statements that name it (SQL text or a stored-procedure component), the methods running each, their callers up to max_depth levels, and the user action each path starts from — a DFM event on a control, an action and the controls using it (with captions), a screen event (OnCreate, OnShow), or a handler assigned in code — on the screen whose own or inherited wiring runs it. A dataset event handler (BeforePost, AfterPost ...) is followed to the code that posts or deletes the dataset; a scroll handler is also a record_change (the user selecting another record). method_chain runs from the handler the user triggers down to the method running the statement. Paths reaching no user action are listed: system_event (a timer, the application’s idle loop), or no_user_action (startup code, utility routines nobody calls). Paged.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      procedure_namestringyesStored procedure name, any spelling.
                      max_depthintegerLevels of callers to follow above the method running it. Default 4.
                      limitintegerHow many paths to return (default 50). Totals always count everything.
                      offsetintegerSkip this many first — pass next_offset from the previous answer for the next page.
                      trace_table_write_chainTrace the complete end-to-end chain for a write operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) on a SQL table.

                      Trace the complete end-to-end chain for a write operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) on a SQL table. Shows: (1) which Delphi code performs that operation — a statement that writes the table (never one that only reads it, as the source of INSERT ... SELECT does), a call to a stored procedure that writes it (directly or through the procedures calling it), or a dataset write (Post, Delete) on a dataset reading it — one row per site and screen, with route, the methods running it and the line; (2) which triggers fire, (3) which tables those triggers cascade into, (4) which procedures those triggers call. The definitive tool for understanding what happens when a record is created, modified, or deleted.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      table_namestringyesSQL table name to trace.
                      operationstringyesWrite operation to trace: INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

                      docs · 6 tools · How is this done, and why?

                      expand_contextFetch parent, child, or sibling chunks of documentation chunks already retrieved via search_docs, using hierarchical…

                      Fetch parent, child, or sibling chunks of documentation chunks already retrieved via search_docs, using hierarchical chunk metadata (parent_chunk_ids, child_chunk_ids, retrieval_group_id). It returns neighbouring chunks, not the full text of the chunks given: for that, call get_adaptive_siblings with their chunk_ids. Each returned chunk’s content is a 500-character preview, flagged as in search_docs (truncated, full_length; truncated_chunk_ids and full_text_hint when any is cut). Given IDs that are not in the collection, or are not chunk IDs at all, are listed in not_found.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      chunk_idsarrayyesChunk IDs from a prior search_docs result to expand.
                      directionstring
                      get_adaptive_siblingsReturn the full stored text of documentation chunks by chunk ID.

                      Return the full stored text of documentation chunks by chunk ID. Use it whenever search_docs, expand_context or search_adjacent_docs marks a passage truncated (their content is a 500-character preview; truncated_chunk_ids lists the cut ones). Returns one passage per requested ID, in the order given: a chunk that is one part of a section split during ingestion comes back as the whole section, its parts merged in order (complete is false if a part could not be found); any other chunk comes back whole. IDs that are parts of the same section share one passage (also_covers). IDs not in the documentation collection, or not chunk IDs at all, are listed in not_found. A passage longer than max_chars (default 20,000) is cut: truncated is true and next_offset says where it goes on; call again with that chunk ID and offset = next_offset to read the rest (more_text lists them).

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      chunk_idsarrayyesChunk IDs from a prior search_docs, expand_context or search_adjacent_docs result, for example its truncated_chunk_ids. Any chunk ID works: each returns its full text, merged with its other parts when its section was split.
                      max_charsintegerMost characters returned per passage (default 20,000). A longer passage comes back cut, with truncated: true and next_offset.
                      offsetintegerWhere each passage starts, in characters (default 0). To read on in a long passage, call again with its chunk ID and offset set to its next_offset.

Each chunk’s content is a 500-character preview, flagged as in search_docs (truncated, full_length; truncated_chunk_ids and full_text_hint name get_adaptive_siblings for the full text).

                      Search nGenue documentation by embedding a query, searching Qdrant, and reranking with a CrossEncoder. Returns ranked chunks with source file, heading, and score. Each chunk’s content is a preview: its first 500 characters. truncated is true when the chunk’s text is longer than that or the chunk is one part of a section that was split into parts; full_length is the stored length. When any chunk is cut, truncated_chunk_ids and full_text_hint name them: call get_adaptive_siblings with those chunk_ids for the full text (field tables and long sections are often past the preview), and do not treat text beyond a preview as missing.                       Differences in the new-UI server

                      The new-UI server has 144 tools. These legacy tools are not in it: find_field_by_caption, get_component_context, get_layout, get_menu_path, get_source_slice, verify_caption_link. It has two tools of its own, for the new UI’s captions and controls:

                      find_control_by_captionFind a screen field or button by the words a user sees: its caption, the label beside it, a grid column’s…

                      Find a screen field or button by the words a user sees: its caption, the label beside it, a grid column’s DisplayLabel, text code puts on it, or — ranked below those — the name derived for a control that shows no caption. Returns each control with its form, where it sits, the label, and what it is bound to (data field, datasource, dataset, field). Exact matches first, then words in order, then substrings. Optionally limit to one form. Graph 2.9. Paged.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      captionstringyesWords on the screen, e.g. ‘Credit Limit’.
                      active_formstringOnly this form’s controls. Optional.
                      limitintegerRows to return (each tool has a default).
                      offsetintegerRows to skip: pass next_offset from the previous answer.
                      get_control_detailEverything about one control: what the user reads (caption, label, derived name, hint), what it shows (data field,…

                      Everything about one control: what the user reads (caption, label, derived name, hint), what it shows (data field, datasource, dataset, the TField and its display label, format and size), what its stored values mean (value_map), what enables it (ENABLED_BY: a checkbox, from code or layout), the code that changes its state (Enabled, Visible, ReadOnly … writes), its popup menu and its event handlers. Pass control_id, or active_form with control_name. Graph 2.9.

                      ArgumentTypeRequiredMeaning
                      control_idstringThe component id.
                      active_formstringThe form, with control_name.
                      control_namestringThe component’s name on that form.

                      B Packages and why each is used

                      Taken from each repository’s pyproject.toml, requirements.txt and project file. Version ranges are the declared ones.

                      The graph builders (both lines)

                      PackageVersionWhy
                      pydantic≥2.10, <2.11Every node and edge is a pydantic model: validation while building, and the JSON Schema that export-schema writes. Held to 2.10 so the generated schema can’t change between machines
                      click≥8.0The command line: delphi-kg (new UI) and delphi-kg-legacy
                      tree-sitter≥0.21, <0.22The parser runtime that compiles and loads the Pascal grammar (the 0.21 API)
                      tree-sitter-languages≥1.10Declared alongside tree-sitter; 1.10 has no wheels for Python 3.12 or later, which is why the builders require Python 3.11
                      pytest, pytest-cov≥7.0, ≥4.0 (dev)The builders’ tests and coverage
                      jsonschema≥4.0 (legacy dev)Tests that check graphs against the exported schema
                      ijsonoptionalLets compare-graphs stream two large graphs instead of loading both
                      Git, a C compilersystemFetching and compiling the Pascal grammar (the legacy builder pins its commit)

                      The MCP servers

                      PackageVersionWhyLegacyNew UI
                      fastapi≥0.115The web application: routes, middleware, the lifespan start-up hookyesyes
                      uvicorn[standard]≥0.30The ASGI server that runs FastAPI; the standard extra adds the fast event loop and HTTP parseryesyes
                      pydantic≥2.5Used through FastAPIyesyes
                      python-dotenv≥1.0Reads .env into the environment at start-upyesyes
                      PyJWT[crypto]≥2.9Checks Entra ID tokens; the crypto extra adds RS256 signature checksyesrequirements.txt only
                      httpx≥0.27Async HTTP: fetching Entra ID’s signing keys and forwarding token requestsyesrequirements.txt only
                      pyodbc≥5.0Live SQL through ODBC Driver 18yesnot declared
                      jsonschema≥4.0Checks structured answers against output schemas before sendingyesnot declared
                      qdrant-client, openai≥1.9, ≥1.30Documentation search: the vector database and Azure OpenAI embeddingsrequirements.txtrequirements.txt
                      sentence-transformers, torch, numpy≥3.0, ≥2.2, ≥1.26The cross-encoder reranker for documentation searchrequirements.txtrequirements.txt
                      pytest, pytest-asyncio≥7.4, ≥0.23The servers’ testsrequirements.txtrequirements.txt
                      sqlglot—Third check layer of the new-UI live SQL, used only if installed—optional, undeclared

                      Watch out

                      The new-UI server’s requirements.txt doesn’t list pyodbc or jsonschema, and its pyproject.toml lists only four packages. An install from either file alone gives a server whose live SQL can’t import its driver (Part 7, C7).

                      C Environment variables

                      Every setting the server code reads, found by scanning the code rather than the template, so it includes four settings that .env.example doesn’t mention (DOCS_MAX_CONCURRENT, INSTRUCTIONS, MCP_VENDOR_ROOTS, and MCP_REPO, which only the scripts use). Settings marked “legacy only” are not read by the new-UI server; all others are read by both.

                      SQL_GRAPH_PATH./graphs/database_graph.jsonRequired. The client’s SQL graph (schema 5.x)
                      DELPHIGENIE_TOOLS_PATH./toolsRequired. The folder holding the tools package

                      Watch out

                      HOST defaults to 0.0.0.0 in the code, but to 127.0.0.1 in the template. An instance whose .env lacks the line listens on every network interface, reachable without going through IIS, unless a firewall blocks its port. Set HOST=127.0.0.1 explicitly on every instance (Part 7, S9).

                      D Command-line reference

                      The builder commands are generated from the legacy builder’s cli.py (delphi-kg-legacy); the new-UI builder (delphi-kg) differences follow. Run any command with --help for the same text.

                      build

                      Build a knowledge graph from a Delphi source folder.

                      OptionDefaultMeaning
                      --sourcerepeatable requiredSource root directory. Pass multiple times to include additional source trees (e.g. --source Ntrack --source ntracklibrary when they are sibling directories rather than nested).
                      --outputgraph.jsonOutput graph JSON file. Diagnostics sidecar written alongside.
                      --notesOptional note recorded in _metadata.source.notes.
                      --skip-pasflagSkip PAS parsing (Phase 2). Use for quick DFM-only builds.
                      --scriptdom-urlScriptDOM REST service URL for SQL parsing. Defaults to lexical fallback.
                      --parallelflagUse process-pool parallelism for Phase 2 (PAS) and Phase 4 (DFM) extraction.
                      --workersNumber of parallel workers (default: cpu_count, capped at 8). Implies --parallel.
                      --incrementalflagIncremental rebuild: only re-parse files whose content changed since the last build. Manifest stored alongside the output graph. Resolvers always re-run on the full graph.
                      --shard-by-typeAfter build, shard the output into per-type JSON files in this directory.
                      --baselinePath to diagnostics_baseline.json. Diagnostics matching the baseline are suppressed from the sidecar list (still counted in summary). Create a baseline with: delphi-kg accept-baseline graph.diag.json.
                      --coverage-baselinePath to coverage_baseline.json — accepted per-type node/edge counts from a previous build. Population changes are diffed against it: a populated type falling to zero is an error, a drop beyond the threshold is a warning. The coverage report is always written to <output>.coverage.json whether or not a baseline is given. Create one with: delphi-kg accept-coverage-baseline graph.coverage.json.
                      --bundle-sourceflagWrite source.zip + source_manifest.json alongside the graph. Zip entry names are identical to the graph’s source_file values, so a reader resolves a path by opening the entry with no translation. Paths in the graph are never rewritten to point at the bundle: one graph works bundled, unbundled, or against a live checkout.
                      --no-schema-validationflagSkip checking the written graph against graph.schema.json. The check is on by default because the schema and the writer had silently drifted apart.
                      --coverage-drop-thresholdDEFAULT_DROP_THRESHOLDFractional population drop that triggers coverage_population_dropped.
                      --census-excludeDEFAULT_CENSUS_EXCLUDEComma-separated source roots excluded from the parse census gate. Third-party trees are vendored, not maintained here, so a body lost in one is not a regression this build can fix. Pass an empty string to census everything.
                      --census-fail-threshold0Method bodies allowed to be missing from the AST before the build fails. Zero is the target; raise it only to land a change with a known, recorded residue.
                      --strict-includesflagFail the build when an {$I} include file is missing (default: a warning listing the units).
                      --build-configWhich .dproj configuration’s conditional symbols to compile with, e.g. Release. Default: the .dproj’s default configuration (Debug for nGenue.dproj). Recorded in the graph’s _metadata.build_config.
                      --prettyflagWrite the graph indented, as before Batch 12. Default: one node/edge per line.
                      --compare-withAfter writing, compare the new graph with this one and print the differences.
                      --allow-unclaimedflagBuild even when a source root’s top-level units are skipped because no .dpr or .dpk sits beside them (Batch B1, audit F-B-01). Default: stop.
                      --allow-structural-fallbackflagBuild even when the tree-sitter-pascal grammar cannot be loaded: Pascal units are then not parsed (no methods). Default: stop (Batch B1, audit F-B-02).
                      --allow-sql-fallbackflagBuild even when ScriptDOM is unreachable or some of its requests fail: that SQL is parsed by the lexical parser (fewer columns). Default: stop at start-up, and an error at the end for failed requests (Batch B1, audit F-B-07).
                      --clientClient id recorded in _metadata.source.client and used to pick this client’s entry of --coverage-baseline. Default: the folder holding the --source roots, without a leading ‘nGenue ‘ (nGenue TEXICAN-RETAIL -> TEXICAN-RETAIL) (Batch L-13, audit OS4).
                      --source-revisionrepeatableRecord COMMIT as the revision of the --source root named NAME (e.g. Ntrack=01c65fb...), overriding its .git and any SNAPSHOT.json beside it. Repeatable (Batch L-13, audit T14).

                      readme-stats

                      Write the build’s numbers into README.md (Batch 19, audit item 31).

                      compare-graphs

                      Compare two graphs node by node and edge by edge (Batch 12).

                      --samples5Example ids shown per difference.
                      --reportAlso write the full comparison as JSON.

                      shard

                      Shard an existing graph.json into per-type files.

                      Arguments: GRAPH_PATH

                      OptionDefaultMeaning
                      --output-dirrequiredDirectory to write shard files into.
                      --compactflagWrite compact (no-indent) JSON for smaller files.

                      accept-baseline

                      Create or update a diagnostics baseline from a .diag.json sidecar.

                      Arguments: DIAG_PATH

                      OptionDefaultMeaning
                      --outputdiagnostics_baseline.jsonPath to write (or update) the baseline file.
                      --exclude-errorsflagExclude error-severity diagnostics from baseline (default: True).
                      --notesHuman-readable note stored in the baseline.

                      --exclude-codesComma-separated list of codes to exclude from baseline.

Options of build only in the legacy builder: --allow-sql-fallback, --allow-structural-fallback, --allow-unclaimed, --build-config, --client, --compare-with, --pretty, --source-revision, --strict-includes. Options only in the new-UI builder: none.

                      E Graph schema reference

                      Generated from the legacy builder’s models (delphi_kg/model/). delphi-kg-legacy export-schema writes the same information as JSON Schema.

                      The graph file

                      A graph file has four top-level keys: _metadata, nodes (40 collections, one per node type, such as forms, methods, sql_placeholders), edges (one collection per edge type that occurs) and snippets.

                      _metadata keyHolds
                      version, line, schema_idSchema version (for example 3.0), product line (legacy), and the schema’s identity
                      built_at, build_duration_secondsWhen the build finished, and how long it took
                      buildername, version and code_hash of the builder that wrote it
                      sourceclient, commit, roots, root_path, fingerprint, file counts per type, notes
                      build_config, conventions_profileThe options and naming conventions used
                      parser_grammarThe Pascal grammar used (and its pinned commit, in the legacy line)
                      sql_backend, sql_backend_version, sql_backend_statsScriptDOM or the lexical fallback, and how many SQL texts each handled
                      features, allowed_valuesWhat the graph contains, and every enum value it may use: the contract with the servers
                      statsnodes_total, edges_total, call_sites, call_sites_resolved

                      The other files

                      FileShape
                      database_graph.json (SQL graph, schema 5.x)Database objects as nodes (tables, columns, views, procedures, functions, triggers, indexes, constraints, types) with dependency edges; built by a separate project from the client’s database (chapter 2.9)
                      code_flows/<object>.jsonOne stored procedure, function or trigger as ordered steps, branches, variables and the tables each step reads and writes
                      data_dictionary.jsonBusiness descriptions of tables, columns and procedures
                      retail_graph.jsonThe retail and wholesale workflow: business steps, their order, and links to screens and procedures
                      source.zip + source_manifest.jsonThe source files the graph was built from; the manifest holds graph_built_at, root_anchor, file_count and per file rel, bytes, encoding and sha256

                      G Glossary

                      Terms used in this handbook, in alphabetical order.

                      Access token
                      A short-lived credential (here a JWT from Entra ID) that a client sends with each request to prove who it acts for.
                      ARR
                      Application Request Routing: the IIS extension that forwards requests to other servers, here to the local Python processes.
                      ASGI
                      The Python standard interface between async web servers (uvicorn) and web applications (FastAPI).
                      Audience (aud)
                      The token claim naming which API the token is for; the server accepts only its own.
                      Behavioural walker
                      A builder phase that follows what code does (validations, dataset operations, transactions) and records it as nodes.
                      Census
                      The builder’s count of what it saw against what it recorded, so silent losses become visible.
                      Code flow
                      A stored procedure, function or trigger described step by step, from the SQL side.
                      Connector
                      A Claude or ChatGPT setting that links the AI client to one MCP server address.
                      Contract graph
                      A small current-version graph in the server tests, used to check the builder and server agree.
                      Cross-encoder
                      A model that scores a question and a passage together; used to rerank search results.
                      Cursor
                      A token returned with a cut answer; get_more_results uses it to send the rest.
                      DFM
                      Delphi’s form file: the screen’s components and their properties, in a text format.
                      Diagnostic
                      A message the builder writes about something it couldn’t do fully, with a severity.
                      Discovery tool
                      A tool that finds something by name and returns its id for later calls.
                      Edge
                      A typed connection between two nodes, such as CALLS or HAS_SQL.
                      Embedding
                      A list of numbers representing a text’s meaning, so similar texts can be found.
                      Entra ID
                      Microsoft’s identity service (formerly Azure Active Directory).
                      Event binding
                      The link from a component’s event (such as OnClick) to the method that handles it.
                      Instance
                      One running server process for one client, with its own .env, port and graphs.
                      Instructions (playbook)
                      The text the server sends at the start of a conversation, telling the model how to use the tools.
                      isError
                      The MCP flag on a tool result meaning the tool ran but failed; the text explains why.
                      JSON-RPC
                      A simple protocol of JSON requests and responses with methods, ids and error codes; MCP is built on it.
                      JWKS
                      JSON Web Key Set: Entra ID’s published public keys, used to check token signatures.
                      Knowledge graph
                      Facts stored as typed nodes and edges, so questions become walks along connections.
                      Legacy line
                      The old Delphi VCL UI of nTrack, with its own builder (delphi-kg_old_UI) and server.
                      Lexical fallback
                      The builder’s simpler SQL reader, used when ScriptDOM isn’t available.
                      Managed identity
                      An Azure identity for a machine or service, used to reach other Azure services without stored secrets.
                      Manifest (tool)
                      tool_manifest.txt: the tools that must load, or start-up stops.
                      MCP
                      Model Context Protocol: the open standard by which AI clients discover and call tools on servers.
                      New-UI line
                      The newer nTrack UI, with its own builder (delphi-kg) and server.
                      Node
                      One thing in the graph, such as a form, method, component or SQL statement.
                      NSSM
                      The Non-Sucking Service Manager: runs ordinary programs as Windows services.
                      OAuth proxy
                      The server’s two endpoints that adjust sign-in requests for Entra ID (chapter 4.3).
                      Output schema
                      A JSON Schema describing a tool’s structured answer, checked before sending.
                      PKCE
                      Proof Key for Code Exchange: protects the OAuth code from being used by anyone else.
                      Provenance
                      Where a node came from: file, line, and how it was found.
                      Qdrant
                      The vector database holding documentation embeddings.
                      Recursive descent
                      A parsing method where each grammar rule is a function that calls the others.
                      Refresh token
                      A long-lived credential used to get new access tokens without signing in again.
                      Registry
                      The part of the server that discovers, checks and runs tools.
                      Reranking
                      Re-scoring search results with a stronger model and keeping the best.
                      Resource server
                      In OAuth, the API that checks tokens; here the MCP server.
                      ScriptDOM
                      Microsoft’s T-SQL parser library, run as a small service for the builders.
                      Source bundle
                      source.zip: the exact source a graph was built from, for get_source_slice.
                      SQL placeholder
                      A node for one SQL statement found in Delphi code or a form, with its tables and columns.
                      State (STATE UPDATES)
                      Ids the model passes between calls, such as active_form; returned in each answer’s trailer.
                      Stateless
                      Keeping nothing between requests; each request carries what it needs.
                      structuredContent
                      An MCP tool result’s machine-readable copy, beside the text.
                      tree-sitter
                      A parser generator and library; the builders use its Pascal grammar.
                      TTL
                      Time to live: how long a client may cache an answer, such as the tool list.
                      Unit
                      A Delphi source file (.pas), with interface and implementation sections.
                      uvicorn
                      The ASGI server that runs the FastAPI application.
                      Vendor code
                      Third-party source (such as DevExpress) kept apart from nTrack’s own code.
                      Visited set
                      The record of nodes already seen during a walk, so loops end.
